Irvin S. Cobb explains how his essay jelled at last in a small seacoast hotel, where, laid up sick over a Sunday, he ran out of newspapers and magazines. In despair he took an old Fifth Reader to bed and read it through. The night's reading stirred his defense of the cheap story papers of his boyhood.

His plea speaks for Old Cap Collier, hero of the dime novels that boys once hid and devoured. Cobb argues that those crude tales of detectives and Indians fed real hunger for story and did less harm than their critics claimed. The essay is funny, fond, and shrewd about how reading tastes form.
a-texas-ranger:
William MacLeod Raine's A Texas Ranger, dated 1910, begins with a foreword to ye gentle reader. The frontier, Raine writes, has passed from rollicking boyhood to responsible majority within living memory. The ranger who patrolled for bad men has yielded to the forest ranger. Tucson, where he writes, is now more civilized than New York.

Part one, The Man from the Panhandle, opens on a desert meeting. A girl crouched in the bear-grass covers a passing driver with her revolver. Steve, the ranger hero, plays second fiddle, by the part's own subtitle, to the lady's distress. Raine builds a border melodrama of rustlers, disguises, and a ranger's divided duty. His West is already nostalgic in 1910. The saga of the strong, as his quoted poem calls it, sings over country the plough has taken.
a-v-laider:
Max Beerbohm tells a quiet, teasing short story about a narrator resting at a small seaside hotel after illness. Rain falls, time hangs heavy, and the narrator falls into talk with A. V. Laider, a fellow guest who writes books nobody seems to know. Laider shares a strange tale about a palm reading and a fate he believes was foretold for him.

Beerbohm lets the talk unfold slowly, with dry humor and polite doubt on both sides. The joke turns on vanity, fate, and how gladly a man believes a story that makes him seem marked by destiny. Readers prize the story for its gentle wit and its neat, ironic close.
a-woman-hater:
Charles Reade opens at the Golden Star hotel in Homburg, a humble house used by modest travelers, not gay gamblers. At two o'clock on a June day, two strangers sit far apart in the dining room. One is a lady of twenty-four with a high white forehead and gray eyes, looking comely and sedate — and not, the narrator warns, the remarkable person she really is.

The other stranger is a sworn woman-hater, and Reade sets these two against each other for thirty-two chapters of argument, adventure, and reluctant feeling. The heroine argues women's cause with her life as much as her tongue. Reade writes with his usual research, energy, and courtroom love of a good cross-examination.
a-yankee-girl-at-fort-sumter:
A Yankee Girl at Fort Sumter, by Alice Turner Curtis, tells a Civil War story for young readers through a Boston child in Charleston. Curtis sets Sylvia Fulton in the South Carolina city with her parents just before the war opens. The introduction promises her perilous adventure in Charleston Harbor and her warm welcome from new southern friends, whose kindness to a northern girl carries much of the book's point.

Philadelphia printed the volume in 1920, with illustrations by Isabel W Caley, as part of Curtis's historical writing for girls. Early chapters bring a new friend, trouble, and an unexpected journey. Later ones take Sylvia to a plantation with Estralla and Elinor, where ways of life she has never seen raise questions the story treats gently. Loyalty to home and fairness to strangers are held up together as the guns approach.
allan-and-the-holy-flower:
H. Rider Haggard's Allan and the Holy Flower, first published in 1915, begins with Allan Quatermain disclaiming any link to orchids. Yet an orchid hunt of remarkable character, he writes, should not be lost. His companion beyond the Limpopo is Charles Scroope, an English sportsman. Scroope fled to Africa after quarrelling with his fiancée over four dances at a hunt ball.

Brother John, a white-bearded missionary figure of the wilds, leads the party inland. Their goal is a gigantic orchid, the holy flower worshipped by the Ponda people. A slave-raiding stronghold, a great ape, and a tribal war guard the treasure. Haggard mixes botany with his usual African adventure. Quatermain narrates in dry hindsight, older and sadder than in King Solomon's Mines. The flower itself, when found, justifies the madness of the quest.
amy-foster:
Joseph Conrad's story Amy Foster is told by Kennedy, a country doctor in the village of Colebrook on the Kent coast. Kennedy's practice runs from the sea-wall towns inland to Darnford, and his cases bring him the parish's secrets. Among them is the history of Amy Foster, a dull, kind servant girl, and of the stranger the sea delivered to her world.

That stranger is Yanko Goorall, a peasant from Eastern Europe and the sole survivor of a wrecked emigrant ship. He learns no English that the village trusts, marries Amy, and has a child with her. When fever takes him, the gap of language and fear between husband and wife turns fatal. Conrad turns a coast village's suspicion of one foreign man into a study of loneliness.
an-adventure-with-a-genius-recollections:
An Adventure with a Genius records Alleyne Ireland and his recollections of Joseph Pulitzer, the great newspaper publisher. Ireland frames the book in a preface about a life spent meeting remarkable men in a score of countries, from kings and viceroys to judges and ward politicians. His first outstanding adventure, he says, was with a stern and formidable man, and the dedication honors Mrs Joseph Pulitzer.

Inside, the chapters follow Ireland's work beside Pulitzer at close range. The publisher appears through daily demands, sharp judgments, and the running of a newspaper empire built on crusades and circulation wars. Ireland writes as a witness rather than a critic, setting down habits, sayings, and scenes from inside the office and the household. Readers curious about how a press lord actually worked, hour by hour, get a portrait drawn by a man who stood in the room.
book-of-mormon-1852-front-matter:
Front matter from the 1852 Liverpool edition of the Book of Mormon fills this entry. Publishers Jas. O. Wright and Co. framed Joseph Smith's scripture for British readers. Only the introduction and synopsis appear here, not the full text.

The publisher explains the book's origin and story in brief. A synopsis walks through its peoples, prophets, and wars. Such framing shows how a new faith packaged its core text for converts abroad. The piece is a small historical artifact. It suits students of Mormon history who study how the movement spread in its first decades.
bound-to-rise-or-up-the-ladder:
Bound to Rise, or Up the Ladder, by Horatio Alger Jr, opens with a life of its author. Alger was a minister turned writer. He settled in New York to work among street boys. The sketch counts more than seventy Alger stories. It also counts over a million copies sold in his lifetime. That frame tells readers what kind of book they hold.

Harry Walton, a poor country boy, carries the story. His family needs his wages. His motto comes from Hiram, the hired man of Chapter III. A calamity opens the tale. An arithmetic sum matters more than sums usually do. The ladder of the subtitle then rises rung by rung. Employers, temptations, and small sums saved mark the climb. Alger's promise sits in the title. Rise is possible, and boys earn it in public, one honest decision at a time.
brother-and-sister:
Josephine Lawrence's Brother and Sister opens the Morrison family at breakfast on a rainy morning. Brother will not drink his milk because rain stops outdoor growing. His brother Ralph promises a birthday present next week, if Brother is tall enough by Wednesday. Louise, the older sister, calls him silly.

Twenty-two short chapters follow Brother and Sister through party preparations and presents. Dick's buttons, a haunted house, and a very sick doll supply the adventures. Mickey Gaffney, a poorer neighbour boy, needs plans and finally owns up. Lawrence wrote the first of her Brother and Sister series for young children. The episodes are gentle, funny, and exact about family life: spilled treats, small jealousies, and making up. Grandma Hastings and Miss Putnam keep the grown-up world kindly in view.
bucky-o-connor-a-tale-of-the-unfenced-bo:
William MacLeod Raine dedicates Bucky O'Connor to his brother Edgar. The Denver letter is dated March 1910. It offers the tale of the unfenced border as a companion for a long northern winter. Sheriff Bucky O'Connor of Arizona enters with Bear-Trap Collins in chapter one. Taxation without representation and a called bluff follow in the contents.

Bucky crosses into revolutionary Mexico and survives the hold-up of the M C P flyer. He pursues a kidnapped girl and stolen money, through stone walls that do not a prison make. He climbs stairs three at a time to meet brown eyes after the night's hazards. Raine, a Colorado schoolteacher turned Westerner, writes clean action with a romantic shine.
business-correspondence-vol-1-how-to-wri:
An anonymous manual, Business Correspondence, Volume One: How to Write the Business Letter, teaches the art of selling and persuading by post. Its twenty-four chapters draw proved principles and practical schemes from extracts of 217 actual letters.

Early chapters prepare the writer: what a postage stamp can do, the advantages of doing business by letter, and gathering talking points. Later parts show how to open a letter, present a proposition convincingly, close effectively, and acquire a forceful, original style. The volume adapts selling appeal to different prospects and aims at orders by letter. Modern readers will find it a vivid record of early twentieth-century salesmanship.
cabin-fever:
B M Bower named Cabin Fever for the malady her first chapter diagnoses: the restlessness that snow, isolation, and a failing marriage breed in a northern cabin. Bud, a young rancher, quarrels with his wife Marie and heads south with ten dollars and a job. The contents promise deserts, barren months, and cabin fever in its worst form.

Bud partners with the older Cash, whose sourdough loaves and silence steady the partnership through mining disappointments. A child, Lovin Child, enters the tangle, and Marie takes a desperate chance of her own. Bower resolves the fever with facts faced and a cure complete. Her Westerns ground romance in work, weather, and money, and this one adds a rare honest look at marriage.
cap-n-dan-s-daughter:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Cap'n Dan's Daughter is a Cape Cod story set in the village of Trumet Centre, where the Metropolitan Dry Goods and Variety Store opens for business with no customers at all. August should bring city visitors hunting white duck hats, oilskin coats, post cards and chocolates, but the shop stands quiet.

Lincoln peoples his village with shopkeepers, sailors and summer folk, telling their doings in the dry, affectionate dialect humour that made his Cape Cod books famous. The daughter of the title, Cap'n Dan's own girl, stands at the centre of the village's hopes and gossip. Readers who enjoy gentle American local-colour fiction, with salt air and small-town comedy, will feel at home in Trumet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-deer:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Deer describes a once-famous Scottish monastery on the Ugie in Buchan. Celtic legend tells how St. Columcille, with his disciple Drostan, founded a missionary centre there on lands given by the local chief, whose son Columcille's prayers had healed.

Columcille soon moved on, leaving Drostan as abbot until his death about 606, and Aberdour's veneration of Drostan supports the legend. In 1219 the Earl of Buchan founded the Cistercian abbey of New Deer two miles west, granting it part of Old Deer's lands. Later a titular abbot held the lands in commendam, and the flourishing monastery fell prey to the troubles of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dorc:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dorchester describes an abbey founded in 1140 by Alexander of Lincoln for Augustinian canons, or Black Canons. Dorchester, a Roman city of Mercia nine miles from Oxford, had held a bishopric from 634, when St. Birinus arrived, until the see moved to Lincoln in 1085.

The abbey, dedicated to Peter, Paul and Birinus, drew rich gifts from the old bishopric's lands and tithes, with twelve parishes subject to it. Its first abbot appears to have been Alured, and its last, John Mershe, elected in 1533, subscribed to the king's supremacy and took a pension of twenty-two pounds a year. Henry the Eighth kept much of the property for a college of his own founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abner:
Abner, son of Ner and cousin of Saul, served as commander-in-chief of Saul's army. After Saul and three of his sons fell at Mount Gelboe, Abner made Isboseth, Saul's fourth son, king over all Israel except Judea, which held to David. For seven and a half years he fought for Isboseth's throne, and near Gabaon he reluctantly slew Asael, brother of Joab, who pursued him hotly.

That killing embittered Joab, who counted himself his brother's avenger. When Isboseth rebuked Abner for marrying Respha, a concubine of Saul, Abner angrily opened talks with David, restored Saul's daughter Michol to him as demanded, and reached a full understanding. Joab then called him back and killed him at the city gate, and David mourned him and charged Solomon to avenge the murder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert-stif:
Adalbert Stifter was a poet and pedagogue born at Oberplan in Bohemia on 23 October 1805. He died at Linz on 28 October 1868; his father had been a linen weaver and flax dealer. The boy's first stimulus came from his mother and grandmother, tellers of fairy tales, stories, and legends. School proved him apt, with talent for music and drawing. After his father's sudden death in 1817, his grandfather placed him at the Benedictine school at Kremsmunster.

In 1827 Stifter went to Vienna University, moving from philosophy and law toward mathematics and natural science. He supported himself by private lessons among leading families, gaining a wide circle including Metternich's family. He wished to teach natural science and passed the written examination with honour in 1830, though not the oral one. At thirty-two, still a teaching candidate, he married, and his later writing and school work made him a noted Austrian author.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-heinrich:
Adam Heinrich Muller was a publicist and political economist, and a convert, born at Berlin on 30 June 1779. He died at Vienna on 17 January 1829. Meant for Protestant theology, he gave himself from 1798 at Gottingen to law, philosophy, and natural science. Back in Berlin, his friend Gentz persuaded him to take up political science. After serving in the Kurmark chamber and travelling in Sweden, Denmark, and Poland, he went to Vienna.

There he entered the Catholic faith on 30 April 1805, then lived at Dresden from 1806 to 1809, tutoring a Saxe-Weimar prince and lecturing on literature, drama, and political science. In 1808 he edited the periodical Phoebus with Heinrich von Kleist. In 1813 he became imperial commissioner and major of the Tyrol rifle corps in the wars of liberty, then a government counsellor reorganizing the country.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-tanner:
Adam Tanner was a controversialist born at Innsbruck in 1571 who died at Unken on 25 May 1632; he joined the Jesuits in 1589, teaching first Hebrew, apologetics, and moral theology. When a Catholic-Lutheran debate was arranged at Ratisbon in 1601, Tanner aided his fellow Jesuit Gretser. Together they argued the Bible's dead word could not be faith's supreme arbiter, and Tanner published an account of the proceedings in 1602.

In 1603 Bavaria's duke called him to Ingolstadt's scholastic theology chair. There he exposed the fallacies of the Augsburg Confession in his work of 1613. He defended Communion under one species and the sacrifice of the Mass against the Utraquists. He also vindicated church freedom against Venice in 1607. After fifteen years at Ingolstadt he moved to Vienna, published his great Universa theologia scholastica, and became Prague's chancellor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelaide-anne:
Adelaide Anne Procter was a poetess and philanthropist born in London on 30 October 1825. She died there on 2 February 1864. Eldest daughter of Bryan Waller Procter, the poet Barry Cornwall, and Anne Benson Skepper, she showed precocious intelligence as a child. She gained French, German, and Italian, as well as music and drawing, and she read widely. Brought up amid literary leanings, she began writing verses early, contributing to the Book of Beauty at eighteen.

In 1851 she and two sisters became Catholics without disturbing the domestic circle's harmony. In 1853, under the pseudonym Mary Berwick, she sent a short poem to Household Words. It so pleased Charles Dickens that he accepted it and invited more. Only late the next year did Dickens learn his unknown correspondent was Barry Cornwall's daughter. Her poems and charitable work made her a beloved Victorian voice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adele-bayer:
Adele Bayer, nee Parmentier, was the eldest daughter of Andrew Parmentier. She was born in Belgium on 4 July 1814 and died in Brooklyn, New York, on 22 January 1892. Her father, a horticulturist and civil engineer born at Enghien in 1780, reached New York in 1824 en route to the West Indies. Persuaded to stay, he bought land near Brooklyn for a horticultural park.

His park soon became famous, and his skill was sought far and wide. He shaped American landscape gardening more than any other practitioner of his day. He introduced the black beech tree and several shrubs, vegetables, and vines, and helped found St. James's, Brooklyn diocese's first Catholic church. After his death in 1830, his daughter Adele and her mother carried on. During the Civil War Madame Bayer took up caring for sailors at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, a task she pursued for thirty years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolf-pfister:
Adolf Pfister was an educationist born at Hechingen in Hohenzollern on 26 September 1810, who died at Ober-Dischingen in Wurtemberg on 29 April 1878. He was educated at Hechingen's Latin school, the Lyceum of Rastatt, and Sasbach, then studied theology at Strasburg's Grand Seminary. Ordained priest on 25 May 1833 at Freiburg, he served as curate at Sasbach and assistant at Freiburg Cathedral.

From 1835 to 1838 he was curate at Steinhofen, then pastor at Dotternhausen, Rosawangen from 1839, and Risstissen from 1841, also serving as school inspector at Ehingen from 1851. In 1857 he founded the Rottenburger Kirchenblatt, and from 1860 he edited Catholic school weeklies. His most valuable work was editing with Rolfus the Real-Encyclopadie of education on Catholic principles, four volumes from 1863 to 1866, with a second edition to 1874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocates-of-:
Advocates of St. Peter are a body of jurists chartered by Leo XIII's brief of 5 July 1878. As the name indicates, their main object is defending the Holy See's rights and privileges, in both the spiritual and temporal order. Members bind themselves to refute calumnies against the church, whether from distortions of history, jurisprudence, or dogma.

Above all they devote their legal knowledge to defending church rights before civil tribunals. The society formed in 1877, on the Golden Episcopal Jubilee of Pius IX, with Count Cajetan Agnelli dei Malherbi of Rome as first president. Pius IX warmly approved the undertaking and desired its wide extension, since church immunities need defence everywhere and under every government. Branches spread rapidly across the Catholic world, with colleges in Italy and England, Austria and France, Spain and Germany, Canada, and South America, each affiliated to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aer:
Aer, Greek aer, the air, is the Greek church's largest, outermost chalice-and-paten covering. It matches the Latin rite's veil, slightly larger than that veil and is embroidered in the style and colour of the priest's vestments. Its name comes either from its former light material or from the priest holding it high in the air during the Nicene Creed.

During the Creed the priest waves it slowly toward the chalice. Its use, like the veil's, was first to cover the chalice and keep anything from falling in before consecration. It is first named in a sixth-century explanation of the liturgy and as the so-called aer in Constantinople's council acts. In the Greek church the veil rests on the deacon's shoulders at the great entrance, a rite kept in Greek Catholic practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alabaster:
Alabaster, from Greek alabastros and Latin alabaster, of uncertain origin, is commonly fine-grained gypsum, calcium sulphate, much used for vase and ornament making. Oriental alabaster, the alabastrites of old writers, is a translucent marble formed from dripstone deposits. Because its banded structure is like onyx, it also goes by onyx marble, or simply, though wrongly, onyx.

From remote times it won high esteem for decoration. Among the ancients Oriental alabaster often held unguents in vases, believed to preserve them. Hence alabasters named the vases even when made of other materials. The sinful woman's alabastrum unguenti, anointing the Saviour, in Matthew, Mark, and Luke, was such a one. The vase, though probably of alabaster, need not have been of that material, as the English alabaster box of ointments seems to imply.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-chartie:
Alain Chartier, French poet of Bayeux, was born about 1390, who died between 1430 and 1440. He is believed to have studied at Paris, as did his brother Guillaume, later Bishop of Paris. In life he counted an eminent writer, and a century later men of letters still called him a noble poet and the father of French eloquence.

He is best known by the story of Margaret of Scotland, said to have kissed his sleeping lips to honour the mouth that spoke so many virtuous words. The story is only legend: Margaret came to France only in 1436, when Chartier was already dead by the best authorities. His love poems include Le debat de reveille-matin and Belle dame sans merci. Praised then, they seem to modern readers lifeless and pedantic. His Breviaire des Nobles codes the perfect knight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alban-butler:
Alban Butler was an English Catholic historian born at Appletree in Northamptonshire in 1710, who died at St-Omer in France in 1773. Schooled first at Dame Alice's School in Lancashire and then at the English College at Douai, he was ordained a priest in 1735. He ranked with Bishop Challoner as a leading Catholic scholar of England. The first half of the eighteenth century was a bleak time for English Catholics.

Butler gave nearly thirty years to his great work, Lives of the Fathers, Martyrs and Other Principal Saints, published between 1756 and 1759 and reprinted many times since. He finished it during his years at St-Omer, where he became president of the English College in 1766. He had earlier travelled with the Earl of Shrewsbury and his brothers in 1745. His other writings include letters on Bower's Lives of the Popes and a life of Mary of the Holy Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albrecht-dure:
Albrecht Dürer was a celebrated German painter and engraver, born at Nuremberg in May 1471 and dead there in April 1528. He left his native city only three times. After his apprenticeships to his goldsmith father and to the painter Wohlgemut, he travelled through Germany. In 1505 to 1507 he spent time in Venice, and he travelled again in 1520 to 1521. Nuremberg itself was then famous for commerce, learning, and art.

The entry divides his work into three periods. Before 1505, he set up his own studio in 1494 after early portraits, Madonnas, and landscape sketches. From 1505 to 1520, his Festival of the Rosary, painted in Venice for German merchants, rivalled the Italian colourists. From 1520 to 1528, his diligence shows in newly found sketches for St. Jerome with the Skull. Dürer emerges as a master of both painting and engraving, rooted in Nuremberg's commerce, learning, and art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-bau:
Alexander Baumgartner was a Swiss poet and writer on the history of literature, born at St. Gall in June 1841 and dead at Luxemburg in September 1910. His father Gallus Jakob Baumgartner was a noted statesman. At the abbey school of Maria Einsiedeln, where he began higher studies at fourteen, the poet and scholar Father Gall Morel shaped the boy's mind. His bent was confirmed at the Jesuit school at Feldkirch.

Baumgartner joined the editorial staff of Stimmen aus Maria-Laach and wrote for it for thirty-six years, scarcely a number appearing without something from him. His fame rests on his writings on literary history, including studies of Lessing, Longfellow, and Joost van den Vondel, gathered toward his larger History of World Literature. He also travelled widely, visiting Iceland, Scandinavia, and St. Petersburg in 1883 and Denmark, Sweden, and Norway three years later, trips recalled in his Northern Journeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alma-redempto:
Alma Redemptoris Mater, Kindly Mother of the Redeemer, opens one of four antiphons sung at Compline and Lauds honouring the Virgin through the seasons. This antiphon is assigned to the part of the year between first Vespers of the first Sunday in Advent and Compline of 2 February. It ceases then even if the Feast of the Purification is transferred. Six hexameter verses in strict prosodial form make it up, followed by versicle, response, and a seasonal prayer.

Hermannus Contractus, or Hermann the Cripple, who died in 1054, gets the credit for the hexameter verses. The antiphon must have been popular in England both before and after Chaucer's Prioress's Tale. The tale rests wholly on a legend about its recitation by the little clerk. Professor Skeat first thought the Alma Redemptoris in Chaucer was the sequence, but corrected the error in Modern Philology in April 1906.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloisius-edou:
Aloisius Edouard Camille Gaultier was a priest and schoolmaster, born at Asti about 1745 to French parents, dead at Paris in 1818. He studied first in France, then in Rome, where he was ordained. Returning to France in 1780, he devoted himself to education. In 1786 he opened a Paris school instructing children while amusing them. The Revolution drove him to England, where former pupils of the French nobility joined his London course for refugees.

Oxford and Cambridge admired his principles and commended his methods. He returned to France in 1801, teaching and publishing. A later London journey studied Bell and Lancaster's monitorial system for French schools. During the Hundred Days, Carnot named him to the public instruction commission. Later he helped found the Society for Elementary Instruction. His textbooks cover every branch of primary instruction, applying his instructive plays. The plays are questions and answers, with credits gained and lost stimulating interest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloys-karl-oh:
Aloys Karl Ohler was an educationist, born at Mainz in 1817 and dead there in 1889. He attended Mainz gymnasium, read theology at Giessen, then took orders at Mainz in 1839. First chaplain at Seligenstadt, he helped Moufang found and teach at the Progymnasium. He directed Mainz's St. Rochus Hospital in 1845, pastored at Abenheim near Worms in 1847. In June 1852 he became director of Bensheim's Hessian Catholic teachers' training college.

For fifteen years there, encouraged by Bishop von Ketteler, Ohler laboured for a better spirit in Hesse's teaching body. In April 1867 he became a Mainz cathedral canon, took charge of education, and lectured in pedagogy and catechetics at the seminary. He held the post until the seminary closed during the Kulturkampf in 1878. His chief work, Textbook of Education and Instruction (Mainz, 1861; tenth edition 1884), holds that Catholic youth should be educated on Catholic principles, Church and school cooperating. It was meant for clergy and teachers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloys-senefel:
Aloys Senefelder, inventor of lithography, was born at Prague in 1771, died at Munich in 1834. His father, a Munich Royal Theatre actor, played at Prague at his birth. Young Senefelder studied at Munich on a 120-florin diligence scholarship, then jurisprudence at Ingolstadt. His father's death in 1791 forced him to quit his studies, supporting his mother and eight siblings.

His experiments led to chemical printing. The design is marked on stone with greasy soap, wax, and lampblack, then washed with water soaking the unmarked parts. Printing ink adheres only to marked places, water protecting the rest, yielding many impressions, with no etching needed, since grease and water do not mix. His improvements won English, Bavarian Polytechnic, and Bavarian Crown medals. Despite financial difficulties, he stayed devoted to high ideals, hoping his invention would benefit mankind, never misused. His Complete Textbook of Lithography (Munich and Vienna, 1818) was translated into French, English, and Italian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alphons-huber:
Alphons Huber was an historian, born in October 1834 at Fügen in the Zillerthal, Tyrol, dead in November 1898 at Vienna. After humanities at Hall and Innsbruck, he studied history under Ficker at Vienna University. Very young, Annegarn's history interested him deeply. In 1859 he became Innsbruck history lecturer, professor in 1863, Academy of Sciences Corresponding Member in 1867, and full member in 1872. In 1887 he became Vienna University professor, succeeding Ottokar Lorenz.

Under Ficker he learned critical accuracy, purity of style, and strictly impartial investigation, and diplomatics, the study of documents. His training showed in his writing and life: sober, opposed to claptrap, liberal in politics, but deeply religious. His earliest writings, on the Austrian Freiheitsbriefe and the forest cantons Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, deal with territorial history. For Austria and Tyrol's union anniversary in 1864 he wrote its history, with a sequel on Duke Rudolf IV in 1865.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosiaster:
Ambrosiaster names the unknown author of a commentary on all St. Paul's Epistles except Hebrews, usually printed among St. Ambrose's works. Each epistle opens with a short prologue on purpose and context, the text given by sections with a natural, logical explanation for each portion. Modern scholars call it excellent, some the best of its kind before the sixteenth century. The commentary's section-by-section method keeps Paul's argument clear for readers following epistle by epistle.

Published in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume seventeen, columns 45 to 508, it stands as a patristic landmark. The name itself marks the work's long misattribution to Ambrose, corrected by modern study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
Chester held a bishop and a cathedral only at intervals before the Reformation. The title Bishop of Chester appears even before the Norman Conquest, for prelates better called bishops of Mercia or Lichfield. After the Council of London in 1075 ordered sees moved into cities, Peter, Bishop of Lichfield, moved his seat to Chester. He took Saint John the Baptist as his cathedral.

His successor moved the see to Coventry for its rich monastery, keeping the palace at Chester. Saint John's still ranked as a cathedral, with its own dean and chapter of secular canons, down to the Reformation. The chief foundation in the city was its Benedictine monastery. Henry VIII created the see anew in 1541, but Rome recognized it only during Queen Mary's reign. One later bishop was sent to the Tower, escaped to the Continent, and died at Louvain in 1564.

Worcester was created in 680, when the Synod of Hatfield under Archbishop Theodore split the great Mercian diocese into five sees. Tatfrith, a monk of Whitby, was named bishop but died before consecration, and Bosel, a fellow monk, was consecrated in his place. The diocese then ran a singularly uneventful course, fortunate above all in never staying vacant long, with an unbroken line of bishops from 680 to 1565.

Mercian kings lavished gifts on the cathedral church, first dedicated to Saint Peter and later to Our Lady. Secular canons served it until Saint Oswald replaced them with Benedictines in the tenth century and rebuilt the church, finishing in 983. Danes burned city and cathedral in 1041, and Saint Wulstan rebuilt it between 1084 and 1089. Fires struck again in 1113, 1180, and 1202. King John was buried there in 1216, between the shrines of Oswald and Wulstan, and the restored cathedral was consecrated two years later before king, prelates, and nobles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Stavanger, in Norway, covered Stavanger, Lister and Mandal, and Nedenes. It was formed early in the twelfth century from southern Bergen, which had till then held all western Norway. Reginald, an Englishman, was its first bishop. With money King Sigurd Jorsalefarer gave him in 1128, for allowing the king to marry Cecilia during Malmfrid's lifetime, Reginald began the cathedral and founded the chapter.

Harald Gille had Reginald hanged at Bergen in 1135. He had refused to impoverish his see by paying fifteen marks of gold to a king who suspected him of hiding royal treasures. His successor John Birgersson moved to Trondhjem in 1152, as did Eric Ivarsson in 1188. Bishop Arne, from 1276 to 1303, quarrelled with his chapter from 1294 to 1303. King Haakon decided for the chapter and gave it a voice in nominations to and removals from benefices. Bishop Gutterm Paalsson, from 1343 to 1350, died of the Black Death.

Winchester's diocese dates to 635, when Dorchester, the missionary diocese Saint Birinus had founded in 634 for Wessex, was divided into Sherborne and Winchester. One bishop ruled both sees until 676, when they separated. Winchester then held Hampshire, Surrey, and Sussex; Sussex later formed Chichester, and the Isle of Wight joined Winchester.

King Cynegils had founded and endowed in 634 the church that became the new cathedral, and his son Coenwealh added more lands. As Wessex grew supreme, the see's importance grew greatly. After Canterbury and York, it stood first among English bishoprics until the Reformation, a rank the Anglican see still keeps. Saint Swithin, its seventeenth bishop, brought fresh honour through his episcopate and canonization: once his relics were enshrined, the cathedral's dedication changed from Saint Amphibalus to Saint Swithin. Its site had held a Roman-era building Saxons turned into a pagan temple, before Cynegils raised a new cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-dacier:
Andre Dacier, a philologist, was born at Castres on 6 April 1651 and died on 18 September 1722. A Huguenot, he studied under Tanneguy Lefevre at Saumur. In Paris the Duc de Montausier engaged him to edit Pomponius Festus for the Ad usum Delphini authors, published in 1681 and 1699. In 1683 he married his teacher's daughter Anne Lefevre. Two years later both abjured Protestantism.

He published a Horace translation with commentary from 1681 to 1689, on Lefevre's Saumur text. The translation is accurate for its period. The commentary runs diffuse and shows the allegorical taste of the seventeenth century. Dacier held that Horace knew everything, even finding Moses and Solomon behind his lines, though his pages also hold judicious remarks. Mainly a translator, he rendered Marcus Antoninus, Aristotle, Sophocles, Plutarch, Hippocrates, Plato, Pythagoras, and Epictetus. He kept the king's books and entered both academies in 1695, serving the French Academy as secretary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-de-boul:
Andre de Boulanger, called Petit-Pere Andre, was a monk and preacher, born at Paris in 1578 and dead on 27 September 1657. His father presided over the Parlement of Paris. He entered the Augustinian order and preached for over half a century in France's pulpits. He used the jesting burlesque of Menot and Maillard freely, despite its bad taste. This jesting kept his name alive.

Boulanger likened the Doctors of the Latin Church to card-suit kings. Augustine stood for the King of Hearts, for large-heartedness. Ambrose stood for the King of Clubs, for flowery eloquence. Jerome stood for the King of Spades, for his biting style. Gregory the Great stood for the King of Diamonds. Anne of Austria and the Prince of Conde enjoyed his sermons. Provincial of his order several times, he left one work in print: an oration for Marie de Lorraine, abbess of Chelles, judged mediocre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-bened:
Andreas Benedict Feilmoser, theologian and Biblical scholar, was born at Hopfgarten in Tyrol in 1777 and died at Tubingen in 1831. He studied at Salzburg from 1789 to 1794 and philosophy at Innsbruck, entering the Benedictine order at Fiecht in 1796. There he studied Oriental languages under Dom Georg Maurer. At Villingen he heard Maurer and Dom Gottfried Lumper, both eminent scholars.

Back at Fiecht, he taught exegesis, was ordained in 1801, and became professor of ethics in 1802 and of church history in 1803. Theses of 1803 drew Brixen's suspicion, and the abbot was rebuked for letting him teach doctrine. His Animadversiones of 1804 brought threats against the abbot unless he dropped opinions. Hofer's men carried him prisoner to Pusterthal in the rising of 1809. He regained New Testament exegesis in 1817 despite opposition. His introduction of 1830 was judged inaccurate, and his rationalist exegesis denied the Comma Johanneum and treated Job, Jonah, Tobias, and Judith as didactic poems.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-hofer:
Andreas Hofer, patriot and soldier, was born in the Passeyr valley of Tyrol in 1767 and executed at Mantua in 1810. His father, the Sandwirth, kept the family inn on a sandy spit of the Passeyr for over a hundred years. Hofer's schooling was very limited. As a youth he traded in wine and horses, travelled widely, and learned Italian, which later served him well.

At first no leader, he won fame capturing a Bavarian detachment in the marsh at Sterzing. At the second battle of Berg Isel he rallied weakening ranks while Haspinger decided the day. With the intendant fled, Hofer ruled from the Hofburg in patriarchal style. A golden medal from Francis II fed his belief that the emperor would never abandon the Tyrolese. He dismissed Archduke John's letter as enemy propaganda and lost the third battle of Berg Isel on 1 November to a superior force.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-koble:
Andreas Kobler, historian, was born at Muhldorf in Bavaria in 1816 and died at Klagenfurt in 1892. He studied at Landshut, theology at Munich, where Mohler and Gorres awakened his love of history. Ordained in 1840, he served four years as a mission curate, then entered the Jesuit novitiate at Graz. The disturbances of 1848 sent him to America, where he spent five years with New York mission teaching mathematics.

Back in Europe, he taught at Presburg until 1857, then became professor of church history at Innsbruck. He held that chair for fourteen years and served as rector from 1861 to 1866. In 1871 he taught mathematics at Linz and served two years as rector. At Innsbruck, he gave nine years to literary work. In 1887 he became superior of the Klagenfurt seminary, vigorous in the pulpit at his death. His books are historical: a Jesuit in Paraguay, the suppression of the Society, and English confessors from 1550 to 1681.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anger:
Anger means the desire for vengeance. How it rates ethically depends on the justice of the vengeance and the strength of the passion. When both match the prescriptions of balanced reason, anger counts as no sin. Rather, it is praiseworthy, justifiable with proper zeal.

Vengeance becomes sinful when sought against one who has not deserved it, beyond what was deserved, against the law's dispositions, or from a bad motive. Then the sin is generally mortal, opposed to justice and charity. It can still be venial when the punishment aimed at is trifling, or when full deliberation is lacking. Anger is likewise sinful when the passion itself is unduly vehement, inwardly or outwardly. Ordinarily that counts as venial, unless the excess seriously counters love of God and neighbour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anne-dacier:
Anne Dacier, née Lefèvre and wife of André Dacier, was born in 1651 and died in 1720. At twenty-three she published Callimachus fragments, having received her brother's instruction. She translated Anacreon and Sappho (1681), Plautus and Aristophanes (1683-1684), Terence (1688), the Iliad (1699), and the Odyssey (1708). She edited Florus in 1674, Dictys and Dares in 1684, and Aurelius Victor in 1681. In shared work, she is the father, with a vigour her husband lacked.

Her 1699 Iliad translation answered Homer's critics in its preface. Houdart de la Motte's verse Iliad appeared only in 1713, cut to twelve cantos, prolixity removed, revised to taste as reasonable and elegant. Dacier refuted that attack in Les causes de la corruption du goût, analysing Tacitus's Dialogue on Orators. La Motte answered in his Réflexions sur la critique. That year Fénelon defended the ancients, aiding their supporters. The quarrel dragged on, and in 1716 Hardouin apologized for Homer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anthony-kober:
Anthony Koberger, German printer, born about 1445, died 1513. He came from an old artisan family on the town council since 1350, a goldsmith before becoming a printer. After his first dated volume, Alcinous, in 1472, his house grew, with about 200 works before 1500, mostly in folio. In 1480 it had outstripped Schöffer of Mainz, and was the world's greatest printing-house until the century's end.

Koberger used twenty-four presses a day. Woodcuts in the 1483 Bible mark a new printing epoch, opening the way for Schedel's Weltchronik, with 2000 woodcuts. This greatest illustrated work of the century greatly influenced the woodcut. Towards the century's end the business diminished. Publication by contract, with war and pestilence, chiefly caused its dissolution. Previously he had printing done at Basle and Strasburg, and from 1510 to 1525 presses at Nuremberg, Paris, and Lyons were busy. After his death in 1513, his cousin Hans took charge for his children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-augus:
Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, a French farm reformer born in 1737, did more than anyone to put the potato on French tables. Orphaned young, he trained as a pharmacist and served with the Hanover army, where capture in Prussia taught him how the potato fed soldiers. Back in Paris, he became pharmacist at the veterans' hospital known as the Invalides.

He pressed for better maize and chestnut growing and for sounder baking methods. During the Revolution he ran the making of salted rations and a hard sea biscuit for troops. His many books on farming and gardening spread practical advice, and the entry credits him with turning a little-used tuber into a staple food.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-de-ga:
Antoine de Gaudier, a French Jesuit born in 1572, wrote on the spiritual life from long practice guiding others. He entered the Society at Tournay about age twenty, taught Scripture and moral theology, and became master of novices. Colleagues soon saw his gift for directing souls, and his talks grew, piece by piece, into a full treatise on ascetic practice.

His Latin works include a short book on love of Christ. They also cover true imitation of Christ and God's presence, plus a guide to meditation in the manner of Ignatius. A thirty-day retreat drawn from the Spiritual Exercises was reprinted often after 1643. The entry values Gaudier as a teacher who had spoken with the immediate disciples of Ignatius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-laure:
Antoine-Laurent Lavoisier, a French chemist born in Paris in 1743, founded modern chemistry on the balance. Trained in law, he left it for science, studying mathematics, botany, geology, and chemistry at the College Mazarin. He learned to weigh every substance before and after a reaction, a habit that changed chemistry from guesswork into measurement.

Building on Priestley's oxygen and Cavendish's work on water, he showed that burning takes a ponderable gas from the air, reversing the old phlogiston theory. He stated the conservation of mass in chemical equations, built a clear system of chemical names, and advanced gas analysis. Guillotined in 1794, he left a science remade by exact weighing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-dereser:
Anton Dereser, a Discalced Carmelite born in Franconia in 1757, won fame as a teacher of Scripture and Eastern tongues. Against his order's custom, he took chairs in hermeneutics, the study of interpreting Scripture, and oriental languages at Heidelberg and Bonn. Refusing the Revolutionary oath in France, he was jailed and sentenced to death, then freed when Robespierre fell.

His writings included a German breviary and prayer book, studies of divinity and Pharisaism, and a work on the founding of Bonn University. His combative temper got him into trouble wherever he taught, and he was expelled at Lucerne for rationalist teaching. The entry presents a brilliant, restless scholar whose clashes matched his learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-guenthe:
Anton Guenther, a Bohemian philosopher and priest born in 1783, tried to prove Christian faith by reason alone. Student reading in Kant, Fichte, and Schelling had shaken his belief, until a parish priest and Saint Clement Hofbauer restored it. Ordained in 1820, he spent his later life in Vienna, serving for years on the state board of book censorship.

His system set God against the world, and spirit against nature, and argued that even the Trinity and Incarnation follow from reason. Set out in his Introduction to Speculative Theology and other works, it drew a school of disciples. Rome investigated his doctrines from 1852, and his followers later drifted toward the Old Catholic movement, ending his influence in Catholic thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-sander:
Anton Sander, a Flemish historian born at Antwerp in 1586, spent his fortune publishing histories of his homeland. After study at Douai and Louvain and ordination at Ghent, he fought Anabaptist preaching in Flanders, then served as secretary and almoner to a cardinal. In 1654 he became penitentiary at Ypres, resigning three years later to write full time.

He left forty-two printed works and nearly as many in manuscript, on Flemish writers, saints, and towns. His chief work described the churches and monasteries of Brabant in a sacred chorography, a geography of holy places, illustrated with engravings. Reduced to poverty by printing costs, he ended his days as a guest of Afflighem Abbey, where he died in 1664.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonius-fisc:
Antonius Fischer, archbishop of Cologne and cardinal, was born at Jülich in 1840 and died at Neuenahr in 1912 after a long rise through teaching and diocesan work. The son of a professor, he studied theology at Bonn and Münster, was ordained in 1863, and taught religion for twenty-five years at the gymnasium, or secondary school, at Essen. He took a doctorate at Tübingen in 1886 with a thesis on the salvation of unbelievers, and became titular bishop of Juliopolis in 1889.

As assistant to the aged auxiliary Bishop Baudri he learned the Cologne diocese, succeeded him in 1893, and became archbishop in 1902, a cardinal under Pius X in 1903. During ten years as archbishop he consecrated several hundred churches and more than a thousand altars. He protected religious orders and won unusual trust from the government, which aided the spread of Catholic life. The entry is a portrait of steady administration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apollinaris-t:
Apollinaris the Elder, a Christian grammarian of the fourth century, taught first at Berytus in Phoenicia, later at Laodicea in Syria. He took priestly orders and stood among the firmest supporters of the Council of Nicaea of 325 and of Athanasius. When Emperor Julian the Apostate barred Christian teachers from lecturing on Greek poets and philosophers in 362, Apollinaris and his son set out to replace the lost classics. They wrote Christian works of their own.

Socrates credits the elder Apollinaris with turning the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible, into Greek hexameters. He recast the first two books of Kings as an epic in twenty-four cantos. He wrote tragedies after Euripides, comedies after Menander, and odes after Pindar. Sozomen stresses the son's work instead. This hurried Greek literature, the article judges, lacked genius and faded, yet it shows Christians answering exclusion with imitation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arnold-forste:
Arnold Förster, a German entomologist, was born at Aachen on 20 January 1810 and died there on 12 August 1884. His father died while he was young, and only strict economy and tutoring let him finish his gymnasium, or secondary school, course, begun in 1824. An apt student with a decided taste for natural history, he was fostered by the entomologist Meigen, who lived nearby, and Meigen's influence runs through Förster's later insect work.

Förster began medicine at Bonn in 1832 but soon left it for natural science alone. While still a student he assisted Goldfuss and tutored his family. In 1836 he became an instructor at his native city's high school, now the Realgymnasium, where he stayed until death. A conscientious teacher, he tried to wake in pupils love for nature's wonders, and his wealth of knowledge made him a leading student of insects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aser:
Aser, correctly Asher in the Hebrew original though Aser appears uniformly in Septuagint, Vulgate, and Douay versions, was Jacob's eighth son. He was born in Paddan-Aram, second son of Zilpah, handmaid of Leah, Jacob's wife. His name comes from the root asher, to make or pronounce happy, since his mother declared that through her childbearing women would call her blessed. Scripture records four sons and one daughter, Sarah, for Aser, and Chronicles lists his descendants.

Aser also names one of Israel's twelve tribes, descended from that son. Its territory, described in Joshua 19:24-31, stretched along the Mediterranean from Mount Carmel north to the Leontes river, now Nahr el-Quasimiyeh, with an irregular eastern border. The entry thus covers both a patriarch and a tribe, correcting a familiar spelling while mapping a coastal inheritance in the promised land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asiongaber-ez:
Asiongaber, more properly Ezion-geber, was a city of Idumea on the northern tip of the Aelanitic Gulf, now the Gulf of Aqaba. Scripture mentions it six times, in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Kings, and Chronicles. Its general site is pointed to in 1 Kings 9:26, but its remains have vanished, so its precise site remains conjecture.

Israel encamped at Asiongaber on its wilderness journey, and Solomon's and Hiram's ships sailed from that port to Ophir. It served as Israel's main port for trade with lands bordering the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. Jehoshaphat of Judah joined the wicked Ahaziah of Israel to build ships there, but God disapproved the impious alliance and the ships were wrecked in port. The entry is a harbour's biblical biography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-athanasius-ki:
Athanasius Kircher, celebrated for versatile knowledge and above all for natural science, was born on 2 May 1601 at Geisa. Geisa is a small town on the northern shore of the Upper Rhone in Buchonia. He died at Rome on 28 November 1680. From his birthplace he took the Latin tag Bucho, or Buchonius, to his name, later preferring Fuldensis after Fulda, capital of his native country. His Christian name honoured the saint on whose feast day he was born.

His father John Kircher had pursued philosophy and theology at Mainz without taking priesthood, and after his doctorate in theology lectured in the Benedictine house at Seligenstadt. Athanasius learned humanities at Fulda's Jesuit college and on 2 October 1618 joined the Society of Jesus at Paderborn, then went to Cologne after his novitiate. The entry opens a life of encyclopaedic learning, from Egyptian hieroglyphs to magnetism and music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attainder:
A bill of attainder was an act of Parliament that punished a named person, even with death, without a regular trial. Parliament thus acted as lawmaker and judge, unlike impeachment, where Commons accused and Lords tried. Strictly, a death sentence by statute was an attainder, while a lesser penalty was a bill of pains and penalties. Common speech, and the United States Constitution, used attainder for both kinds.

English use reached back to the Despensers' banishment in 1321, and abuse peaked in the civil war passions of the 1600s. Attainder brought forfeiture of property and corruption of blood, so the condemned could neither inherit nor pass on land. Its force faded after an 1870 statute provided that no conviction for treason, felony, or self-murder should cause attainder or forfeiture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-august-friedr:
August Friedrich Gfrorer was a German historian born at Calw in Wurtemberg in 1803 who died at Karlsbad in 1861. Against his own bent, he studied theology at Tubingen at his parents' wish. He served briefly as vicar at Stuttgart, then resigned, having lost belief in revealed religion. Through a friend's recommendation he became third librarian of the Stuttgart public library in 1830, with the title of professor, and used his free hours for literature and history.

His early book on Philo and Jewish-Alexandrine thought prepared his larger Critical History of Early Christianity, published in five volumes in 1838. Writing as a rationalist, he still denied that he followed David Strauss, whose Life of Jesus had spurred him. Later works ranged over German folk law, Byzantine history, and old Latin pseudepigrapha. The entry credits him with bold and keen combination, though his research sometimes lacked method.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-august-reiche:
August Reichensperger was a German politician and author born at Coblenz in 1808 who died at Cologne in 1895. After studying law at Bonn, Heidelberg, and Berlin, he entered Prussian civil service, served as counsel and chamber president in the Cologne courts, and retired in 1875. From 1848 to 1885, save for the years 1863 to 1870, he sat almost without break in parliaments. He served at Frankfort, Berlin, and Erfurt, and in the Reichstag from 1871 to 1884.

He helped found the Catholic party in Prussia and co-founded the Centre, earning esteem as an orator even from opponents, though Windthorst led the party in fact. A skeptic in youth, he returned to the faith after the imprisonment of Archbishop Clemens August in 1837. He backed the Borromaeus Society, the Catholic press, and religious freedom. He wrote widely on church art, politics, and Shakespeare, while his legal studies remain his least known work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-de-b:
Augustin de Backer was a Jesuit bibliographer born at Antwerp in 1809 who died at Liege in 1873. He studied at Jesuit colleges in Belgium and France, entered the Society of Jesus in 1835, and taught at Namur before studying for the priesthood at Louvain. Even as a student he collected Elzevirs, early printed books from a famous Dutch press, and planned a history of Europe's first printing presses. Visits to the chief libraries of Belgium and Paris prepared him for that work.

At Louvain he found Southwell's unfinished Bibliotheca of Jesuit writers from 1676 and resolved to complete the task. With his brother Aloysius he published the Bibliotheque des Ecrivains de la Compagnie de Jesus in seven volumes between 1853 and 1861. A new edition in three large folios, listing eleven thousand Jesuit authors with editions, translations, and refutations, followed between 1859 and 1876. He died during its third volume, and his brother finished it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustin-thei:
Augustin Theiner was a German theologian and historian, a shoemaker's son born at Breslau in 1804 who died at Civitavecchia in 1874. He studied theology, then, on his brother's advice, turned to law and took a degree at Halle in 1829. A Prussian grant let him hunt canon-law sources abroad. At Rome, under Count Reisach's influence, his views changed, and he became a priest of the Oratory of St Philip Neri.

Pius IX gave him a Vatican Library post in 1850 and charged him with a history of Pope Clement XIV. In that work he turned against the Jesuits, once his friends. After he passed outsiders the Council of Trent's secret order of business, he lost his dignities and offices, and whether he died at peace with the Church remains doubtful. His posthumous Acta Genuina of Trent, issued in 1874, was imperfectly edited, yet his scholarship and service to history stand clear.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustine-van:
Augustine Van de Vyver was the sixth Bishop of Richmond, born at Haesdonck in Belgium in 1844, who died at Richmond in 1911. He studied at St Nicholas and at the American College of Louvain, and he was ordained priest in 1870. He served at Richmond cathedral, pastored Harper's Ferry from 1875 to 1881, and became vicar general of the diocese. Rome named him to succeed Bishop Keane in 1889, aided by a petition from the diocesan priests.

His consecration brought together his two predecessors, Cardinal Gibbons and Bishop Keane. Under him, Thomas Fortune Ryan of New York gave the Sacred Heart Cathedral building, and his wife gave its furnishings, at near half a million dollars. The cornerstone was laid in 1903 and the cathedral consecrated in 1906. A quasi-synod in 1907 set new laws. Deep humility moved him to seek resignation several times, but he died in office, revered as a father to all ranks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthasar-cor:
Balthasar Cordier, or Corderius, was an exegete and editor of patristic works, born at Antwerp in 1592, who died at Rome in 1650. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1612, taught Greek, moral theology, and Sacred Scripture, then gave himself to Greek manuscripts. Searching Europe's libraries, he translated and edited Greek catenae and works of the Greek Fathers.

His editions include chains of Fathers on Luke (1628) and John (1630), Philoponus on Genesis, and Cyril's moral apologies. Later came Dionysius with Maximus's notes (1634), a Greek exposition of the Psalms (1643-46), and Dorotheus's ascetic rules (1646). His Jeremiah homilies ascribed to Cyril are in fact Origen's, a slip in his critical judgment. He also wrote Job Illustratus, a commentary on Job published in 1646.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomeus-:
Bartholomeus Welser was a German merchant prince born at Augsburg in 1488, who died in Swabia in 1561. After his father Anton's death in 1518, he founded Welser and Company with his brother Anton. Their loans to Charles V won Bartholomeus imperial nobility in 1532, a safe-conduct in 1541, and court exemptions in 1546. By treaty of 1528, the Welsers gained supremacy in Venezuela, monopolizing its trade and planting a colony.

Their first regent, Ambrosius Ehinger, explored Venezuela's interior, but disputes with Spain killed hopes of rich profit. Bartholomeus's son was murdered in 1546, and Spain retook the province by legal decision in 1556. Accused of cruelty, the colonizers' uprightness is now fully proved. Back at Augsburg, he funded Charles V in the Smalkaldic War, sat on the privy council from 1548 to 1556, and kept his family Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-h:
Bartholomew Holzhauser was a parish priest, ecclesiastical writer, and founder of a religious community, born in Bavaria in 1613, who died in 1658. One of eleven children of a poor shoemaker, he loved books and longed for the ministry. At Augsburg's free school for poor boys, he sang at doors and begged to live. Aided by friends and Jesuits, he studied at Neuburg and Ingolstadt, taking his philosophy doctorate in 1636.

Ordained in 1639, he became dean and pastor of Tittmoning in 1640 and pastor at Leukenthal in 1642. He was much sought after as a confessor. His Apocalypse commentary, borrowing from Joachim di Fiore, pictures a strong ruler and holy pope, seven church ages, and the Empire as earth's last. Its 1260 days and Chosroes as Antichrist's forerunner also follow Joachim. The commentary is still counted instructive and edifying.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilica-of-s:
The Basilica of St Peter stands where Agrippina's gardens lay at the first century's start. Her son Caligula built a circus there, setting the Heliopolis obelisk, now in St Peter's Square, in its spine. Nero staged spectacles in that circus, including the Christians' martyrdoms, and tradition marks Peter's crucifixion spot with an altar. Past the circus ran the Via Cornelia, lined with tombs, and a small city of churches and hospices grew nearby.

After Saracens pillaged the basilica in 847, Leo IV walled the suburb, giving the Vatican district its Leonine City name. Two of his towers and a wall fragment still stand in the Vatican gardens. Maintaining the colossal building falls to a corps of architects and the sampietrini, permanent artisans under a head master. Few institutions boast so chosen a body of clever, reliable, fearless workmen, and the maintenance is exemplary throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beda-weber:
Beda Weber was a Benedictine professor, author, and member of the National German Parliament, born in the Tyrol in 1798, who died at Frankfort in 1859. His father had him learn shoemaking alongside peasant work, but Weber finished high school at Bozen in four years and studied philosophy at Innsbruck. Entering Marienberg Abbey, he took the name Beda for Johann Chrysanth, studied theology at Innsbruck and Brixen, and was ordained in 1824. After a short pastorate he taught at Meran's high school for twenty years, refusing calls from Innsbruck, Augsburg, and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen.

The events of 1848 called him to Frankfort's national Parliament, where his labors drew attention. Succeeding Frankfort's town priest, his zeal won him a Limburg canonry and diocesan offices. An excellent preacher, he gave his sermons' proceeds to charity and founded Frankfort's Catholic Church paper in 1853. His Charakterbilder of 1853 and Cartons aus dem deutschen Kirchenleben of 1858 collected his journalism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-stat:
Benedict Stattler, a Jesuit theologian of Bavaria, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Kötzting in 1728, he died at Munich in 1797 after teaching philosophy and theology at Solothurn, Innsbruck, and Ingolstadt. Even after the Jesuits were suppressed, he kept his Ingolstadt chair until former Jesuits were barred from teaching in 1783.

Controversy marks his later work. He exposed the Illuminati, a secret society founded by Adam Weishaupt, in an anonymous book, and answered Kant's Critique of Pure Reason with his Anti-Kant of 1788. Yet several of his own works, including his Catholic Demonstration, fell under Roman censure and landed on the Index of forbidden books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beverley-mins:
Beverley Minster, a collegiate church in the East Riding of Yorkshire, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Served by secular canons until the Reformation, it began with St. John of Beverley, in the early 700s, when the place was forest clearing in Deira. Its name, Beverlac, may come from beaver colonies on the River Hull.

St. John founded communities of monks and nuns there, then retired to the minster after resigning York and died in 721, his shrine drawing pilgrims. Later building made it one of England's great Gothic churches. The entry follows a forest clearing to a pilgrim church of national fame.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biblical-crit:
Higher criticism, the study of the Bible's literary origins and historical value, receives a very long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. The name, first used by Eichhorn, covers a field distinct from textual criticism, which seeks the purest text. Higher criticism asks who wrote each book, when, from what sources, and how it changed.

Rationalist critics, the entry says, treat Scripture as merely human and set inspiration aside, while moderate Protestants keep inspiration with freedoms Catholic teaching rejects. Catholic critics hold full inspiration and inerrancy as starting points. The piece maps a contested science with unusual fairness to its opponents.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-german-gar:
Blessed German Gardiner, the last martyr under Henry VIII, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth date is unknown, and he died at Tyburn on 7 March 1544. Secretary and probably kinsman to Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester, he defended the old faith ably in a tract against John Frith dated 1534.

Years of fiery trial followed, and Gardiner took courage from the martyrs, above all Thomas More, a layman like himself. His witness came eight years later, when Henry's shifting wrath sacrificed the Catholic in place of the heretic Cranmer. Indicted for denying the king's supremacy, he died with John Larke and John Ireland, while a fellow condemned man, Heywood, recanted and lived.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-roche:
Blessed John Rochester, priest and martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born probably at Terling in Essex about 1498, he died at York on 11 May 1537. Third son of John Rochester of Terling, he joined the Carthusians as a choir monk of the London Charterhouse and opposed Henry VIII's royal supremacy with all his strength.

Arrested, he was sent to the Charterhouse at Hull, then removed to York and hanged in chains, with a fellow Carthusian, James Walworth, about whom little is known. Leo XIII beatified him in 1888. His elder brother Sir Robert, comptroller to Princess Mary and later chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster under Queen Mary, closes the entry as a faithful Catholic courtier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-sarka:
Blessed John Sarkander, martyr of the seal of confession, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Skotschau in Austrian Silesia in 1576, he died at Olmütz in 1620. He took a master's degree in philosophy at Prague in 1603. After four years of theology he was ordained priest at Graz. He then served parishes in the Olmütz diocese, becoming parish priest of Boskowitz in 1613 and Holeschau in 1616.

Hussites and Bohemian Brethren had seized many Catholic churches since the fifteenth century, and Sarkander worked to restore them. Arrested during the Bohemian revolt, he was tortured to reveal confessions and died rather than break the seal. The entry presents a priest who died guarding a secret.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-cleme:
Blessed Clement Mary Hofbauer, second founder of the Redemptorists and Apostle of Vienna, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born John Dvorák at Tasswitz in Moravia in 1751, youngest of twelve children of a grazier and butcher, he died at Vienna in 1821. His father died when he was six, and longing for priesthood without means, he became a baker's assistant, studying in spare hours.

Service in the Premonstratensian monastery of Bruck and years as a hermit led to Rome, ordination, and the Redemptorists. With Thaddeus Hübl he planted the congregation in Warsaw and then Vienna, preaching to the poor. The entry presents a baker's boy who became Vienna's apostle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-gunth:
Blessed Gunther, a hermit in Bohemia, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born about 955, cousin of St. Stephen of Hungary, he died at Hartmanitz in 1045. Court life of pleasure and intrigue filled his early years until St. Gotthard converted him in 1005 at fifty, and he gave all his goods to Hersfeld Abbey with his heirs' consent.

Thirty-four years of poverty and mortification followed in the Bohemian forest, with water itself measured out to the brothers. Though he knew little beyond the Psalter, God granted him, his biographer says, deep Scripture knowledge, and his sermons on John the Baptist drew tears. Visits to King Stephen won alms and churches for the poor, and he founded Rinchnach monastery, endowed by Conrad II in 1029.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-peter:
Peter of Montboissier, better known as Peter the Venerable, reformed the great Cluniac order and sheltered Abelard after his condemnation. Born in Auvergne about 1092, he was offered to Cluny's monastery at Sauxillanges. He became prior of Vezelay at twenty and general of an order counting some two thousand houses at thirty.

He faced a violent bid by his deposed predecessor Pontius. He answered Bernard of Clairvaux's attacks with firmness and meekness, and wrote a full code of Cluniac life. During a Spanish visit in 1139 he had the Koran first rendered into Latin. He resisted the antipope Anacletus II, and reconciled Abelard with Bernard and the pope before dying at Cluny on Christmas Day 1156.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-wimm:
Boniface Wimmer, archabbot of Saint Vincent in Pennsylvania, transplanted Benedictine life to the United States for German immigrants. Born at Thalmassing, Bavaria, on 14 January 1809, he studied law at Munich, then won a scholarship to the Gregorianum and was ordained in 1831. After a year as curate at Altotting, he entered Metten Abbey and made solemn vows in 1833.

Reading of neglected German settlers in America, he sailed with five students and fifteen brother candidates, landing at New York on 16 September 1846. Undeterred by warnings of failure, he settled forty miles east of Pittsburgh on land from Bishop O'Connor, where Saint Vincent Archabbey, College, and Seminary now stand. His community grew, organized scattered settlers into parishes, and supplied German-speaking priests across the country. He died at Saint Vincent on 8 December 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-commo:
The Book of Common Prayer, imposed by the first Act of Uniformity on 21 January 1549, replaced Latin worship in England with an English liturgy. Before that date, services ran in Latin under local uses like Salisbury, York, and Hereford, all drawn from the Roman liturgy with its Roman Canon. The stated motives were uniformity, simplicity, and the people's edification.

The entry argues the real motive was to strip doctrines the Reformers rejected. These were the Real Presence, the Mass as sacrifice, invocation of saints, prayer for the dead, seven sacraments, auricular confession, and a sacrificing priesthood. Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury, stands behind almost every line down to Edward's reign, the book's history being largely his biography. Convocation, the entry notes, had no part in the first Act; laymen made the book a schedule of a penal statute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesar-of-spe:
Caesar of Speyer, a Friar Minor born late in the twelfth century, became the first provincial minister of the order in Germany and died in 1239. As a preacher he won so many Albigenses from their errors that their anger drove him from his home city. He studied theology at Paris in 1212, joined the Franciscans in the Holy Land in 1217, and returned to Italy with Saint Francis in 1221.

At the Pentecost chapter at Assisi in 1221 he and twenty-five companions were sent to Germany, and that October he held the order's first German provincial chapter at Strasburg. The Rule of 1223 was likely written by him at Saint Francis's dictation. In later years he urged the friars to hold fast to their rule against the Relaxati, and for that stand the minister general had him imprisoned. Jordan of Giano called him the most saintly friar after Saint Francis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caius-and-sot:
Caius and Soter share a feast on 22 April, though a few martyrologies give Soter the 21st and Caius the 19th or 21st. Soter's pontificate lasted about eight years, from around 167 to 175. A fragment survives of a letter to him from Saint Dionysius of Corinth. It praises Rome's age-old custom of sending alms to churches in every city and aid to brethren in the mines.

Soter's own letter to Corinth is lost, though some scholars take it for the so-called Second Epistle of Clement, and nothing more is known of him. Caius held the papacy from 17 December 283 to 22 April 296, twelve years, four months, and seven days in all. He was laid in the popes' chapel in the cemetery of Callistus. Nothing whatever is known of his life, lived in the peace before the last great persecution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caspar-castne:
Caspar Castner, also called Kastner, was a Jesuit missionary born at Munich in October 1655 who died at Peking in November 1709. He joined the Society in 1681 and finished theology at Ingolstadt in 1694. After teaching logic briefly at Ratisbon, he sailed for China in 1696 at the head of Jesuits from Portugal and Genoa. He worked with success on Shang-chuen island and at Fatshan, then a rival of Canton.

In 1702 he traveled with Franciscus Noel to Lisbon and Rome for the Bishops of Nanking and Macao, seeking settlement of the Chinese Rites question. He returned to China in 1706 with fresh missionaries. Beyond his apostolic work he won praise in navigation, astronomy, and cartography. He showed Portugal a shorter Macao route past the Cape of Good Hope by the Sunda Islands. He mapped the Chinese Empire with a mathematician's reputation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caspar-schatz:
Caspar Schatzgeyer was a leading opponent of the Protestant Reformers, born at Landshut in 1463 or 1464, who died at Munich in September 1527. Guardian at Munich for many years, he became in 1517 first provincial of the Friars Minor in Strasburg and definitor-general. In 1523 he became inquisitor for Germany. He fought the new errors in speech and writing with energy.

He shares much of the credit for Catholicism's hold in southern Germany and for Bavaria's staunch defense with his confreres. Within a few years he published more than twenty-three works defending grace, veneration of saints, monasticism, indissoluble marriage, the Mass, and purgatory. John Eck praised his writings highly, collected them, and published them at Ingolstadt in 1543, and Bavarian dukes commended them to all clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestine-ord:
The Celestine Order, whose members were also known as the Murrone hermits or the hermits of St. Damian, was a Benedictine congregation founded in 1254 by Pietro di Murrone, afterwards Pope Celestine V. At first the saint gave his monks no written rule, offering his own life as their ideal. Urban IV confirmed the order in 1264 and gave it the Rule of St. Benedict, and Gregory X confirmed it again in 1274.

Celestine confirmed constitutions drawn up by Abbot Humphrey and granted his order many privileges, including a general chapter every year. Run on the pattern of Cluny, all houses answered to Sulmona's Abbey of the Holy Ghost, divided into provinces. The order counted 96 Italian houses, 21 French ones, and a few in Germany, most of which later joined the Reformers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-censer:
A censer is a vessel hung by chains for burning incense at the great offices, solemn Mass, Vespers, Benediction, and processions. Today it is called a thurible. In its usual shape it has a cup or bowl on a firm base. It holds a hollow movable pan for lighted charcoal, a lid, and four chains about three feet long. Three join the bowl to a disc, and the fourth raises the lid.

To carry it, the chains are grasped just under the disc. The base is held six or eight inches off the ground, and the censer swung gently so the moving air feeds the fire on the fragrant gums or incense. The censer mattered in ancient Jewish and pagan worship alike, so its Christian use reaches back to the earliest times. Its first form was a vase with a perforated cover, chains being added later for handling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chair-of-pete:
The Chair of Peter covers two subjects: the annual feast of the Chair at Rome and the chair itself. From the earliest times the Roman Church kept 18 January as the memory of the day the Apostle first served the faithful of the Eternal City. The Martyrologium Hieronymianum records the dedication of the chair in which Peter first sat at Rome. A second feast on 22 February appears in its ninth-century form.

All manuscripts assign that February feast to Antioch, not Rome, though the words placing Peter's sitting at Antioch look like a later addition. Both feasts, the article argues, are Roman in origin, and the February feast was originally the more important of the two. The second part of the article turns from the feasts to the chair itself, its history, and its veneration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chapter:
Chapter, from Latin capitulum, names corporate ecclesiastical bodies. The name is said to come from the chapter of the rule book read in monks' assemblies. By degrees the meeting itself took the name chapter, and the meeting place became the chapter house. From conventual chapters, meetings of monks over monastery or order business, the name passed to analogous assemblies of other ecclesiastics, hence collegiate and cathedral chapters.

In general a chapter is a body of clerics of one church, joined as a moral body by church authority to promote divine worship through choir service. For a cathedral chapter, however, the main object is assisting the bishop in governing his diocese, with choir service secondary. Members are called canons. The article traces the origin of chapters from the cathedral clergy, the Presbyterium, common dwelling, and monastic example. It surveys constitution, officials, rights, meetings, and chapters in vacancy and mission lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-character:
Character in Catholic theology means a lasting spiritual mark left on the soul by Baptism, Confirmation, and Holy Orders. The mark cannot be erased, which is why none of these three sacraments may be given twice to the same person. The word echoes Hebrews, where the Son is called the figure of the Father's substance. The teaching was set out by the Councils of Florence and Trent.

It grew clearer over time. Early hints gave way to fuller statement, and medieval theologians who doubted it could be proved from revelation still held it true and part of Catholic teaching. The word is used differently elsewhere. In Protestant writing on the Trinity, hypostatic character names what marks each Divine Person as distinct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-butle:
Charles Butler was among the most prominent English Catholics of his day, born in London in 1750 and dead in 1832. From an old Northamptonshire family, he was nephew of Alban Butler, who wrote the Lives of the Saints. After a private school at Hammersmith and the preparatory house at Equerchin, he finished the full course at Douai. Back in England he turned to law. His religion barred him from the Bar, so he became a conveyancer practising in chambers, studying under Duane and Maire.

From 1775 he practised for over forty years. For more than half that time he ranked as the first conveyancer of the day. His pupils included the future attorney-general Sir Thomas Denman.
