Exclusion from the Bar mortified him and drove him into Catholic efforts to repeal the Penal Laws. He also wrote widely, continuing his uncle's Lives and publishing lives of Erasmus and Grotius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-cahie:
Charles Cahier was an antiquarian born at Paris in 1807 and dead there in 1882. After studies at the College of Saint-Acheul he entered the Society of Jesus in 1824, and taught in Jesuit colleges at Paris, Brieg in Switzerland, Turin, and Brugalette in Belgium. Most of his life, though, went to collecting, classifying, and interpreting surviving medieval art treasures. He worked in France and Belgium, in Germany, and across Europe, valuing them chiefly as evidence of Catholic faith.

From 1840 he worked with Father Arthur Martin, a fellow Jesuit and fine draughtsman, who gathered most of the material Cahier interpreted in the light of faith and theology. Their first major work treated the thirteenth-century stained glass of Bourges cathedral, published between 1841 and 1844. Their most characteristic work is the four quarto volumes of archaeological, historical, and literary mélanges issued from 1848 to 1859.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-edmon:
Coussemaker was a French historian of music born at Bailleul in 1805 and dead at Lille in 1876. He served musical science by drawing students' attention to the early history of harmony and counterpoint, as shown in the diaphony section of the Musica Enchiriadis. His work on Hucbald, a monk of Saint-Amand who lived from about 840 to 930 and wrote the Enchiriadis, opened that field.

Even after becoming a lawyer at Douai, he took counterpoint lessons under Victor Lefebvre. His early wish to compose, above all church music, came to little permanent result, since most of those pieces remain in manuscript. While sitting as judge in five towns in turn, Bergues, Hazebrouck, Cambrai, Dunkerque, and Lille, he pursued the researches behind works of lasting historical importance. His writings helped the revival of true church music and the restoration of chant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-garni:
Charles Garnier was a Jesuit missionary born at Paris in 1606 and dead in 1649. He studied classics, philosophy, and theology at the Jesuit college of Clermont and joined the order in 1624. Begging for the Canadian mission, he sailed in 1636 with Governor Montmagny's fleet. Sent at once to the Huron country, he spent fourteen years there in heroic apostolate.

His zeal for converting infidels brooked no delay: neither distance, weather, nor danger of death kept him from hurrying to the stake. His frail frame resisted the strain, and his patience under endless trials earned him the mission's title of lamb. He strove repeatedly to convert the Tobacco nation, until their obstinacy gave way and they asked for the black robes in 1646. He lived among them until death, receiving the final blow in an act of charity in 1649.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-mauri:
An entry on Charles Maurice Le Tellier, Archbishop of Reims and a leading churchman of Louis XIV's France. Born at Turin in 1642, son of minister Michel Le Tellier and brother of Louvois, he took his doctorate in theology. Ordained in 1666, he held the see of Reims from the age of twenty-nine. His rule was marked by zeal for schooling, the training of clergy, parish organisation, and the rooting out of Protestantism around Sedan.

Royal favour pushed Le Tellier to the front of French Church affairs. There he reported for the king against the pope on disputed rights, including the régale, the crown's claim to revenues of vacant sees. He steered the Gallican Assembly of 1682, which backed royal encroachment on Church affairs. He presided over the assembly of 1700 that judged Jansenism and lax moral teaching. The entry judges him a capable administrator despite grave errors of loyalty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-plumi:
An entry on Charles Plumier, a French Minim friar and botanist, a student of plants, ranked as the most important plant explorer of his time. Born at Marseilles in 1646, he joined the Minims at sixteen, studied mathematics and physics, and became a skilled draughtsman, painter, and maker of instruments. Sent to Rome, he learned botany eagerly under the Cistercian Paolo Boccone, and back in France he joined the excursions of Tournefort, the leading French plant classifier.

Plumier's lasting work began in 1689, when the government sent him with Surian to the French Antilles. Named royal botanist, he made two more voyages there and to Central America in 1693 and 1695, aided by the Dominican Labat. In 1704, about to sail for Peru to seek the home of the true cinchona tree, he fell ill with pleurisy and died near Cadiz.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chichester:
A history of the ancient Catholic Diocese of Chichester in England, born from the Council of London of 1075, which moved bishoprics from villages into towns. The old South Saxon see, founded late in the seventh century by Saint Wilfrid of York at Selsea, was transferred to Chichester in 1082 by Bishop Stigand. The town took its name from Cissa, son of the Saxon chief Aelle, whose fort gave Cissa's Ceaster, in time Chichester.

Ralph de Luffa, bishop from 1091 to 1123, built the cathedral, consecrated in part in 1108, burned in 1114, completed in 1184, and burned again in 1186. Seyffrid the Second rebuilt it with Early English work inside the Norman shell, giving the nave its mixed character. Later bishops included Richard Poore, builder of Salisbury, Ralph Neville the statesman, and Saint Richard of Chichester, whom Henry the Third first denied the revenues of his see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-may:
An entry on Christian Mayer, a Moravian Jesuit astronomer born in August 1719 and dead at Heidelberg in April 1783. He joined the Society of Jesus at Mannheim in 1745, taught humanities at Aschaffenburg, and became professor of mathematics and physics at Heidelberg. In 1755 the Elector Palatine Charles Theodore asked him to build and run the observatory at Mannheim, and he built another at Schwetzingen.

Mayer's observations filled many memoirs, some in London's Philosophical Transactions, and he observed the transit of Venus at Saint Petersburg in 1769 at the invitation of Empress Catherine. His most disputed claim, that bright southern stars were ringed by smaller stars he took for satellites, failed before the stronger telescopes of Herschel and Schröter. Mayer defended it in print in 1778, but the sightings, made in good faith, were evidently an optical illusion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christoph-bro:
An entry on Christoph Brouwer, a Jesuit historian born at Arnhem in March 1559 and dead at Trier in 1617. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1580, trained in the humanities, and gave himself to church history, teaching philosophy at Trier and serving as rector first at Fulda, then at Trier. His chief work was the Antiquities and Annals of Trier and its suffragan bishops, reaching the year 1600.

Two archbishops asked for the work to answer a partisan book by Hermann Kyriander, syndic of Trier, who had defended the city against the archbishop. Brouwer spent most of his life on it, and Hontheim honoured his love of truth and method. Yet the archbishop's councillors disliked it, printing was sanctioned only in altered form, and the eighteenth book was suppressed. Masenius continued the work to 1652 and issued it whole at Liège in 1670.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-s:
An entry on Christopher Scheiner, a German Jesuit astronomer born near Mindelheim in July 1575, he died in Silesia in July 1650. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1595, studied mathematics at Ingolstadt, and taught at Dillingen, then at Ingolstadt, where he taught Hebrew and mathematics and took up research. He had invented the pantograph, a copying instrument, and now built a telescope to study the sun.

With a student helper, Scheiner projected the sun's image on a screen. In March 1611 he found sunspots, a sight so against the philosophy of the day that his superiors barred his name from print. His letters, issued by Welser at Augsburg in 1612 under a false name, described the spots' rotation and the bright faculae. Galileo claimed priority, and Fabricius had seen the spots earlier still, but Scheiner's continuous observations stand undisputed. His Rosa Ursina of 1626 to 1630 remains a standard treatise on the sun.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrysostomus-:
An entry on Chrysostomus Hanthaler, a Cistercian historical researcher born in Austria in February 1690. After schooling he professed at Lilienfeld in 1716 and gave himself to history with untiring zeal. The abbey archives and rich library gave him a splendid field, and as librarian he first built a reliable catalogue, then gathered every document on Lilienfeld and Austria.

Copies and impressions of tablets, seals, and coins filled twenty-two folio volumes of transcripts. From them Hanthaler wrote the Fasti Campililienses in two large volumes. It covers his monastery's complete history, from the thirteenth century through the Middle Ages' end, with the Babenberg dukes of Austria and Styria also treated. Death delayed the work, and after the abbey's suppression in 1789, Abbot Pyrker published its continuation at Vienna in 1819 and 1820. Hanthaler also wrote on coins for amateur collectors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-buffie:
Claude Buffier, a philosopher and author, was born in Poland of French parents on 25 May 1661 and died at Paris on 17 May 1737. Schooled at Rouen's Jesuit college, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1679, taught literature in Paris, and returned to Rouen for a chair of theology. Archbishop Colbert's pastoral recommending Gallican and Jansenist books drew Buffier's pamphlet attack. Refusing to retract, he went to Rome and justified himself there.

From 1701 to 1731 he worked on the Journal de Trevoux, publishing on history, asceticism, biography, education, and literature, above all philosophy. He was no disciple of Descartes: he rejected methodic doubt and followed the scholastics. The Encyclopedists printed whole pages of his books without credit, Tabaraud reports, and Reid the Scottish metaphysician acknowledged great debt to him. His chief works include a French grammar on a new plan and a course of the sciences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-claude-franco:
Claude-Francois Menestrier, an antiquarian, was born at Lyons on 9 March 1631 and died at Paris on 21 January 1705. He inherited a taste for antiquities from a great-uncle who collected art and medals for Cardinal Barberini. A pupil of the Jesuit College of the Trinity at Lyons, he entered the Society. At fifteen he taught rhetoric, composing ballets for Louis the Fourteenth's Lyons visit in 1658.

He was more than an organiser of spectacles. His heraldry publications drew disputes with Claude le Laboureur, and he studied emblems and mottoes. From 1670 he preached in Paris for twenty-five years. He wrote Latin inscriptions for LeBrun's prints and Van der Meulen's battle pictures. His books include a history of Louis the Great told through medals and arms (1689) and a history of Lyons (1696). In 1682, at Villiers, he found the tomb of Russia's Queen Anne, or Agnes. A diploma bearing her seal vindicated him in 1825.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clement-schra:
Clement Schrader, a Jesuit theologian, was born at Itzum in Hanover in November 1820 and died at Poitiers on 23 February 1875. He studied at the German College in Rome from 1840 to 1848. He entered the Society of Jesus on 17 May 1848. Then he lectured on dogmatic theology at the Roman College, and later joined Vienna's theological faculty.

In 1867 he joined the theological commission preparing preliminaries for the Vatican Council. Refusing the Constitution's fidelity oath of 1867, he lost his Vienna professorship soon after the council was prorogued. His remaining life went to teaching theology at the Catholic University of Poitiers, where pneumonia ended it. His grasp of scholastic theology shows in many works, chiefly De Deo Creante and De triplici Ordine. Eight series treat questions such as predestination, actual grace, faith, and human society. De unitate Romana, judged by Hurter his ablest work, stands among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clogher:
Clogher, a suffragan of Armagh in Ireland, covers Monaghan, almost all Fermanagh, southern Tyrone, and parts of Donegal, Louth, and Cavan. Its name comes from Clogher, seat of the Prince of Oriel, whose territory matched the old diocese. Saint Patrick founded the see and appointed one of his household, Saint Macarten, as first bishop. No evidence shows Patrick governing Clogher before settling at Armagh, as Jocelyn states.

Tracing Clogher's bishops from the sixth to the eleventh century is very difficult, since bishops blur with abbots of monastic houses. The Irish Annals differ from the Register of Clogher, compiled by Bishop Patrick Culin and Archdeacon Roderick Cassidy. In 1241 Henry the Third ordered Clogher united to Armagh for the poverty of both sees, but the union was not carried out. Tyrone portions went to Ardstraw, and much of Louth, including Dundalk, Drogheda, and Ardee, passed to Armagh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cloister:
Cloister renders the Latin clausura, from claudere, to shut up. In Roman law the word meant rampart or barrier, and in Benedict of Aniane's work it meant case or cupboard. In modern church usage clausura means, materially, an enclosed space for religious retirement, and formally, the legal restrictions on egress of the enclosed and entry of outsiders. The legislation distinguishes religious orders from simple-vow institutes, and men's houses from women's.

For male religious orders, common law requires every convent or monastery of regulars to be encloistered on completion. A convent is a building serving as a fixed dwelling where religious live by their rule. Jurists hold that houses with two or three religious dwelling permanently fall under the law. In missionary countries Propaganda applied cloister even to mission houses of two or three regulars. Houses merely hired by religious, not fixed and definitive homes, escape the law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college-of-sa:
Bernard Ward's entry tells of the Jesuit college at St. Omer, often called St. Omers. Father Parsons founded it in 1592 or 1593. Catholic schooling was banned in England, so Englishmen had built colleges abroad at Douai, Rome, and Valladolid. Those schools trained clergy first. Parsons saw a need for a college meant first for the laity. He chose a spot near England: St. Omer, twenty-four miles from Calais, in Artois, then under the King of Spain.

His first students came from a small house he had set up at Eu in Normandy. Boys soon poured in from England, and within ten years the college held over a hundred. Artois passed to France in 1678, but the French government stayed friendly. The college prospered until 1762, when the Parlement suppressed the Jesuits and its long first chapter closed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-peutin:
Arthur F.J. Remy's entry follows Conrad Peutinger, antiquarian and humanist born at Augsburg on 14 October 1465, died on 28 December 1547. Young, he studied law and belles-lettres at Padua, Bologna, and Florence. At Rome his enthusiasm for antiquity awoke. Returning to Germany he entered his native city's service in 1490, winning definite appointment as syndic in 1497. To life's end he served Augsburg in various capacities, always with distinction.

He enjoyed Emperor Maximilian's friendship and special confidence, and the emperor frequently used him on diplomatic or literary missions. Through that friendship Peutinger won valuable privileges for Augsburg, notably in 1506 while staying with Maximilian in Vienna and Hungary, where he led negotiations between emperor and rebellious Hungarian subjects. In 1512 he acted as intermediary between emperor and other powers. Of his literary work only part has been published, yet his antiquarian collections and civic service mark him among Augsburg's leading Renaissance figures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-tanner:
Francis Mershman's entry follows Conrad Tanner, Einsiedeln's abbot, born at Arth, Schwyz, on 28 December 1752, died on 7 April 1825. He studied at Einsiedeln, took vows on 8 September 1772, and was ordained in May 1777. He taught at Einsiedeln and Bellinzona, served as abbey librarian in 1787, and directed Bellinzona's college in 1789. During the Revolution he fled to the Tyrol with the statue, Saint Meinrad's head, and valuables, restoring them when safe.

Pastor of Saint Gerold from 1802, he returned as novice master, then won election as abbot in 1808. With prudence he met the political situation and saved the monastery. He encouraged studies, renovated buildings, and rebuilt the Holy Chapel destroyed in 1798. Though Einsiedeln village left his rule, fatherly care marked the famine years of 1816 and 1817. Pius VII's plan for a Waldstätten diocese with Tanner as bishop, proposed in 1818, met refusal. His writings include Betrachtungen zur sittlichen Aufklärung and Bildung des Geistlichen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-vetter:
Nikolaus Scheid's entry follows Conrad Vetter, preacher and polemical writer born at Engen, Baden, in 1547, died at Munich on 11 October 1622. He entered the priesthood and championed the Catholic cause in speech and writing. While prefect of music in the nobles' church at Hall, he learned more of the Society of Jesus. All he learned matched his desires, so he entered Munich's novitiate in 1576.

After studies he became Munich's academic preacher for unusual oratory gifts. He then preached years at Ratisbon, where many Lutherans returned to the Church through his sermons. His writings number nearly one hundred, chiefly polemical. Tone runs unrefined: Vetter deployed Swabian coarseness to disparage Luther, recalling Luther's own style. Yet the little books sold largely and reprinted often. Catholic contemporaries defended his method, Duke Maximilian among them against Neuburg's Count Palatine. Bavaria's Dukes William V and Maximilian held him in high regard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantine-b:
Friedrich Lauchert's entry follows Constantine, Baron von Schazler, theologian born at Ratisbon on 7 May 1827, died at Interlaken on 9 September 1880. Protestant by birth and training, he studied at Ratisbon's Protestant gymnasium of Saint Anna. He took philosophy at Erlangen in 1844 and 1845, then law at Munich from 1845 to 1847 and Heidelberg from 1847 to 1848. Choosing military life, he became a Bavarian officer.

In 1850 he left the army, won a Doctor of Laws degree at Erlangen, and practiced law. That year he entered the Catholic Church at Brussels on 10 October and began theology. At Louvain in 1851 he joined the Society of Jesus and was ordained priest at Liège on 11 September 1856. He left the Society in 1857 and continued studies at Munich, taking a Doctor of Theology degree in 1859. A work on dogma history from the Catholic standpoint, edited by Thomas Esser at Ratisbon in 1884, crowns the bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-jan:
Patricius Schlager's entry treats Cornelius Jansen the Elder, also Jansenius Gandaviensis. The exegete was born at Hulst, Flanders, in 1510, and died at Ghent in 1576. He was schooled at Ghent by the Brethren of the Common Life, called there the Hieronymites, then studied theology and Oriental languages at Louvain. Licentiate of theology in 1534, he lectured at Tongerloo's abbot's request to young monks on Scripture until 1542.

From 1542 until 1562 he served as pastor of Saint Martin's at Courtrai, Kortryk. Doctor of Theology in 1562, he became Louvain's professor of theology, and next year dean of Saint James's seminary. His writings include the Concordia evangelica, later expanded by his Commentarius, Louvain, 1572. One of the century's leading exegetes, his Concordia Evangelica proved epoch-making in Catholic exegesis. He insisted on literal sense against his predecessors' mystical reading, stressing the original text and deep Oriental language study for grasping the Vulgate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-alexand:
A biographical entry follows Count Alexander Huebner, an Austrian statesman born in 1811 and dead in 1892. His career ran from Metternich's chancery to the highest posts of the empire. It traces his rise through Paris, Lisbon, and Leipzig, and his close standing in Metternich's household. He later wrote the account of the chancellor's last days.

The narrative lingers on the revolutionary year 1848. Huebner was arrested at Milan and held three months. He then served as secretary to the prime minister at Olmutz, and drafted manifestos for the accession of Francis Joseph. Later he became ambassador and minister. His journals and memoirs remain valued sources for Austrian diplomacy, and sources are listed for readers who want the fuller record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crosier:
This liturgical entry explains the crosier, or pastoral staff, conferred on bishops at consecration and on mitred abbots at investiture. It corrects a common error: archbishops do use the crosier, and also have the archiepiscopal cross borne before them. The Roman pontiff, by contrast, does not use one today, though early images of popes show it.

Symbolism comes first: the staff stands for authority and jurisdiction, and the words of presentation charge the bishop to correct faults with mercy and judge without anger. Origin and antiquity follow, then early forms and artistic development, from simple shepherds' crooks to richly worked metal. The entry draws on Kraus, Pugin, and standard works on vestments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cross-bearer:
A liturgical entry defines the cross-bearer, the minister bearing the processional cross, a crucifix on a long staff. An archbishop's cross has its figure turned toward the prelate. In all other cases the figure faces forward.

Whenever possible the bearer should be a cleric, though in lay processions the most worthy layman is chosen. At solemn processions such as Corpus Christi, Palm Sunday, and Candlemas, a subdeacon in amice, alb, and tunic carries the cross. On lesser occasions a clerk in surplice serves. The staff is held with both hands, figure well above the head, and the bearer walks at the head of the procession, flanked by acolytes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-fitter:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Fitter, an English priest born in Worcestershire in 1628 and dead at Saint Thomas Priory near Stafford in 1700. Entering Lisbon College at nineteen, he was ordained in 1651 and returned as chaplain to William Fowler at Saint Thomas Priory, where he stayed for life. Under James II he opened a Stafford school, suppressed at the revolution of 1688.

In the excitement after the Titus Oates plot, Fitter upheld the lawfulness of a tendered oath, subscribed it, and defended his act on the common legal use of the word spiritual. Chosen vicar-general of four counties, he was required to sign a Paris declaration against the oath of supremacy. He became first provincial president of Holzhauser's institute of clergy living in common, and left funds that became the Johnson Fund for the district clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-of-win:
A biographical entry follows Daniel of Winchester, Bishop of the West Saxons from 705 to 744, dead in 745. Friend of Aldhelm at Sherborne, Bede at Jarrow, and Boniface in Germany, he succeeded Bishop Hedda. The vast Wessex diocese was then split, and Daniel kept Hampshire, Surrey, and Sussex while Aldhelm took the west.

Taught at Malmesbury by the Irish scholar Maildubh, Daniel retired there when blindness forced his resignation. Bede turned to him for the church history of southern and western Britain. He is best remembered for Boniface, who took commendatory letters from him to Rome and counsel from him through the German mission. Two of his letters to Boniface survive, admired for piety and good sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daughters-of-: A brief congregational entry notes the Daughters of the Divine Redeemer, whose motherhouse stood at Oedenburg in Hungary. It sprang in 1863 from the Daughters of the Divine Saviour of Vienna, the congregation counted 37 filial houses and 300 sisters. Its sisters ran schools of all kinds and cared for the sick. Teaching and nursing together shaped the daily work of the houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-augusti:
A biographical entry follows David Augustine Baker, a Benedictine mystic and ascetic writer born at Abergavenny in 1575 and dead of plague in London in 1641. Son of Lord Abergavenny's steward, he studied at Christ's Hospital, Oxford, and the Inns of Court. At Oxford he lost faith in God's existence, but a brush with death that seemed miraculous led him back to the Catholic Church.

Joining the Benedictines at Padua in 1605, he returned to reconcile his dying father to the Church, then gave his inherited means to research. He investigated and refuted the claim that England's ancient Benedictines depended on Cluny, aided by the Cottonian Library's spoils of dissolved monasteries. His writings on prayer and the interior life remain valued by students of mysticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-benjami:
A life of Denis-Benjamin Viger, a French-Canadian statesman and writer born at Montreal in 1774 who died in 1861. Called to the bar after study at the Sulpician college, he sat in Parliament from 1808 and later travelled to London in 1828 to plead French-Canadian interests against Lord Dalhousie. Imprisoned for nineteen months in 1838, he refused bail and demanded a trial.

Following the union of the Canadas he returned to Parliament and, as premier under Governor Metcalfe, split the Liberal party by backing the governor, a step friends read as ambition. His pamphlet on the ministerial crisis of 1844 defends responsible government in plain constitutional terms. He also helped found two newspapers, La Minerve and L'Aurore, and served as first president of the Saint Jean-Baptiste society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominical-let:
The dominical letter is a device taken over from the Romans by old chronologers to find the weekday of any date. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains its use in fitting the movable feasts to the fixed feasts when building the church calendar for a year. The Church, charged from early days with ordering time, supplied a computus, a system of reckoning that joined the solar and lunar years and fixed Easter.

Seven letters, A through G, mark the Sundays of the year in turn, shifting with leap years and with the concurrents, a companion set of numbers. The entry works through the tables that link concurrents to letters, giving calendar makers the key to the whole year. It is a small but exact piece of the machinery behind the feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dower:
Dower is the provision for lifelong support that law grants a wife who outlives her husband. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry stresses that dower differs from a marriage portion such as the Roman dos, the French dot, or the English dowry. Those are gifts settled by agreement, while dower comes by law and belongs to the widow herself. Tacitus found a like marriage gift among the Germans, made by husband to wife.

Roman law knew a gift from the husband's family tied to the wife's portion, but it bound the gift to the portion's presence. The entry follows dower through English statutes and French and Canadian codes, citing Park, Crabbe, and Beauchamp. For readers of family law, it sets out an old shield for widows in plain terms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eadmer:
Eadmer was precentor of Canterbury and a historian, born in 1064 and dead in 1124, both dates uncertain. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he was brought up at Christ Church from childhood and, after Saint Anselm's consecration in 1079, became the saint's intimate companion. After Anselm's death his chief work was writing, drawing on notes of the saint's deeds and discourses.

From those notes he built his chief works, the History of Recent Events and the Life of Saint Anselm. His shorter works hold verses and lives of Dunstan, Edward, Wilfrid, Odo, Oswald, and Bregwin. His tract on the conception of Saint Mary matters greatly for the growth of the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception. In 1121 he was chosen for Saint Andrews, but he barred his own rise by refusing ordination save by York.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-easter:
As Bede wrote, Easter's English name comes from Estre, a Teutonic goddess of day's rising light and spring, unknown elsewhere even in the Edda. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives the old forms, easter and eastron, with April called easter-month. The plural form fits a seven-day feast, matching the French Paques, which renders the Latin paschal feasts of the whole octave.

The Greek pascha has no link with the verb for suffering, though later writers joined them. Pascha is the Aramaic shape of Hebrew pesach, passover. Greeks named Easter the pascha of resurrection and Good Friday the pascha of the cross. The entry follows the feast through history and reckoning, citing Duchesne, Krusch, and Rock.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eberhard-wach:
Eberhard Wachter was a painter born at Stuttgart on 29 February 1762 who died there on 14 August 1852. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he studied at Paris under Regnault, David, and Gros, then went to Rome, where Italian art softened his French classical manner. He prized Carsten's freer style and took up the ideas of the Romantic school. At Rome he became a Catholic.

His fine sense of the feeling locked in a subject swayed his contemporaries. His best years produced a Child Jesus on the Lamb, a Belisarius at the Porta Pinciana, and Job and His Friends. Driven from Rome by the French in 1798, he settled at Vienna, finding no place at Stuttgart after his conversion. He excelled in lyrical and elegiac subjects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ebner:
Ebner is the name of two German mystics whom research has shown to be wholly unrelated. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry opens with Christina Ebner, born of a patrician house at Nuremberg on Good Friday 1277. From her mother she took a deep religious spirit, shown early in prayer and mortification. Soon after her first communion her parents let her enter the Dominican convent at Engelthal, a wish she had held since age seven.

After her novitiate she fell into a dangerous illness that returned three times a year from thirteen to twenty-three, and each year after she suffered a relapse. Yet she kept her diary of visions, including words of the infant Christ heard even in sleep, preserved in a manuscript of 1353 at Medingen. She died at Engelthal in 1355, loyal to Louis the Bavarian, whose soul she believed saved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-auger:
Edmond Auger was a Jesuit preacher born near Troyes in 1530 and dead at Como in 1591, in the years when French Calvinists fought for power. He joined the Society of Jesus while Ignatius still lived and won fame as a speaker, so crowds came to hear him, even his foes. At Valence he was seized and set to burn, yet his words from the pyre won his release.

Later he nursed plague victims at Lyons, and in thanks the town set up a Jesuit college where Calvinist children too could learn. He served as provincial and rector, stood by troops in two battles, and became the first Jesuit confessor to King Henry III. Readers meet a restless pastor caught between pulpit, court, and a land split by faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-bonner:
Edmund Bonner was Bishop of London through the storms of the English Reformation, born about 1500 and dead in 1569. A lawyer trained at Oxford, he served Cardinal Wolsey and then Henry VIII as a diplomat at Rome and in France. He became Bishop of Hereford in 1538 and was moved to London in 1539, taking up the see in 1540.

Under Henry he tried heretics under the Six Articles. Under Edward VI he lost his see and went to prison in the Marshalsea, and under Mary he took London back in 1553. Under Elizabeth he lost it again and spent his last years a prisoner, dying in 1569. The entry weighs a able, harsh bishop whom friends praised and foes painted as cruel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-tanner:
Edmund Tanner was Bishop of Cork and Cloyne for a brief, perilous term, born about 1526 and dead in 1579. Little is known of his youth beyond a note that he came from the province of Dublin. At Rome in 1565 he joined the Jesuits, studied at Dillingen, and took a doctorate, but failing health made him leave the Society.

Named bishop on 5 November 1574 and consecrated at Rome, he reached Ireland in May 1575 with wide powers for his own diocese and for sees whose bishops were absent. Seized at Clonmel while at work, he was soon freed through a noble earl, then spent four years in secret ministry across the south, giving sacraments at constant risk. He died worn out by hardship in the diocese of Ossory on 4 June 1579.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egbert-archbi:
Egbert was Archbishop of Trier from 977 until his death in December 993, and a restorer of his diocese after the Northmen's raids. Son of Count Theodoric I of Holland and Countess Hildegarde, he was schooled at Egmont Abbey and rose to head the imperial chancery under Archbishop Willigis of Mainz. Records of 976 and 977 already show him in that office.

At Trier he repaired churches, rebuilt abbeys, and revived schools, finishing Saint Mary ad Martyres and building Saint Eucharius outside the city with help from Otto II. He deposed an unworthy abbot at Mettlach, raised Saint Martin's at Munstermaifeld to a collegiate church, and endowed Saint Paulinus. A friend of Otto II, whom he followed to Italy in 983, he first backed Henry the Wrangler, then turned to the young Otto III and his mother Theophano.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth-cel:
Elizabeth Cellier was a noted London midwife caught up in the pretended Meal-Tub Plot of 1680. Little is known of her before her marriage to Peter Cellier, a Frenchman, and her conversion from Anglicanism. In 1678 Titus Oates's fabricated plots filled prisons with Catholics. Her charity led her to visit and relieve prisoners. Her trade brought her among leading Catholic ladies whose alms she often carried.

Among them was the Countess of Powis, who had helped Thomas Dangerfield, a clever impostor. Cut off by the countess, Dangerfield in revenge denounced her and Cellier as plotters, claiming a treason paper lay hidden in a meal-tub in Cellier's house. A search found such a paper, and both women were arrested. Tried for high treason on 11 June 1680, Cellier showed Dangerfield unworthy of belief and was found not guilty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-engelbert-mue:
Engelbert Muehlbacher was an Austrian historian, born at Gresten in 1843 and dead at Vienna in 1903. Schooled at Vienna, his father's home city, he became a novice among the Austin Canons at Saint Florian in 1862 and was ordained in 1867. Historical study already flourished at Saint Florian, and Muehlbacher soon joined it, writing on Gerhoh of Reichersberg and the house's literary output.

In 1872 he studied under Julius Ficker at Innsbruck, took a doctorate in theology two years later, and finished his training at Vienna under Sickel. Ficker gave him the Carolingian part of Boehmer's Regesta, a field where he did lasting work. His masterly edition of the imperial Regesta of the Carolingian age came out between 1880 and 1889 and became a model for the whole new edition. From 1892 he edited Carolingian documents for the Monumenta Germaniae Historica.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistles-of-s:
The Epistles of Saint Peter are treated under authenticity, recipients and occasion, date and place, and analysis. The First Epistle's authenticity, admitted by the early Church, was denied in the past century by critics such as Baur and the Tübingen School, Von Soden, and Harnack. But the entry holds it cannot seriously be questioned. It rests on outside and inside arguments.

Outside arguments cite first- and second-century writings. They include Justin's letter to Lyons and Vienne, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Papias, Polycarp, Clement of Rome, the Didache, and the Pastor of Hermas. The Second Epistle, admitted to be very ancient even by doubters, alludes to an earlier epistle by the Apostle. Tradition is also unanimous for Peter's authorship, from Clement and Origen at Alexandria to Tertullian and Cyprian in Africa and Irenaeus in Gaul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernest-meisso:
Ernest Meissonier was a French painter, born at Lyons on 21 February 1815 and dead at Paris on 31 January 1891. A family friend introduced him to the much frequented studio of Leon Cogniet. These are portraits, generally busts, of the neighbourhood bourgeois, life-size and somewhat commonplace, one of them now at the Louvre.

At the 1834 Salon appeared a more significant picture: the Visit to the Burgomaster's, showing three middle-class Hollanders in eighteenth-century dress, seated at a table, smoking. Here he first tried small genre scenes in period costume, whose pleasing picturesqueness would do much for his fame. But fame was to be delayed for ten years, since Meissonier had to earn his living by illustration. He made vignettes for works today much sought after as romantic editions, including Paul et Virginie and Les Français peints par eux-mêmes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernst-deger:
Ernst Deger was a historical painter, born in Bockenem, Hanover, on 15 April 1809, and dead in Düsseldorf on 27 January 1885. In 1828 he went to the Berlin Academy of Fine Arts to study art under Professor Wach. He was so impressed by pictures of the Düsseldorf School that he placed himself under Schadow, director of the Düsseldorf Academy. Banz says Deger lived in religion, deeply convinced of his art's nobility, painting what he felt, believed, and hoped.

Only twenty-one, he won fame with his Pietà, and thereafter devoted himself to religious painting. Deger was entrusted with the most important frescoes in the church of Saint Apollinaris at Remagen. Fully equipped after four years' study, he returned from Rome in 1843 and began the work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernst-friedri:
Ernst Friedrich Zwirner was an architect, born at Jakobswalde in Silesia in 1802 and dead at Cologne in 1861. He studied at Breslau and Berlin, and worked at Berlin under Schinkel. From 1833 he was the architect of the cathedral at Cologne. Completing the great cathedral at Cologne was the task that would bring the highest honour to the Gothic style. Schinkel's school supplied the men, first Ahlert, and after his death, Zwirner.

Before long Zwirner won more confidence than his predecessor, because he grasped the old masters' work more perceptively. After the restoration was finished, he presented his plans for completing the structure in 1841 to King Frederick William IV, and the work began the next year. However, neither Zwirner nor his successor Voigtel, who completed the work, succeeded in uniting free play of imagination with technical correctness and architectural sequence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernst-maria-l:
Ernst Maria Lieber was born at Camberg in the Duchy of Nassau on 16 November 1838 and died on 31 March 1902. After Dr. Windthorst died, Lieber became the principal leader of the Centre Party in the Reichstag and the Prussian Landtag. From the gymnasium he went on to study law at Würzburg, Munich, Bonn, and Heidelberg, receiving on 30 July 1861 the degree of Doctor of Civil and Canon Law.

A university post was his first aim, but he gave up that purpose and retired to his native town. Meanwhile Nassau's political life drew his active interest. The Catholics of that small state wanted separate schools, as in Prussia, rather than mixed public schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-esprit-flechi:
Esprit Flechier, a bishop, was born at Pernes in France in 1632 and died at Montpellier in 1710. He belonged to the Academy, and his century counted him among its greatest sacred orators, beside Bourdaloue, Bossuet, Fénelon, and Mascaron. His uncle, superior of a religious congregation, guided his earliest studies at Tarascon. Flechier entered that congregation and received holy orders, but he soon left it for Paris, arriving in 1660.

Soon he gained a name as a wit and spiritual writer. A Latin poem honouring Louis XIV first brought him the Court's favour. After his duties as tutor in Caumartin's household, his spare time went to literature and history. Mémoires sur les grands jours tenus a Clermont en 1665, his chief historical work, came from that period. While tutoring the Dauphin, his preaching first made him famous, and his funeral eulogies in particular earned him more than one comparison with Bossuet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-esther:
Esther, from the Hebrew for star, happiness, was Queen of Persia and wife of Assuerus, identified with Xerxes, who reigned 485 to 465 before Christ. She was a Jewess of Benjamin, daughter of Abihail, first named Hadassah. Her family had been deported from Jerusalem to Babylon in 599 before Christ. On her parents' death her uncle Mardochai of Susan adopted her.

Assuerus, angered at Vasthi's refusal to attend a banquet in his third regnal year, divorced her and ordered the kingdom's most attractive maidens brought before him. Among them was Esther, whose rare beauty moved the king to place her on the throne. Her uncle Mardochai remained near the palace to advise her. While at the palace gate he discovered a plot of two eunuchs to kill the king. He revealed it to Esther, who informed the king; the plotters were executed, and Mardochai's service entered the chronicles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-alexa:
Etienne-Alexandre Bernier was a French bishop, born at Daon on 31 October 1762 and dead at Paris on 1 October 1806. He taught theology at Angers, then became pastor of Saint Laud's parish there. During the Revolution he refused the Civil Oath, and his eloquence aroused the peasants of Anjou and Vendée. He then became one of the movement's most important leaders, through his influence with the chiefs and on the military councils. He was called L'Apôtre de la Vendée.

Historians do not agree on his real conduct during the insurrection, especially towards its end. After the 18th Brumaire, Bernier negotiated between the First Consul and the insurgents. When Bonaparte resolved to unite the French nation and the Catholic Church, he chose Bernier to represent the French Government in preparatory negotiations. This choice was happy, for none denies his deep intelligence, untiring activity, and seductive influence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-exeter:
Exeter is an English see Leofric of Crediton chose for his cathedral city in 1050. Devonshire and Cornwall had formed the Bishopric of Sherborne about 703, then split in 900, with the Devon bishop at Crediton. The sees joined again under Leofric as first Bishop of Exeter. The present cathedral began under Bishop Warelhurst in 1112, and its Norman transept towers still stand.

Later bishops built it in decorated style, and Grandisson, bishop for forty-two years, left it much as it stands. Its marks are the transeptal towers, the choir with early glass and a fine throne, and a choir screen dated 1324. Its bishops kept much independence, and the see ranked among England's largest and richest. Henry VIII plundered it, Coverdale was intruded under Edward, and Turberville, restored under Mary, was deprived in 1559 and died in prison.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fall-river:
Fall River is a diocese in Massachusetts, erected on 12 March 1904. Pius X formed it from the diocese of Providence, as the first act of his pontificate. It then held some 309,000 people, of whom about 152,000 were Catholics. William Stang served as first bishop from 1904 to 1907.

Daniel Feehan succeeded him as bishop in 1907 and still held the see at writing. The diocese ran parishes, schools, and charities across its towns. Its clergy and religious orders staffed a growing network of parishes and institutions. The article gives full figures for priests, parishes, schools, and charitable works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Most Holy Redeemer feast thanks God for the work of Redemption. Venice began it after the deadly plague of 1576 had passed. The Senate vowed a splendid temple to the Redeemer and yearly solemn thanksgiving. Palladio designed the church, consecrated in 1592 and placed in Capuchin care.

The Redemptorists keep the feast as a first-class double on the third Sunday of July. They also mark it on 23 October and 25 February each year. Rome assigned it to 23 October by a decree of the Sacred Congregation of Rites in 1830. White vestments mark the joy of Redemption, not red.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-faber:
Felix Faber was a German Dominican and the most famed pilgrim writer of his century. Born about 1441 at Zurich, he studied under Dominicans at Basle. He preached at Ulm and rose to provincial of the German province in 1486. In 1483 he made a pilgrimage to Palestine and Syria.

His Latin Evagatorium describes the Holy Land, Arabia, and Egypt. Scholars prize it as the most distinguished and learned pilgrim account of the fifteenth century. He also wrote a versified pilgrim book and a history of the Swiss to 1489. Faber died at Ulm in 1502, praised by few but copied by many.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-jan:
Ferdinand Janner was a Bavarian theologian, church historian, and archaeologist. Born in 1836, he studied at the Latin school of Amberg, then at Wurzburg and Ratisbon. Ordained in 1858, he taught religion and history at Speyer, then church history at Ratisbon. He became diocesan consultor in 1883 and retired from active life in 1888.

Janner's chief work was a three-volume history of the bishops of Ratisbon. Three volumes carried the story down to the sixteenth century. He also wrote on dogmatic facts, the Holy Land, and medieval builders' lodges. His German Breviary translation ran to four large volumes in 1890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-ste:
Ferdinand Steinmeyer was a Jesuit missionary better known as Father Farmer. Born in Swabia in 1720, he entered the Jesuits in 1743. Hoping for China, he was sent to America in 1752 instead of China. He served at Lancaster, then at St Joseph's Church in Philadelphia.

Farmer rode mission circuits across the east of Pennsylvania and the north and centre of New Jersey. He crossed into New York despite the death penalty for priests under British rule. There he kept the faith alive and all but founded St Peter's Church. A noted philosopher and astronomer, he died in 1786 at Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-von:
Ferdinand von Miller was a Munich bronze founder of world-wide fame. Born in 1813, he learned varied bronze technique in Paris under Soyer and Blus from 1833. He took over his teacher and uncle Stiglmayr's Munich foundry workshop. His casting of the colossal Bavaria brought him his greatest fame.

Miller cast famous Herder, Goethe, and Schiller statues for Weimar. He also cast two Washington monuments for Boston and Richmond respectively. His great 1876 Munich exhibition joined fine art with crafts and trade in harmony. His son followed him, casting famous works in America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-wal:
Ferdinand Walter was a German jurist and strenuous defender of church rights against the state. Born at Wetzlar in 1794, he fought against Napoleon in 1814. He studied law at Heidelberg and taught many branches of law at Bonn from 1819. Blindness forced his retirement from his teaching chair in 1875.

Walter sat in the Prussian National Assembly in 1848 and defended ecclesiastical freedom against civil encroachment. His famous oration of 1849 upheld the Church's independence in its affairs. His Lehrbuch des Kirchenrechts of 1822 became a classic textbook of canon law. Translated widely, it reached a fourteenth edition, prepared by Gerlach, by 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fintan-mundwi:
Fintan Mundwiler was a Swiss-born Benedictine who became abbot of St. Meinrad in Indiana. Born at Dietikon in 1835, he took the habit at Einsiedeln in 1854 and was ordained in 1859. He reached St. Meinrad in 1860 with Martin Marty and taught in its seminary. Elected abbot in 1880, he enlarged the college and founded houses in Arkansas and Louisiana.

He won Rome's leave to erect the Helvetico-American Congregation and became its first president. When fire destroyed the abbey in 1887, he rebuilt it on an even greater scale. He also founded a commercial college at Jasper and helped found a priory in North Dakota. A man of prayer amid temporal cares, he spread devotion to the Blessed Sacrament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florence-of-w:
Florence of Worcester was an English chronicler, a monk of Worcester who died in 1118. His Chronicon ex Chronicis was England's first attempt at a universal chronicle from Creation. Its universal part rests wholly on Marianus Scotus, an Irish monk dead at Mainz about 1082. Florence added English matter from Bede, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and saints' lives.

His use of a lost version of the Chronicle gives his borrowings special value. From 1030 he speaks as an independent authority, in annals running down to 1117. John of Worcester carried the work to 1141, and later writers carried it to 1295. The chronicle remains a very useful record of events in annalistic form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-forgery-forge:
Forgery in canon law means a deliberate tampering with truth meant to deceive and harm a third person while wearing the outward look of honesty. Canon writers divide it by word, by writing, and by deed, with false witness, falsified public papers, and counterfeit money as the chief examples in each class. Using a forged document counts as forgery itself, and the harm is seen as striking public order first, not just one person.

Most of the discussion concerns the falsifying of Apostolic letters, the papers issued by the Roman Curia and bishops' courts. Forging such letters brought excommunication reserved to the pope alone. The entry also notes famous cases, from a forged papal election law dated 1873 to a false 1905 report that priests in South America might marry, which nobody believed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fortunatus-hu:
Fortunatus Hueber, who died at Munich on 12 February 1706, was a Franciscan historian and theologian born at Neustadt on the Danube. He entered the Bavarian province of the Franciscan Reformati in 1654 and rose through a string of offices: general lector in theology, cathedral preacher at Freising from 1670 to 1676. He became provincial of Bavaria in 1677. He later served as definitor-general and chronicler of the order in Germany in 1679, and official writer of the order in 1698.

He also served as confessor to the Poor Clares at St. Jacob on the Anger in Munich, visited Bohemia and Hungary as commissary. He was esteemed by Bavarian dukes and the Elector of Cologne. He left more than twenty works. Best known is the Menologium Franciscanum of 1698, lives of Franciscan saints and blesseds arranged by month and day, alongside a German chronicle of the order's history in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-a-pau:
Francis a Paula Triesnecker, born at Kirchberg on the Wagram in Lower Austria on 2 April 1745 and dead at Vienna on 29 January 1817. He was a Jesuit astronomer of exacting accuracy. He entered the Society at sixteen, studied philosophy at Vienna and mathematics at Tyrnau, taught at Jesuit colleges, and after the suppression completed his theology at Graz and was ordained. He soon won a name as mathematician and astronomer, became assistant to Father Max Hell at the Vienna Observatory, and succeeded him as director in 1792.

He held that post for the rest of his life, observing sun, moon, planets, and stars in spite of ill health into advanced age. With Burg he edited the Vienna Ephemerides after Hell's death. Between 1787 and 1806 he published there his tables of Mercury, Mars, Venus, and the sun, most of his micrometrical observations, and in 1802 his new tables of the moon's motions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-asbur:
Francis Asbury Baker, born at Baltimore on 30 March 1820 and dead on 4 April 1865, was a priest of the Paulist Fathers whose conversion bridged American Protestant and Catholic life. The son of a noted Baltimore physician, he graduated from Princeton in 1839, took orders in the Episcopal Church in 1846, and rose to rector of St. Luke's, Baltimore, winning rank at once as an eloquent preacher of refinement, wealth, and engaging personality.

The Oxford Movement, with its return to primitive and patristic theology, moved him deeply, and though breaking intimate ties cost him much, he made his profession of Catholic faith in April 1853. Entering the Redemptorists and ordained a Catholic priest, he later shared with companions in founding the Paulist Institute for English-speaking missions, giving it a tradition of exact rubrics and splendid ceremonial. He died of typhoid pneumonia caught while ministering to the sick.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-coste:
Francis Coster, born at Mechlin on 16 June 1532 and dead at Brussels on 16 December 1619, was a Jesuit theologian of the Counter-Reformation. Received into the Society of Jesus by St. Ignatius himself on 7 November 1552, he was sent young to Cologne to lecture on Scripture and astronomy, and in 1564 Cologne University made him Doctor of Philosophy and Theology. By word and writing he defended Catholic teaching against heresy and brought many back to the Church.

He served two terms as provincial of Belgium and one of the Rhine province, and attended three general congregations of his order. His catalogue lists forty-two works, including ascetical writings, meditations on the Blessed Virgin, and sermons for every Sunday. Most famous was his Enchiridion of the chief controversies of religion, published at Cologne from 1585, revised repeatedly, translated widely, and defended against Protestant attackers such as Marbach, Gommar, and Osiander.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-de-sa:
Francis de Sales Brunner, baptised Nicolaus Joseph, was born at Muenliswil in Switzerland on 10 January 1795 and died at Schellenberg in Liechtenstein on 29 December 1859. He founded the Swiss-American congregation of Benedictines. Entering the Benedictine monastery of Maria Stein in 1812, he took vows two years later and was ordained in 1819. After ten years he sought a stricter life with the Trappists of Oehlemberg, but that house was suppressed.

Offered a mission to China that was recalled before departure, he instead founded a school for poor boys at Lowenberg castle. On a pilgrimage to Rome with his mother in 1833 both joined the Archconfraternity of the Most Precious Blood. His mother gathered pious women for perpetual adoration, orphan education, and vestments for poor churches, founding the Sisters of the Most Precious Blood. She died in 1836, and the community later came to America under its second superior, Sister Clara.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-josep:
Francis, Joseph, and Paul Mezger were three learned Benedictine brothers of St. Peter's monastery in Salzburg and professors at Salzburg University. Francis, the eldest, born at Ingolstadt on 25 October 1632 and dead at Salzburg on 11 December 1701, took vows in 1651 and was ordained in 1657. He taught philosophy and moral theology at Salzburg, then at Ettal in Bavaria, before serving as master of novices until his death. His philosophical treatises and translations from French Capuchin and Maurist authors fill the entry's first part.

Joseph and Paul, his younger brothers, taught and wrote in the same Benedictine school. They produced works on philosophy, theology, history, and academic oratory, including Joseph's history of Salzburg and Paul's sacred history of the Hebrew people. Together the three show the strength of Salzburg's Benedictine university in the later seventeenth century. There monks combined teaching, translation, and publication in the service of Catholic learning across the German lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-richa:
Francis Richard Wegg-Prosser, born at Newnham Courtney in Oxfordshire on 19 June 1824 and dead near Hereford on 16 August 1911, was an English convert, landowner, and Catholic layman. Only son of Prebendary Francis Haggit, he was educated at Eton and Balliol College, Oxford, graduating first class in mathematics in 1845. He sat as a member of Parliament from 1847 to 1852. In 1849 he inherited his great-uncle's Belmont estate and took the name Wegg-Prosser. In 1852 Bishop Grant of Southwark received him into the Catholic Church, an event that changed his career entirely.

He built a handsome church on his estate, which became the pro-cathedral of the Newport diocese by agreement with the bishop and the English Benedictines. He gave adjoining land for a monastery as their novitiate and house of studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-silve:
Francis Silvester, a Dominican theologian born at Ferrara about 1474 and dead at Rennes on 19 September 1526, rose to lead his order in the first years of the Reformation. He joined the Dominicans at fourteen, became a master in theology in 1516, served as prior at Ferrara and Bologna, and in 1519 was chosen vicar-general of the Lombard congregation.

On 3 June 1525, at the general chapter at Rome, he was elected master general. As general he visited almost all the convents of Italy, France, and Belgium, reviving primitive fervour and discipline, and was planning a visitation of Spain when illness carried him away. His monumental commentary on the Summa contra Gentiles of St. Thomas, published at Paris in 1552, heads a long list of works, including explanations of Aristotle and a 1525 defence of Roman institutions against the new evangelical liberty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-xavie:
Francis Xavier Schmalzgrueber, born at Griesbach in Bavaria on 9 October 1663 and dead at Dillingen on 7 November 1735. He was a Jesuit canonist whose judgment and clearness still command esteem. Entering the Society in 1679, he studied at Ingolstadt, taking doctorates in theology and canon law. He taught humanities at Munich, Dillingen, and Neuburg, philosophy at Mindelheim, Augsburg, and Ingolstadt, and dogmatic theology at Innsbruck and Lucerne.

From 1703 to 1716, with a two-year break teaching moral theology, he held the canon law chair, alternating between Dillingen and Ingolstadt. Twice chancellor of Dillingen University, twice censor of Jesuit books at Rome, and prefect of studies at Munich, he poured his learning into his chief work, Jus Ecclesiasticum Universum. It was first published at Ingolstadt and last at Rome in twelve quarto volumes in 1843 to 1845, with compendiums at Augsburg in 1747 that spread his teaching widely.

Francis Xavier Weninger, born at Wildhaus in Styria on 31 October 1805 and dead at Cincinnati on 29 June 1888. He was a Jesuit missionary and author who preached across America for forty years. A priest and doctor of theology when he joined the Society of Jesus in 1832, he taught theology, history, and Hebrew at Innsbruck from 1841. The Revolution of 1848 blocked his work at home. He sailed for the United States.

There he visited every state, preaching to crowds in English, French, or German as suited his hearers. He delivered nearly a thousand sermons in 1854 alone and about forty-five missions in 1864. His pen matched his voice. He wrote forty works in German, sixteen in English, eight in French, and three in Latin. They include a Manual of the Catholic Religion, Easter in Heaven, and volumes of sermons published at Mainz between 1881 and 1886. The entry presents a tireless preacher of the immigrant Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franciscan-or:
The Franciscan Order is the family of religious foundations, for men and women, that profess the Rule of St. Francis of Assisi in one of its several forms. Tradition says Francis founded three orders. They are the Friars Minor, the Poor Ladies or Clares, and the Brothers and Sisters of Penance, counted as First, Second, and Third Orders. The division is recorded in the Office for 4 October.

The First Order dates from 1209, when Innocent III gave unwritten approval to Francis's simple rule for his first companions. It was later rewritten and solemnly confirmed by Honorius III on 29 November 1223, the rule still professed throughout the First Order. The Second Order, the Poor Ladies, grew around Clare at Assisi, and the Third Order gathered lay penitents of both sexes. Later divisions, reforms, and branches, from Observants to Capuchins, all claim that same Franciscan rule, and the entry maps how they relate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-jacq:
Francois Jacquier, born at Vitry-le-Francois on 7 June 1711 and dead at Rome on 3 July 1788, was a French Franciscan mathematician and physicist. An ecclesiastic tutor soon saw his bent for science and mathematics. At sixteen he entered the Friars Minor, completing his studies at the French convent of La Trinite du Mont in Rome. With his superiors' leave he specialised in mathematics, and for diversion studied ancient languages, growing so proficient in Hebrew and speaking Greek as if it were his mother tongue.

 The King of Sardinia named him physics professor at Turin in 1745. But Cardinal Valenti, eager to keep so learned a man at Rome, gave him the experimental physics chair at the Roman College. There he remained in continual demand as a teacher and scholar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-le-m:
Francois Le Mercier, born at Paris on 4 October 1604 and dead at Martinique on 12 June 1690, was one of the early Jesuit missionaries of New France. He entered the Society at Paris in 1620 and taught every class of grammar and humanities in the Jesuit college of the capital. After philosophy and theology he was sent to Canada, arriving on 20 July 1635. Three days after landing at Quebec he set out with Father Pijart for the Huron country, reaching it on 13 August, and gave fifteen uninterrupted years to the Huron mission.

 Stationed at Ihonatiria, Ossossane, and Sainte-Marie, he left Huronia only after the Iroquois laid waste the country and the mission was abandoned on 10 June 1650. Returning to Quebec, he later served in the islands, and we owe him nine annual Relations, including those of the Huron mission for 1637 and 1638.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-phil:
Francois-Philippe Charpentier, born at Blois in 1734 and dead there on 22 July 1817, was a French engraver, inventor, and mechanician whose machines revolutionised reproductive art.

His fame rests less on his own burin or aquatint than on invention. His purely mechanical process for engraving in aquatint and in colour copied wash drawings and watercolours with marvellous exactness. Sketches by great masters reached ordinary people. Count Caylus was among the first to use the machine. Louis XVI made him Royal Mechanician with a Louvre studio, where he melted metals without fire by burning mirror, invented a widely adopted fire engine, and in 1771 a machine for drilling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-xavi:
Francois Xavier de Feller, born at Brussels on 18 August 1735 and dead at Ratisbon on 22 May 1802, was a Jesuit author and apologist of prodigious memory. Educated at the Jesuit college at Luxemburg, he studied philosophy and exact sciences at Reims, joined the Society at Tournai, and taught humanities and edited his pupils' Latin poems as Musae Leodienses. He then taught theology at Luxemburg and Tyrnau in Hungary. After the suppression he preached at Liege and Luxemburg until the French army drove him to Paderborn in 1794.

Two years later the Prince of Hohenlohe brought him to Bavaria, to the court of the Prince-Bishop of Freising and Ratisbon, where he divided his time between Freising, Ratisbon, and Berchtesgaden. His chief work, a philosophical catechism defending Christianity against its enemies, first appeared under the pen name Flexier de Reval in 1772, and he attacked Febronius's anti-papal tenets in 1770.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-anton-s:
Franz Anton Staudenmaier, born at Donzdorf in Wurttemberg on 11 September 1800 and died at Freiburg im Breisgau on 19 January 1856, was a leading theologian of the Catholic Tubingen school. Schooled at Gmund and Ellwangen, he studied theology and philosophy at Tubingen from 1822 to 1826 under Drey, Herbst, Hirscher, and Mohler, entered Rottenburg seminary, and was ordained on 15 September 1827. After a year as parish priest he became tutor at Tubingen's Wilhelmsstift in 1828 and professor of dogmatic theology at Giessen in 1830. There with Kuhn he gave the new faculty its brief prosperity.

In 1837 he became professor of dogmatic theology at Freiburg and from 1843 a cathedral canon. With colleagues he founded journals at Giessen and Freiburg, the Yearbooks for Theology and Christian Philosophy and the Journal for Theology, which won high scholarly standing largely through his contributions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-grillpa:
Franz Grillparzer, born at Vienna on 15 January 1791 and dead on 21 January 1872, was an Austrian poet and dramatist who ranks beside Schiller and Kleist. After desultory home schooling and the gymnasium he studied law and philosophy at university, but literature and music drew him more, and at sixteen, under Schiller's influence, he tried dramatic writing. In 1813 he entered the civil service in customs, an unhappy official life under ill-will, distrust, and rigid censorship, rising slowly and never beyond director of the Court Chamber archives in 1832.

His mother's suicide in 1819 prostrated him. A furlough took him to Italy in the Empress's retinue, where his poem on the ruins of the Campo Vaccino offended the Catholic party and drew the emperor's censure. The setback dogged his career. His fame rests on his dramas, edited in many complete editions, with letters and diaries published by Glossy and Sauer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-hetting:
Franz Hettinger, born at Aschaffenburg on 13 January 1819 and died at Wurzburg on 26 January 1890, was a Catholic theologian who defended the faith by reason. He attended his native gymnasium and academy, took philosophy and early theology there, then entered Wurzburg seminary in 1839, following Bishop Stahl, his former teacher of doctrine and dogma. On Stahl's advice he went to Rome in 1841 for four years at the German College, was ordained by Cardinal Patrizi in 1843, and took his doctorate in theology in 1845.

 Back home he served as chaplain at Alzenau in 1845, assistant at Wurzburg seminary in 1847, subregent in 1852, and professor of the church fathers and of first courses in 1856. He became ordinary professor in 1857. He then taught apologetics and preaching, with charge of the seminary for preachers, and his Apology of Christianity, edited repeatedly after his death, remains his monument.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-ignaz-v:
Franz Ignaz von Streber, born at Reisbach in Lower Bavaria on 11 February 1758 and died at Munich on 26 April 1841. He was a numismatist, a coin scholar, and theologian who saved Bavaria's coin cabinet. Made court chaplain in 1783, auxiliary bishop in 1821, and cathedral provost of Munich in 1822, he had been appointed curator of the elector's coin cabinet as early as 1782. His task was to unite the Mannheim, or Palatine, collection with the Munich, or Bavarian, Wittelsbach collection, disordered since the Thirty Years' War, and arrange the combined cabinet in scientific order.

War forced him to carry off and hide the cabinet five times, rearranging it anew each time. He wrote a history of Bavaria's royal coin cabinet and several treatises on Bavarian and Greek coins, most in the Munich Academy's transactions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-michael:
Franz Michael Permaneder, born at Traunstein in Bavaria on 12 August 1794 and dead at Ratisbon on 10 October 1862, was a German canonist, an expert in church law. He studied theology and jurisprudence at Landshut and was ordained priest at Ratisbon in 1818. He became professor of church history and canon law at the Freising Lyceum in 1834, and in 1847 joined the theological faculty of Munich University.

He contributed to the first edition of the Kirchenlexicon, the great German church encyclopaedia. He wrote a handbook of generally valid Catholic church law with constant reference to Germany, published at Landshut in 1846. He also wrote a work on the church's building burden at Munich in 1853. An incomplete patristic library at Landshut between 1841 and 1844 and a continuation of the annals of Ingolstadt University at Munich in 1859 complete the list. The entry presents a steady, useful scholar of the sources and literature of canon law.

Franz Michael Vierthaler, born at Mauerkirchen in Upper Austria on 25 September 1758 and died at Vienna on 3 October 1827, was a distinguished Austrian pedagogue, a reformer of teacher training. His parents were poor. He sang as a choirboy at Michaelbeuren Abbey and at Salzburg, attended the gymnasium there, and took law at university in 1776 and 1777, though classical languages were his favourite study. In 1783 he became instructor at Salzburg's Virgilian college for nobles.

Teaching history led him to write a Philosophical History of Mankind in seven volumes between 1787 and 1819. Its first volume won him in 1790 the directorship of Salzburg's new seminary for teachers, founded to improve primary schools. Ahead of his time, he championed practical teacher training, natural science, physical training, and opposition to corporal punishment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-pfanner:
Franz Pfanner, an abbot born at Langen in Vorarlberg in 1825 and dead at Emmaus in South Africa on 24 May 1909, was a Trappist founder and missionary to southern Africa.

Professed at Marienwald in November 1864 and made sub-prior weeks later, he reorganised Tre Fontane at Rome in 1866. He then founded Mariastern in Bosnia in 1869, raised to an abbey in 1879. That year Bishop Richards of the Eastern Vicariate of the Cape sought Trappists to evangelise the Kafirs and teach them work. When all others declined, Abbot Franz gave up his settled abbey for South Africa, reaching Dunbrody at the end of July 1880. Drought, winds, and baboons drove him on to found Mariannhill, whose monks, shortly before his death, became the Missionary Religious of Mariannhill under a milder rule for missionary work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-quirin-:
Franz Quirin von Kober, born of simple country folk on 6 March 1821 at Warthausen in Wurttemberg and dead at Tubingen on 25 January 1897, was a German canonist and teacher. Schooled at Biberach and the Rottenburg training seminary at Ehingen, he studied at Tubingen's Wilhelmsstift from 1840 to 1844 and was ordained at Rottenburg on 4 September 1845.

He became extraordinary professor of Catholic theology on 28 January 1851, teaching methods, didactics, and Paul, and ordinary professor of canon law and teaching on 8 September 1857. With good method in history and law he wrote fine works on church ban in 1857, suspension of church servants in 1862, and deposition and degradation in 1867. Further studies of penance, marriage, and church discipline made him a standard guide for German canonists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-seraph-:
Franz Seraph Streber, nephew of Franz Ignaz von Streber, was born at Deutenkofen in Lower Bavaria on 26 February 1805 and died at Munich on 21 November 1864, a numismatist and archaeologist. He first studied theology and philosophy, then archaeology and numismatics, and in 1830 his Erlangen doctoral dissertation treated the genealogy of Nuremberg's burgraves. In 1827 he became clerk of the royal coin cabinet, assistant in 1830, and curator in 1841. He was professor of archaeology at Munich University in 1835, twice its rector, and member of the Munich Academy in 1854.

He also worked on Vienna's numismatic collection, preparing a critical catalogue of eighteen thousand Greek coins. His numismatic and iconographic lexicon held drawings of about six thousand Greek coins from Vienna and Munich. His 1834 work on certain Greek coins corrected false designations and won a Paris Academy prize, as did his investigation of rainbow patina, which he first recognised as Celtic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-d:
Franz Xaver Dieringer, born at Rangendingen in Hohenzollern-Hechingen on 22 August 1811 and dead at Veringendorf on 8 September 1876, was a German Catholic theologian who restored Bonn's theological faculty. He studied theology at Tubingen and was ordained at Freiburg on 19 September 1835. He taught priests-in-training there, became professor of dogma at Speyer's school in 1840 and of philosophy at its lyceum in 1841. In spring 1843 he became ordinary professor of dogma and homiletics at Bonn, with inspection of its training school.

 At his instance a school for preachers and catechists opened in 1844, which he led in preaching. He founded and conducted the Catholic Journal for Science and Art in 1844 against the Hermesians' periodical, continuing it as a Catholic quarterly from 1847 to 1849. Later writings covered Kleutgen and Tertullian's teaching on the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-xaver-v:
Franz Xaver von Baader, born at Munich in 1765 and dead there on 23 May 1841, was a German Catholic philosopher who answered Kant, Hegel, and Schopenhauer from mysticism and faith. Entering Ingolstadt University at sixteen and taking his doctorate at nineteen, he studied medicine two more years at Vienna and assisted his father, the court physician. He then turned to mining engineering, travelled Germany, and spent about five years in England from 1791 to 1796, meeting Bohme's mysticism and the opposite empiricism of Hume and Hartley.

Godwin's Enquiry concerning Political Justice turned him to moral and social questions and to Kant. For Kant's ethical autonomism, the claim that human reason alone, apart from God, is the supreme rule of conduct, he felt only disgust. Calling it devil's morality, he declared that were Satan visibly to reappear, he could preach nothing worse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-wil:
Frederick William Faber, an Oratorian and devotional writer, shaped English Catholic worship with his hymns and sermons. Born at Calverley in Yorkshire in 1814, he studied at Harrow and Balliol and took Anglican orders in 1839. He threw himself into the Tractarian movement, served as rector of Elton, and was received into the Catholic Church in November 1845, weeks after Newman.

Faber founded a small community at Cotton Hall, then placed himself under Newman as a novice of the Oratory. Sent to London in 1849, he built the Oratory around poor schools, nightly services, and hymns sung in procession. His hymns joined sound doctrine with warm feeling and true poetic gift. He also issued the Lives of the Modern Saints, a series of forty-nine short lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-lud:
Friedrich Werner, a convert, poet, and pulpit orator born at Königsberg in 1768, lived a restless life before finding the Church. A disciple of Kant in youth, he clerked twelve years in the War Office and married and divorced three times. In 1804 his mother and his friend Mnioch died on the same day, a double grief that titled his best-known tragedy, Der 24 Februar.

After years of wandering, Werner was received into the Catholic Church at Rome in April 1810. Ordained in 1814, he preached at Vienna during the Congress to crowded, curious audiences. His sermons drew notice for their odd power. His plays, from Sons of the Valley to The Cross on the Baltic, show real dramatic gift without the self-command to make it last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-wil:
Friedrich Wilhelm Weber, a Westphalian doctor, deputy, and poet, won fame with an epic named for thirteen linden trees. Born at Alhausen in 1813, he studied medicine at Greifswald and Berlin, then practiced twenty-six years at Driburg. Honors followed: a medical title in 1863, a Munich doctorate, and the Order of the Red Eagle. He sat in the Prussian House of Deputies for the Centre Party until 1893.

His Dreizehnlinden of 1878 spread across Germany and beyond in translation and stage versions, earning him the name Dreizehnlinden-Weber. His Goliath of 1892, reprinted some thirty times, stands higher in poetic worth. He also carried Scandinavian and English verse into German, and his late poems, Autumn Leaves, appeared after his death in 1894.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frobenius-for:
Frobenius Forster, prince-abbot of Saint Emmeram at Ratisbon, opened a golden age of learning in his monastery. Born in Upper Bavaria in 1709, he took Benedictine vows in 1728, taught philosophy and Scripture, and became abbot in July 1762. He stood among the first churchmen to wed scholastic thought with the new systems of Descartes, Leibniz, and Wolff, keeping his own judgment throughout.

Forster filled his house with science, founding cabinets of physics, minerals, and coins, and drew scholars from across Germany to its courses. He brought a Maurist teacher of Eastern tongues to Ratisbon for four years. His chief book remains his careful two-volume edition of Alcuin's works, issued in 1777 and later reprinted in Migne's Latin Patrology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gallus-jacob-:
Gallus Jacob Baumgartner, a Swiss statesman born in 1797, shaped modern Saint Gallen and nearly reshaped Switzerland. Schooled at Saint Gallen, he studied law at Fribourg and Vienna, was wrongly arrested there in 1819, and rose from cantonal archivist to chancellor. In 1831 he became Landammann, chief magistrate of Saint Gallen, holding the post until 1846.

Baumgartner pressed for a tightly united Swiss republic on the American model, with cantons keeping wide freedom, and he improved roads and waterways. His plan to cut the Church from Rome and rule it by the state, voiced at Baden in 1834, met clerical resistance. When his friends sacked Aargau's monasteries in 1841, he saw where his policy led, changed sides, and later founded Saint Gallen's bishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspar-de-cra:
Gaspar de Crayer, a Flemish painter born at Antwerp in 1582, rose to court painter at Brussels and retired to Ghent. A pupil of Raphael van Coxcie, he soon outstripped his master, won a pension from the governor of the Low Countries, and filled Brussels churches and halls with his work. He later gave up the court post for Ghent, where his finest pictures were made.

Rubens is said to have praised his Centurion and Christ for the Afflighem refectory, saying none would surpass Crayer. Though no profound genius, he drew perfectly and colored with a clear freshness matched in his school only by Van Dyck. His Death of the Virgin at Madrid leads his work, and his mounted portrait of the Cardinal Infant ranks first among his portraits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-chapt:
A General Chapter is the assembly of representatives of a whole religious order or congregation, named for the chapter of the rule read at its daily meetings. Conventual, provincial, and general mark its scope, and the general chapter gathers the entire family of houses. The entry traces the idea from its germ to its settled modern form.

Benedict of Aniane sketched a confederation early in the ninth century, Cluny revived the pattern a hundred years later, and daughter centers from Fleury to Fulda spread it.
