The Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 fixed the congregational system, and chapters have met ever since, yearly at Cîteaux, every three or four years elsewhere. They elect generals, settle discipline, hear appeals, and guard constitutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-general-sir-w:
Sir William Francis Butler, an Irish soldier and writer born in Tipperary in 1838, served the empire from Canada to Egypt. Schooled by Jesuits at Tullabeg, he took a commission in the 69th Regiment in 1858, visited Saint Helena out of reverence for Napoleon, and sailed for Madras. The famine of 1847 and its evictions stayed among his earliest memories.

Wolseley sent Butler to Canada's Red River country in 1867 and 1870, a winter journey told in The Great Lone Land of 1872. In Ashanti in 1873 he led Akim allies toward Coomassie, a failure he owned in Akim-foo. He married the battle painter Elizabeth Thompson in 1877, missed fighting in the Zulu War by ill luck, and served hard in Egypt in 1882. Gladstone once barred him as private secretary for being Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-chau:
Geoffrey Chaucer, the English poet born in London between 1340 and 1345, stands as the father of English verse. Son of vintner John Chaucer, he served as page to Elizabeth de Burgh from 1357. He followed Prince Lionel to France and was captured and ransomed by the king before the Peace of Brétigny in 1360. A life pension followed in 1367, and diplomatic missions filled his middle years.

Italy in 1372 and 1373 turned his art, likely bringing him to Petrarch at Florence or Padua. Troilus and Criseyde came from 1379 to 1383, then the Parliament of Fowls, the House of Fame, and the Legend of Good Women. The Canterbury Tales grew from 1386 past 1390, first printed by Caxton about 1476. He died in London on October 25, 1400.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georg-friedri:
Georg Friedrich Daumer, a German poet and philosopher born at Nuremberg in 1800, traveled from Pietism to pantheism to Rome. Schooled under Hegel at his city's gymnasium, he entered Erlangen for theology in 1817, swapped it for philosophy, and taught at Nuremberg until ill health pensioned him in 1832. His early books attacked Christian doctrine and proposed a new religion of love and peace in 1850.

Settled at Frankfurt, Daumer changed course and publicly embraced the Catholic faith at Mainz in 1858, defending it thereafter against Strauss and others. His best work remains his poetry: Hafis, graceful free versions of the Persian singer, many set by Brahms, and Marian verse from his later years. His Mahomed of 1848 assailed the hypocrisy he once tied to orthodox faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georg-raphael:
Georg Raphael Donner, an Austrian sculptor born at Essling in 1692, brought classic calm to an age of rococo excess. His fancy caught fire at Heiligenkreuz, he trained at Vienna's Academy, entered imperial service in 1724, and passed to Prince Esterházy in 1729. Lifelike and noble in conception, he sometimes prized elegance over character, yet stands as South Germany's classic answer to mannerism.

Donner carved Charles VI for the Belvedere, an Andromeda and Perseus fountain for Vienna's old town hall, and reliefs of Hagar and the Samaritan Woman. At Pressburg he raised Saint Martin on horseback and adorned the primate's burial chapel. His fame rests on the Neuer Markt fountain of 1738 and 1739, where Providence crowns four sporting children pouring Austria's four Danube rivers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georg-ratzing:
Georg Ratzinger, a political economist and social reformer born in Lower Bavaria in 1844, fought for Christian ethics in economics and politics. Schooled at Passau and Munich, he was ordained in 1867, took his doctorate in 1868, and mixed parish work with journalism at Würzburg and Munich. He sat in the Bavarian Diet from 1875 and the Reichstag from 1877 as a Centre man.

Ratzinger later left the Centre for the Peasants' Union, returning to the Diet in 1893 and the Reichstag in 1898. His History of Poor Relief won a prize in 1868, and his Political Economy on Its Moral Foundations, revised in 1895, set Christian ethics against Adam Smith's classical system. His Bavarian history researches, gathered in 1898, and his defense of the peasant estate round out a busy pen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georg-scherer:
Georg Scherer, a Jesuit pulpit orator born in the Tyrol in 1540, kept Austria Catholic by preaching for over forty years. He entered the Society in 1559 and was famed as a preacher even before ordination. From 1577 to 1600 he served as court preacher to Archduke Matthias, then led Vienna's Jesuit college in 1590 before moving to Linz, where he died of apoplexy in 1605.

Scherer fought Tübingen professors courting Greek schismatics, answered Lutheran divines like Osiander, and roused his people against the Turks. On witches he held, with his age, that the state might kill them, but urged spiritual arms, exorcism and prayer, over bodily torment, a view his general Acquaviva disliked. His eloquence won many converts, among them the future Cardinal Khlesl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-cassan:
George Cassander, a Flemish humanist and theologian born in 1513, labored for peace between Catholics and Protestants. Schooled at Louvain, he taught letters at Bruges in 1541, quit over pro-Reformation stir, traveled with a friend's purse, and settled at Cologne in 1549. There he left classics for Bible and church questions, publishing hymns and a liturgy that the Index condemned.

His anonymous Duty of a Pious Man in Religious Division, issued in 1561 for the Poissy colloquy, angered both sides, Calvin most loudly. Cassander split doctrine into fundamental and lesser articles, defended private judgment, and urged communion under both kinds for the laity. His Consultation for Maximilian II in 1564 pleased neither camp. He likely died in 1566 still submitting to the Catholic Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-elder:
George Elder, a Kentucky educator born in 1793, founded and led the West's great Catholic college. Son of Maryland settlers at Hardin's Creek, he was schooled largely by his Scripture-wise father and entered Mount Saint Mary's at Emmitsburg at sixteen. With his friend William Byrne he studied theology at Baltimore and was ordained at Bardstown in September 1819.

Bishop Flaget charged Elder with founding a lay college, first a day school in the seminary basement. A separate building raised between 1820 and 1823 ranked among the West's largest and best equipped. Fifty southern students in 1825 began its long southern patronage. Elder served as president, with a break from 1827 to 1830, edited Louisville's Catholic Advocate, and wrote Letters to Brother Jonathan. Overwork at the 1838 college fire brought his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-joseph:
George Joseph Vogler, a theorist, composer, and organist born at Würzburg in 1749, taught two of the century's great opera men. Son of a violin maker, he schooled with Jesuits, quit Martini at Bologna after six weeks, and spent six months with Vallotti at Padua. From these short studies he forged his own theory system, to his teachers' displeasure. Ordained after Roman theology studies, he returned to Mannheim in 1775 as court chaplain and school founder.

Vogler's Mannheim treatises on singing, theory, and composition drew fire for iconoclasm, and his portable organ-orchestrion, built to a simplified plan, drew crowds across Europe for his virtuosity and showmanship. His large sacred and secular output is now largely forgotten. Settling at Darmstadt as court conductor in 1807, he founded a music school whose pupils included Weber and Meyerbeer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-michae:
George Michael Pachtler, a controversial and educational writer born in Württemberg in 1825, documented the Jesuit school system for posterity. Schooled at Tübingen and ordained in 1848, he taught at Ellwangen, entered the Society of Jesus in 1856, and taught at Feldkirch. He served as chaplain to Tyrolese troops in 1866 and to German volunteers serving the papal army in 1869 to 1870.

After the Society's 1872 expulsion from Germany, Pachtler lived in Holland and Austria and became first editor of Voices from Maria Laach. He wrote ably on the Vatican Council, the Roman question, labor, Freemasonry, and Liberalism, and his 1883 reform of the gymnasia drew Germany's leading educators. His four volumes on the Ratio Studiorum, 1887 to 1894, remain the standard source on Jesuit schooling in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-oliver:
George Oliver, a priest and antiquary born in Surrey in 1781, spent his life at Exeter and wrote Devon's history. After Sedgley Park he entered Stonyhurst in 1796, taught humanities five years, and was ordained in 1806. Sent the next year to the former Jesuit mission at Exeter, he stayed there for life. He was no Jesuit himself, since the Society then had no canonical standing in England, and he lived and died a secular priest.

Oliver became a known authority on Devonshire history and antiquities, his industry and judgment praised despite conclusions later rejected. His best-known Catholic work, Collections, gathers biographical notices of western clergy and laity. On the Plymouth chapter's erection in 1852 he was named provost, though retired. His books run from Monasteries of Devon in 1820 to Lives of the Bishops of Exeter in 1861.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-porter:
George Porter, Archbishop of Bombay, spent a Jesuit lifetime in classrooms before his Indian see. Born at Exeter in 1825 of Scottish descent, he was schooled at Stonyhurst and joined the Society in 1841. After philosophy at Stonyhurst and teaching there and at Liverpool's Saint Francis Xavier's, he studied theology at Saint Beuno's in Wales. Ordained in 1856, he finished studies in Rome under Passaglia and Schrader.

Porter taught dogmatic theology four years at Saint Beuno's, then served as Liverpool rector, London master of novices from 1873, Farm Street rector in 1881, and assistant to the general at Fiesole. In December 1886 he became Archbishop of Bombay, where he died in September 1889. His collected Letters of 1891 show a versatile mind and skill in direction, and his Priest's Manual for the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass dates from 1858.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georges-etien:
Georges-Etienne Cartier, a French Canadian statesman born on the Richelieu in 1814, built Confederation to save French Canada. Schooled at Montreal College, he fought at Saint Denis in the 1837 rebellion and fled across the Vermont frontier, reported frozen to death. Practicing law in Montreal, he entered Parliament for Verchères in 1849 behind Lafontaine and Baldwin, founders of responsible government.

Cartier served four times as attorney-general of Lower Canada and as premier in 1858. He drove the Grand Trunk Railway of 1852, the 1854 settlement of seigniorial tenure, Victoria Bridge of 1860, normal schools, and the 1865 civil code. To avert legislative union he brokered Confederation, securing Quebec's autonomy and minority rights. He then helped add Manitoba, British Columbia, and the North-West, and launch the Canadian Pacific Railway. Made a baronet in 1868, he led his province uncontested for twenty-five years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gobban-saer:
Gobban Saer, or Gobban the Builder, is regarded in traditional lore as the greatest Irish architect of the seventh century, popularly canonized as Saint Gobban. Born at Turvey near Malahide in County Dublin about 560, he built churches, oratories, and bell-towers for many Irish saints. A Catholic Encyclopedia article insists he is historical, not mythical, despite the wonders told of him.

An eighth-century Irish poem, now in a monastery in Carinthia, already alludes to him. The Life of Saint Abban prophesies that his fame as a builder in wood and stone would last in Ireland to the end of time. He stood far ahead of his age as an architect and took commissions all over Ireland. Innumerable stories of him still circulate in the Irish tongue, and he labored as late as 645.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gottfried-lum:
Gottfried Lumper was a Benedictine patristic writer born on 6 February 1747 at Füssen in Bavaria. He died on 8 March 1800 at the Abbey of Saint George at Billingen in the Black Forest. He entered the abbey school young, took the habit, made solemn profession in 1764, and was ordained priest in 1771. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a man of irreproachable character and untiring diligence.

He never left the monastery except to help in the sacred ministry. He served as director of the gymnasium, professor of church history and dogmatic theology, and later prior. All his spare time went to early Christian literature. Catholic Germany owes him grateful remembrance above all for his thirteen-volume Historia theologico-critica of the Fathers and church writers of the first three centuries, published at Augsburg from 1783 to 1789.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregor-aichin:
Gregor Aichinger was an organist and composer of sacred music, born at Ratisbon in 1565, who died at Augsburg on 21 January 1628. As early as 1590 he was organist to the patrician Jacob Fugger at Augsburg, and he visited Rome in 1599. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a priest shaped by the Venice school and by Gabrieli.

Returning to Augsburg about 1601, he re-entered the Fugger service and produced many works. They include Liturgica of 1603, Sacrae Cantiones of 1590 for four to ten voices, Tricinia Mariana of 1598, and Fasciculus Sacrarum Harmoniarum of 1606. Proske praised him for joining solid German art with refined Italian forms. Warmth and tenderness marked him, with deep devotion, and, in his longest pieces, grandeur and solemnity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorius-tho:
Gregorius Thomas Ziegler was Bishop of Linz, born at Kirchheim near Augsburg on 7 March 1770, who died at Linz on 15 April 1852. He joined the Benedictines at Wiblingen in 1788, was ordained in 1793, and taught in Benedictine houses until he became prior in 1802. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a bishop who fought government encroachment.

After Wiblingen's suppression in 1806 he moved with confreres to Tiniec in Poland and taught theology at Cracow. Then he served as professor of church history at Linz from 1809 to 1815 and of theology at Vienna to 1822. He became Bishop of Tiniec in 1822, moved his see to Tarnow, and was promoted to Linz in 1827. There he fostered clerical retreats, popular missions, and religious orders. He wrote on confirmation, the principle of faith, and the life of Sebastian Franz Job.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-fra:
Jesuit writer Guillaume-François Berthier, born at Issoudun in 1704, taught philosophy in Rennes and Rouen, theology in Paris before editing the Mémoires de Trévoux from 1745 to 1762. His strong opposition to the infidel encyclopédistes drew bitter attacks, above all from Voltaire, while he also carried on a French church history from volume thirteen to eighteen.

When the Society was suppressed in France in 1762, the Dauphin made him tutor to his sons and court librarian. Court life soured within two years and he spent a decade in Germany. Retiring to Bourges in 1774, he wrote until his death in 1782, leaving a much-reprinted translation of the Psalms with notes, five volumes on Isaiah, and five volumes of spiritual reflections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-pel:
Languedoc bishop Guillaume Pellissier, born at Melgueil about 1490, served Francis I as diplomat, scholar, and defender of the old faith. Canon and then bishop of Maguelonne by 1529, he helped seal peace with Charles V at Cambrai. He arranged the marriage of Henri II and Catherine de' Medici at Marseilles in 1533 and moved his see to Montpellier in 1536.

Sent as ambassador to Venice in 1540, he brought home a haul of Greek, Syriac, and Hebrew manuscripts. Arrested on suspicion of heresy by the Toulouse parliament and held at Beaucaire, he cleared himself with ease. He spent his remaining years fighting Protestantism, though the Protestants destroyed his cathedral in 1567, a year before his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hanover:
Hanover, a Prussian province since 1866 after centuries as a Guelph duchy, electorate, and kingdom, is surveyed here from Saxon tribes. The survey runs through its union with Britain in 1714 to annexation after the Austro-Prussian war. Its nucleus lay in old Saxony, and its lands grew by steady additions, from Hoya in 1582 to East Friesland and Bentheim in 1814.

Christianity came with Charlemagne's thirty-year Saxon wars, and bishoprics rose at Osnabrück, Münster, Paderborn, Minden, Verden, Bremen, Hildesheim, and Halberstadt, with Corvey Abbey carrying missions to Scandinavia. Bishops and abbots grew as powerful as dukes, the Old Saxon Heliand poem stands as early witness to Saxon faith, and later chapters follow the Reformation and church life into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-decker:
Nuremberg sculptor Hans Decker, active in the middle of the fifteenth century, is a shadowy figure known from a register of 1449 and works dated 1432 and 1437. Though his stone carving runs rough, the entry says he stands alone among his contemporaries for energy and realism, and his few known works open a new style.

His chief pieces are the colossal St. Christopher bearing the Christ Child at St. Sebald's south-west portal and the great Entombment of 1446 in St. Egidius's St. Wolfgang chapel. Eight heroic figures fill that group. Christ's body is handled hard but with an attempt at anatomy, Mary is full of grief, and John lifts his Master's arm for a kiss, in draperies simple and finely set.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-holbein-:
Augsburg's elder Hans Holbein, born about 1460 and dead at Isenheim in 1524, was the father and first teacher of the famous younger Hans. He was a pioneer who brought Renaissance softness into German painting. A leather-worker's son, poor and in debt all his life, he may have studied under Schongauer and moved between Ulm, Frankfurt, Basle, and Alsace.

Early work follows van der Weyden and Memling in Passion scenes of sincere devotion. Then Italian influence loosened his draperies, added architectural backgrounds, and made him among the first Germans to paint a Renaissance setting. His St. Paul altarpiece, showing himself pointing proudly to young Hans, and his St. Sebastian triptych, now recognised as his greatest work, anchor a career long overshadowed by his son.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-niessenb:
Late medieval architect Hans Niessenberger, said to have been born at Graz in Styria, is named often in his own time yet remains hard to pin down as a man. His documented work runs from the choir of Freiburg cathedral, entrusted to him in 1471 and worked until 1480, when he was made to leave and swear off revenge, to St. Leonhard at Basle in 1480 and Strasbourg cathedral in 1482.

A Johannes of Graz at Milan cathedral in 1483 may be the same man, on a salary of 180 guilders a year. Freiburg's choir, long and lofty with twelve chapels, fluted columns, a netted vault, and delicate Late Gothic windows, stands as his masterwork. Its building contract survives as a window on medieval wages and working hours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-brew:
German historian Heinrich Brewer, born at Puffendorf in 1640, earned the title of Imperial Historiographer by hunting original sources when most chroniclers copied one another. Schooled at Cologne's Tricoronatum, ordained in 1664, lecturer in theology at Cologne from 1667, and rector of a Cologne nunnery from 1669 to 1682, he used that leisure for history.

His chief work continues a universal history in two volumes of 1672 to 1675, followed by a revised eight-volume edition, each volume enriched with copies of official documents, pictures, and maps. A biography of Thomas à Kempis of 1681 argues, creditably even today, that Kempis wrote the Imitation of Christ. A 1685 tract on Charlemagne and Aachen's relics shows his strong local feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-jose:
Würzburg scholar Heinrich Joseph Dominicus Denzinger, born at Liège in 1819, wrote the handbook of councils and definitions that Catholic theology still uses. Brought to Würzburg in 1831, doctor in philosophy, seminarian, Roman student, and priest in 1844, he became extraordinary professor of dogmatic theology at Würzburg in 1848. He became ordinary professor in 1854, holding the chair despite ill health until his death.

A pioneer of positive theology and history of dogma after Möhler and Döllinger, he prized exact historical research over guesswork. His Enchiridion of 1854 gathers creeds, council decrees, and condemned propositions from the oldest Apostles' Creed onward, growing through editions to include the Immaculate Conception, the Syllabus. Vatican decrees, beside works on Eastern rites and the Ignatian letters.

Hesse Orientalist Heinrich Joseph Wetzer, born at Anzefahr in 1801, taught Arabic, Persian. Syriac at Freiburg and helped build the first great Catholic Kirchenlexikon. After Marburg, Tübingen, and Freiburg doctorates in 1824 and eighteen months in Paris under De Sacy and Quatremère, he found and edited an Arabic history of Egypt's Coptic Christians in 1828.

Professor extraordinary in 1828 and ordinary in 1830, he defended Freiburg's Catholic character against a Protestant professorial majority that shut him from academic posts after 1846. He became chief librarian in 1850. An anonymous 1844 tract defended the university's Catholic origin, a study of the Arian controversy stayed unfinished. His lasting work was the Kirchenlexikon, for which he drafted the index and edited jointly with Welte.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-webe:
Bamberg church historian Heinrich Weber, born at Euerdorf in 1834, taught history at Bamberg's lyceum for over twenty-six years and wrote the diocese's history from its schools to its saints. Ordained at Würzburg in 1857 after seminary and university study, he served as chaplain and parish priest before becoming religion and history teacher at Würzburg in 1865 and Bamberg professor in 1871.

His chief work traces Bamberg's learned schools from 1007 to 1803, beside histories of catechetical teaching, confession books, church song, and the diocese's divisions and patronage. Town histories of Forchheim, Kronach, and Vierzehnheiligen, two biographies, fifty Kirchenlexikon articles, and pamphlets on guild life, Trappist missions. The medieval emperor idea filled a career crowned by an honorary Würzburg doctorate in 1899, a year after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-joseph-:
Swiss priest Henri-Joseph Crelier, born at Bure in 1816, spent his leisure as a Hebrew scholar answering Renan's attacks on Scripture. Professor at Porrentruy from 1845 to 1855, then chaplain to the Sacred Heart sisters at Besançon and pastor at Rebeuvelier and Bressancourt, he turned spare hours to the Bible he loved.

His books translate the Psalms literally from Hebrew with commentary and defend Job and the Song of Songs against Renan's false and impious readings. They charge Renan with warring on the supernatural and betraying Christ by a novel. For Lethielleux's Bible commentaries he wrote Acts in 1883, Exodus and Leviticus in 1886. Genesis in 1889, the year he died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-ignatiu:
Henry Ignatius Dudley Ryder, an English Oratorian priest born in 1837, entered the Catholic Church at Rome in 1846 and became a private pupil of Newman at about twelve. After a year at the English College in Rome and months at the Catholic University in Dublin, he began his Oratorian novitiate in 1856 and was ordained in 1863. After Newman died he became superior of the Birmingham Oratory.

Ryder's one public stand came in 1867 and 1868, when he attacked W. G. Ward's extravagant claims for papal infallibility, which treated every doctrinal instruction in encyclicals and the Syllabus as infallible. In three pamphlets of notable literary style and theological knowledge he protested, earning, as he put it, the prophet's portion of stones. Time proved him mainly right: Ward soon had to retract many of his pronounced opinions before Roman theologians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-rutter:
Henry Rutter, whose true family name was Banister, was born in 1755, went to Douai College in 1768, and taught at St. Omer's College, which trained secular clergy, from 1781. On the English mission he served several northern places before his appointment in 1817 to Yealand in Lancashire. There he remained until 1834, spending his last years at Dodding Green, where he died in 1838.

The Orthodox Journal praised Rutter as a sterling priest marked by old-world learning and solid piety. He wrote an Evangelical Harmony, re-edited in 1857, along with scriptural exegeses and devotional translations catalogued by Gillow. His Answer to Dr. Southey joined the controversy over Southey's Book of the Church of 1824, where Charles Butler spoke for the Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herder:
Herder names a German publishing and bookselling firm founded by Bartholomäus Herder, born at Rottweil in 1774. Destined at first for holy orders, he planned instead to earn his living by disseminating good books, beginning at Meersburg in 1801 as publisher to the episcopal court of Constance. Moving to Freiburg in 1810, he broadened his list, published Rotteck's history, the gospel of the educated middle classes, and served as director of the allied field press in Paris.

Bartholomäus also founded an art institution for lithography and engraving whose illustrations marked an epoch, including biblical engravings and an atlas of Central Europe in two-colour lithography. Profits never matched expenditure, and the house was unsound at his death in 1839. His sons Karl Raphael and Benjamin succeeded him. Benjamin, impressed by the Cologne troubles of 1837, devoted the firm to Catholic revival through collections, periodicals, and the Kirchenlexikon begun in 1847.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herman-scholl:
Herman Scholliner, a scholar born at Freising in Bavaria in 1722, entered the Benedictine abbey of Oberaltaich in 1738. He read philosophy and theology at Erfurt and Salzburg and directed the Benedictines' house of studies from 1752 to 1757. He taught dogma at Salzburg from 1759 to 1766 and travelled to Vienna for his monastery in 1770. He became prior in 1772, taught at Ingolstadt from 1776 to 1780, then became provost at Welchenberg, dying there in 1795.

He wrote about fifty works on theology and history. From 1759 he belonged to the Bavarian Academy of Sciences, for which he composed the records of Niederaltaich and Oberaltaich, forming volumes eleven and twelve of Monumenta Boica. His other key works treat church leaders' origin, the discipline of the secret, East-West agreement on transubstantiation, and the hierarchy of the Catholic Church. They include the history of first-century Christian theology, with lectures for Bavarian Benedictine students in twelve volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-hueff:
Hermann Hueffer was a German historian and jurist, born at Münster in 1830 and dead at Bonn in 1905. Eye disease pushed him from literary study into law, but he never lost his love of history. He taught canon and Prussian civil law at Bonn and rose to full professor in 1873. He also sat in the Prussian Chamber of Deputies and the North German Reichstag, refusing to join a sectarian Catholic party.

Hueffer believed the key question was what binds people together, not what divides parties, nations, and creeds. His large-scale books treat literary figures such as Heinrich Heine and Annette von Droste-Hülshoff with close detail, alongside historical studies of his own. Readers find a scholar who joined legal training, political life, and deep historical reading in one career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-streb:
Hermann Streber was a German priest and scholar, born at Munich in 1839 and dead at Tölz in 1896. A nervous fever kept him from the usual school-leaving examination. He still entered university by private examination, studied philosophy and theology, and catalogued ancient coins in the Royal Cabinet of Medals. Ordained in 1864, he taught religion at a Munich school and took a doctorate in theology at Rome in 1869.

Dismissed from teaching over alleged support for the dogma of infallibility, he became a parish pastor. He then joined the editing of the Kirchenlexikon, a Catholic church encyclopedia, where he did notable work on its index of names. Illness forced his retirement to Tölz in 1892. The entry traces a career cut short twice by sickness but still rich in editorial service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hieronymus-em:
Hieronymus Emser was the most ardent literary opponent of Luther, born at Ulm in 1477 and dead at Dresden in 1527. He studied Greek and Latin at Tübingen, then law and theology at Basle, where he barely escaped prison for circulating satirical verses. Service as secretary to the legate Cardinal Raymond Peraudi followed, and in 1500 he published a work on crosses supposedly fallen from heaven.

At Erfurt in 1504 he lectured brilliantly on Reuchlin and counted Martin Luther among his hearers, later claiming a pioneer share in German classical humanism. His Leipzig lectures on the classics in 1505 drew little praise, so he turned to theology and won his bachelor's degree with help from George of Saxony. The entry traces the humanist who became Luther's sharpest literary foe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holy-water:
Holy water in the earliest Christian era is attested only by documents of fairly late date. The Apostolic Constitutions, redacted about the year 400, attribute a precept for holy water to the apostle Matthew. A letter ascribed to Pope Alexander I, a second-century pope, is apocryphal and later, so the first solid testimony reaches back only to the fifth century.

Still, water likely served expiatory and purificatory ends from the start, much as under Jewish law. Baptismal water, often flowing sea or river water, could not take the same blessing as water in baptisteries. Two finds matter greatly here: Serapion's fourth-century Pontifical and a Syriac Testamentum Domini of the fifth or sixth century, both holding a blessing over oil and water during Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hubert-walter:
Hubert Walter was archbishop of Canterbury from 1193 to 1205, dying on 13 July 1205. Son of Hervey Walter and Matilda de Valoines, he came of Norman stock holding lands in Lancashire and Norfolk. His elder brother Theobald became ancestor of the Butlers of Ormonde. Hubert first appears as a chaplain in Ranulf de Glanville's household, sharing, a contemporary says, in England's government.

He served as baron of the exchequer in 1184 and 1185, and in 1189 Richard I chose him as bishop of Salisbury. He joined Richard's Third Crusade, became chief chaplain of the whole host on Baldwin's death, commanded English troops, and mediated between Richard and Saladin. His firmness against disorder in the crusading army won praise, and the entry follows his rise to Canterbury and his rule there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-st-ch:
Hugh of St. Cher was a thirteenth-century Dominican cardinal, born at St. Cher near Vienne about 1200 and dead at Orvieto in 1263. He studied philosophy, theology, and law at Paris and taught law there before joining the Dominicans in 1225. He served as provincial and then, in 1230, as prior of the Paris Dominican house.

Hugh became confidant and adviser to several bishops and Gregory IX's trusted envoy to Constantinople in 1233. Innocent IV made him cardinal in 1244, leaned on him at the Council of Lyons in 1245, and later sent him as legate to Germany after Frederick II's death. Alexander IV named him an examiner of the so-called Eternal Gospel. Chiefly through Hugh, Dominicans gained a new biblical Correctorium, still known by his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hurter:
Friedrich Emmanuel von Hurter was a Swiss convert and historian, born at Schaffhausen in 1787 and dead at Graz in 1865. He attended Göttingen University from 1804 to 1806 and took a country parish in 1808. The first volume of his life of Innocent III, twenty years in the making, appeared in 1834 and caused a sensation in Catholic and Protestant circles alike.

Translated into French, English, Italian, and Spanish, the life made Hurter antistes of Schaffhausen's clergy in 1835 and later president of the school board. His open sympathy with Catholic clergy and his aid to Catholics roused colleagues to abuse, and he resigned his dignities in 1841. After three years in retirement he went to Rome and professed the Catholic faith before Gregory XVI in 1844, then served as imperial counsellor at Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyacinthe-de-:
Hyacinthe de Valroger was a French Oratorian, born at Caen in 1814 and dead in 1876. He first studied medicine, then was ordained priest in 1837 and directed the lesser seminary of Bayeux. In 1847 he became titular canon of Bayeux cathedral. In 1852 he joined Père Gratry in restoring the French Oratory, serving as theology professor, master of novices, and assistant general.

A man of great learning and equal modesty, Valroger hesitated to publish lest his works prove inopportune or inexact. Besides many articles in Catholic reviews, he published critical studies of contemporary rationalism in 1846. An essay on the credibility of gospel history against Strauss followed in 1847. Later works covered Christianity and paganism in teaching, the New Testament, the age of the world, the genesis of species, and Maistre's thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-knob:
Ignatius Knoblecher was a Catholic missionary in Central Africa, born in 1819 at St. Cantian in Lower Carniola and dead at Naples in 1858. He studied at Rudolfswerth, Laibach, and Rome's Propaganda College, was ordained in 1845, and graduated as doctor of theology a year later. When the Vicariate for Central Africa was erected in 1846, Propaganda chose him as one of its missionaries.

Before leaving, he spent eight months in Lebanon and Syria learning Oriental Christian rites and customs. In September 1847 he left Cairo with Maximilian Ryllo, pro-vicar apostolic, and four other missionaries, reaching Khartoum in February 1848. There they built a school for young Africans bought in the slave market, who later aided the missions, and through them Knoblecher learned the interior's languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignatius-von-:
Ignatius von Weitenauer was a German littérateur, exegete, and orientalist, born at Ingolstadt in 1709 and dead at Salem near Constance in 1783. His family had been knighted by Bavaria's Elector Maximilian Joseph. Joining the Jesuits in 1724, he taught poetry and rhetoric for eleven years in several colleges, mainly at Eichstätt. In 1753 he took the chair of philosophy and oriental languages at Innsbruck.

Suppression of his order in 1773 abruptly ended his professorship, and he accepted the Cistercians of Salmansweiler's invitation to continue writing in their monastery until his death. Before Innsbruck he had published festive odes and plays of high merit. At Innsbruck he composed his learned works, above all a Biblia Sacra commentary comparing Vulgate and original text, and a Lexicon Biblicum explaining difficult Hebrew words and phrases.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignaz-assmaye:
Ignaz Assmayer was an Austrian musician, born at Salzburg in 1790 and dead at Vienna in 1862. Brunmayr and Michael Haydn taught him first, Eybler later in Vienna. In 1808 he took the organist's post at his native town's St. Peter's, writing his oratorio The Deluge and his cantata Words of Consecration. He moved to Vienna in 1815 and took the Schottenkirche choirmastership, and in 1825 became imperial organist.

After eight years as vice-choirmaster, he became second court choirmaster in 1846, succeeding Weigl. His chief oratorios, The Vow, Saul and David, and Saul's Death, were repeatedly performed by the Tonkünstler Society, which he conducted for fifteen years. His pen produced fifteen masses, two requiems, a Te Deum, plus smaller church pieces and sixty published secular works including symphonies, overtures, and pastorales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignaz-kogler:
Ignaz Kögler, called Lai in Chinese, was, with Adam Schall, the most important of fifty German Jesuits who worked in the old Chinese missions between 1650 and 1750. Born at Landsberg in Bavaria in 1680 and dead at Peking in 1746, he joined the Jesuits in 1696. He taught mathematics and Hebrew at Ingolstadt from 1712 to 1714, then went to China in 1715.

For his extraordinary wide learning he enjoyed great consideration at the imperial court, presiding over the mathematical and astronomical tribunal for thirty years. A mandarin of the second class, he joined the supreme court of equity in 1731, a post never before held by a foreigner. He refused the stipends attached to his offices, and his successor Hallerstein called him one of the most cultivated minds ever to reach those lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaac-joseph-:
Jesuit Isaac Joseph Berruyer was born at Rouen on 7 November 1681. He died at Paris on 18 February 1758. He spent his life on a vast History of the People of God. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1697. The first part runs from the world's origin to the Messiah's coming. It appeared in seven volumes at Paris in 1728. A revised and enlarged edition followed in 1733. A supplement in 1734 added Old Testament prophecies, the story of Job, and maps.

By 1736 seven editions had already appeared, and translations followed into German, Italian, Spanish, and Polish. The second part runs from the Messiah's birth to the end of the synagogue. It came out at Paris in 1753. A more exact Antwerp edition followed in 1754, and a Paris edition in 1755. The entry follows a publishing success that later drew sharp theological fire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaac-thomas-:
New York missionary, author, and founder of the Paulists, Isaac Thomas Hecker was born 18 December 1819 and died in his home city on 22 December 1888. His father, a Wetzlar native, professed no faith, while his mother, first Lutheran then ardent Methodist, raised three sons who joined no Protestant body. A family reverse set Isaac to work at eleven, helping his brothers bake bread.

Lack of full schooling might have barred an intellectual life. The boy was studious by nature and read Kant's Critique of Pure Reason propped before his eyes while kneading dough. Original, intuitive, and eager for knowledge, he grew into a preacher and writer who founded an American missionary congregation. The entry follows a baker's boy toward the pulpit and the printed page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacinto-verda:
Catalan poet Jacinto Verdaguer was born at Riudeperas near Barcelona on 17 April 1845. He died at Vallvidrera on 10 June 1902. While training for holy orders, he entered the Jochs Florals poetry contests. Those yearly contests spurred writing in the eastern Iberian vernacular. Faith, country, and love were their main themes.

Verdaguer won his first prize in 1861, writing with success on faith and country. He was ordained in 1870. In 1877 he published La Atlantida, his most famous work. It ranks among the notable works of modern Catalan letters. It was translated into Spanish, French, Italian, English, and German. His Oda a Barcelona followed in 1883, then the epic legend Canigó. The entry traces a priest-poet of Catalan renewal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-gretser:
Jesuit writer Jacob Gretser was born at Markdorf in 1562. He died at Ingolstadt in 1625. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1578. Nine years later he publicly defended theses covering all theology. Ingolstadt was his main field of work. There he taught philosophy for three years. He taught dogmatic theology for fourteen years. He taught moral theology for seven years.

He gave at least ten hours a day to study. He often worked late into the night. He saved part of each day for charity and pastoral zeal. He ranked among the best controversialists of his age. Pope Clement VIII, Emperor Ferdinand II, and Maximilian I of Bavaria esteemed him. Bellarmine and Marcus Welser consulted him in difficulties. The entry sketches a tireless scholar of the Counter-Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacob-keller:
Controversialist Jacob Keller was born at Säckingen, Baden, in 1568. He died at Munich on 23 February 1631. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1589. After his studies he taught classics at Freiburg. He became professor of philosophy and of moral and dogmatic theology at Ingolstadt. In 1605 he became rector at Ratisbon college. In 1607 he became rector at Munich college. He held that post until 1623.

In 1628 he was reappointed rector at Munich. He still held the office when apoplexy ended his life. Beyond his learning, he showed uncommon executive skill. Despite deep humility, superiors consulted him often. Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria, sought his advice and trusted him with weighty affairs. He discharged them with much success. The entry presents a scholar-administrator of Catholic Bavaria.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-carti:
Jacques Cartier, discoverer of Canada, was born at Saint-Malo, Brittany, in 1491. He died on 1 September 1557. Little is known of his youth. He likely followed countrymen on ventures to Newfoundland or Brazil. He offered his services to Admiral Philippe de Chabot. France's king was renewing colonization attempts after Aubert, Denys, Léry, the Parmentiers, and Verrazzano.

Cartier's reputation as a mariner won him command. Two small ships of sixty tons, each with sixty men, were placed at his disposal. He sailed from Saint-Malo on 20 April 1534. In twenty days he reached Cape Bonavista, Newfoundland. He then explored northward, entering the Strait of Belle Isle and coasting Labrador. The entry opens the story of French Canada with its first great navigator.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-charl:
Orator and church writer Jacques Charles de Brisacier was born at Bourges in 1641. He died at Paris on 23 March 1736. He came from a rich and distinguished family. His father collected general taxes for Berry province. At twenty-five he entered the Paris Society of Foreign Missions. He gave seventy years of his life to that work. He served as chaplain in ordinary to Queen Marie-Thérèse, wife of Louis XIV.

High church honors he might have sought, and many bishoprics were offered him, but he refused them all to stay with the Foreign Missions. Elected superior in 1681, he filled the office for eight terms, since society rules barred more than three straight years as superior, alternating the charge with Louis Tiberge. He also helped frame the society's rules in 1698, a preacher who chose missions over mitres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-gravi:
Jesuit missionary Jacques Gravier, born at Moulins in 1651 and dead in Louisiana in 1708, learned classics and philosophy from the Jesuits at Moulins before joining their order in 1670. Theology at Louis-le-Grand college, Paris, prepared him for Canada, where he was sent in 1685, reaching Michilimackinac in 1686.

The Illinois mission begun by Marquette became his life's work when he succeeded Allouez there in 1687, and he is counted its true founder. A decade of incredible hardship and suffering followed. He became the first to master the Illinois language and reduce it to grammar. He gathered Kaskaskia and Peoria Indians at the Rock near Fort St Louis. Despite medicine-men's plots, he shaped his flock into a model Christian church, aided by a saintly Kaskaskia chief's daughter. In 1696 he also served as superior at Michilimackinac and vicar-general to Bishop St Vallier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-lemer:
Jacques Lemercier, an architect born at Pontoise about 1585, died at Paris in 1654. With Mansart and Le Muet, he stands out as a brilliant figure of French building under Louis XIII and Richelieu. He worked also as a sculptor and engraver. In some measure he copied the strong but prosaic manner of Salomon de Brosse. By then the French Renaissance had come to its final stage, yet it still held a weighty inheritance from Lescot's days.

He was presumably in Italy from 1607 to 1613, and while at Rome he probably engraved a model of St Peter's. By 1618 at the latest he shows up as royal architect, paid a salary of 1,200 livres, and in 1639 he rose to chief architect, overseeing all royal building works. In that post he fell out unpleasantly with the cultivated Poussin over Louvre decorations. He is judged a well-meaning, discreet man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-viger:
Jacques Viger, a French-Canadian antiquarian, first saw light in Montreal on 7 May 1787 and died there on 12 December 1858, after schooling at the Sulpician college in his home city. In the War of 1812 he held a captain's rank in the Voltigeurs, serving under de Salaberry. Montreal chose him as its first mayor in 1833, and he worked hard to better the city's sanitary state. He published little, yet his standing as an archaeologist spread everywhere.

Behind that standing lay a manuscript collection built up through forty years of study, consulted by the leading historians of France and the United States. His chronicle Sabretache, filling 28 volumes, brought together plans, maps, and portraits, plus useful notes on disputed points of history. He set up Montreal's Historical Society, and Pius IX made him a knight of the Order of St Gregory the Great.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-alphons:
James Alphonsus McMaster, editor and convert, was born at Duanesburg, New York, on 1 April 1820 and died at Brooklyn on 29 December 1886. His father, a leading Presbyterian minister, sent him to Union College. He quit before graduating and worked as a private tutor, and in the days of Tractarianism and Brook Farm he became a Catholic in 1845. Thinking he had a call to the priesthood, he joined the Redemptorists as a novice and travelled to Belgium.

There he soon found that religious life did not suit him, so on returning to America he turned to journalism. His forceful and prolific pen opened doors at several papers and periodicals, with pieces in the New York Freeman's Journal, then in the hands of Bishop John Hughes. In 1848 he mapped out a semi-monthly magazine, followed by a semi-weekly independent Catholic paper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-archer:
English missionary priest James Archer was born in London on 17 November 1751. He died on 22 August 1832. While working at a public house called The Ship in Lincoln's Inn Fields, where Catholics secretly met for worship, he caught Dr Challoner's favorable notice. Challoner sent him in 1769 to study at Douai College. He returned in 1780 after ordination to serve the mission in that same public house.

For many years he served as vicar-general of the London district. He received a papal doctorate in divinity at the same time as Lingard, Gradwell, and Fletcher. His published works were chiefly sermons. They included Sermons on Various Moral and Religious Subjects in several series from 1787 onward. They also included Sermons on Matrimonial Duties in 1804. A letter to Milner, vicar-apostolic of the Midland district, completes the list. The entry presents a London mission priest turned popular preacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jan-stephanus:
Flemish painter Jan Stephanus van Kalcker, also called Giovanni da Calcar, was a native of Cleves duchy. He was born between 1499 and 1510 and died at Naples in 1546. Vasari mentions him several times, mainly as Titian's pupil, entering his school in 1536, and for copying Titian's works with extraordinary accuracy. Kalcker seems to have worked first at Dordrecht, but most of his life was spent at Naples.

There, as Vasari tells us, the fairest hopes were conceived for his future progress. He drew the eleven large anatomical plates engraved for Andrea Vesalius' anatomy work as illustrations. Vasari praises them very highly. Kalcker is also said to have drawn portraits of artists in the early edition of Vasari's Lives. Some writers call him a close imitator of Giorgione. The entry presents a copyist whose anatomy plates outlived his paintings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste Bouvier, bishop of Le Mans, was a French theologian born in 1783 and dead at Rome in 1854. A carpenter's son with only school learning at first, he studied classics with his parish priest, entered Angers seminary in 1805, and was ordained in 1808.

Bouvier taught philosophy and moral theology at Le Mans, led its seminary, and became bishop in 1834. His Institutiones Theologicae ran to fifteen editions and served seminaries across France, the United States, and Canada. As the first manual fitted to a time when Gallicanism and Jansenism were fading and church learning was being remade, it gave him a rare place in nineteenth-century theology.

Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, a French scholar of the early Church fathers born at Nîmes in 1629 and dead in Paris in 1686, was a child prodigy. Schooled by his father, once a Reformed minister turned Catholic, he read the Bible aloud in Hebrew and Greek before the French clergy at Mantes in 1641. He was still a boy.

Cotelier studied theology at Paris, joined the Sorbonne without ever taking priestly orders, and in 1667 was set with Du Cange to list the Royal Library's Greek manuscripts. Made professor of Greek at the Collège Royal in 1676, he edited ancient Christian writings whose texts scholars still consult. His editions gave the fathers a sounder footing in print.

Jean-Baptiste de Saint-Vallier, second bishop of Quebec, was born at Grenoble in 1653 and died at Quebec in 1727. A Sorbonne doctor at nineteen, he served as almoner to Louis XIV, kept his piety amid court life, and nursed the wounded in Flanders. He refused Tours and Marseilles, preferring hard mission ground.

Chosen to succeed Laval in 1684, Saint-Vallier visited every parish from Quebec to Montreal and distant Acadia, and in 1687 printed a warm report on the colony's clergy and people. His eager zeal to reform clashed at times with Laval's gentler rule and stirred fear. Still, his energy built up the young Canadian Church he served for over forty years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-brisa:
Jean de Brisacier, a French Jesuit controversialist born at Blois in 1592 and dead there in 1668, joined the Society in 1619 and preached for years with zeal. He later led colleges at Aix, Blois, and Rouen, visited Portugal's province, and served the foreign missions and the Paris professed house.

Brisacier loved mission work above all else, counting years outside it as nothing. He fought Jansenism at every turn, and a 1651 Blois sermon denouncing its deceit, above all around Cour-Cheverny, sparked a fierce pamphlet war. His reply, defending his sermon and naming its foes, was condemned at Paris for personal attacks, yet the dispute ran on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-garnier:
Jean Garnier, a French Jesuit historian and scholar born in Paris in 1612 and dead at Bologna in 1681. He entered the Society at sixteen and taught humanities, philosophy, and theology at Clermont-Ferrand and Bourges. He counted among the most learned Jesuits of his day, versed in Christian antiquity and much consulted on hard cases of conscience.

Garnier first printed in 1618 the Libellus Fidei sent to Rome during the Pelagian dispute, with notes and history. His 1655 Rules of Catholic Faith treated grace through Christ, and his 1673 edition of Marius Mercator added seven dissertations on Pelagian authors, synods, imperial laws, and professions of faith. Sent to Rome on order business in 1681, he fell ill and died on the road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-jacques-:
Jean-Jacques Olier, founder of Saint-Sulpice seminary and society, was born in Paris in 1608 and died there in 1657. Schooled by Jesuits at Lyons, encouraged by Saint Francis de Sales, he studied philosophy at Harcourt and theology at the Sorbonne, preaching in the ambitious style of the day. He moved in fashionable circles.

A pilgrimage to Loreto cured his failing sight and converted him wholly to God. Refusing a court chaplaincy, Olier gathered beggars and the poor for catechism at his home and on Paris streets, a practice first mocked, then widely copied. Under Saint Vincent de Paul he trained priests, and his Sulpician seminary reshaped French clergy formation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-adam-m:
Johann Adam Möhler, a German theologian born at Igersheim in 1796 and dead at Munich in 1838. He studied at Mergentheim and Ellwangen, turned to theology in 1815, and was ordained at Rottenburg in 1819. After curacies at Weilderstadt and Riedlingen he became tutor at Tübingen's Wilhelmstift in 1821.

A year steeped in Greek history and philosophy gave Möhler the clear judgment, fine diction, and feeling for beauty that mark his writings. Touring German and Austrian universities, he met leading Catholic and Protestant minds, above all Neander, then lectured on church history at Tübingen. His Unity in the Church, on Catholicism's principle, opened a career cut short at forty-two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-and-we:
Johann and Wendelin von Speyer were German printers at Venice from 1468 to 1477, among the first to carry printing from Mainz to Italy after 1462. Little is known of their lives beyond their Speyer origin and Johann's early work as a Mainz goldsmith, where he likely learned the craft.

Johann reached Venice in 1468 with wife, children, and brother Wendelin, welcomed by a Senate that granted him a five-year printing monopoly. His Cicero letters appeared in 1469, and during Augustine's City of God in 1470 Johann died, leaving Wendelin to finish it. Wendelin then issued over seventy great works by 1477, in antique type after fine Italian manuscripts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-august:
Johann Augustanus Faber, a Dominican theologian born at Fribourg about 1470 and dead about 1531. He entered the order probably at Augsburg, where he spent most of his religious life, hence Augustanus. Master and doctor of divinity, he became vicar-general of Upper Germany's Dominican congregation in 1511 and prior at Augsburg for twenty years.

Faber rebuilt Augsburg's Dominican church from 1512 to 1515, partly with jubilee preaching funds. He served as court preacher and royal counsellor to Maximilian and, on Erasmus's word, to Charles V. Sympathising with Lutherans' classical revival, he proposed a treatment of Luther his superiors rejected. Breaking with humanists, he drew abuse from Luther and from Erasmus himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-baptis:
Johann Baptist von Hirscher, a German theologian born in 1788 and dead in 1865. He studied at Weissenau, Constance, and Freiburg, was ordained in 1810, and taught at Ellwangen before taking Tübingen's moral and pastoral theology chair in 1817 for twenty years. From 1837 he taught moral theology and catechetics at Freiburg for a quarter century.

Hirscher shaped moral theology, preaching, and catechetics. His Christian Morality of 1835, through five editions, defined the field as the science of man's effective return to divine sonship through Christ's merits, reacting against rationalist morals. Early phrases drew censure, which he softened by degrees, until Kleutgen judged the last editions fully orthodox.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-caspar:
Johann Caspar Aiblinger, a Bavarian composer born at Wasserburg in 1779 and died at Munich in 1867. He began piano and organ at Tegernsee Abbey at eleven, studied at Munich gymnasium, and entered Landshut university in 1800. Drawn to the Church, he finished philosophy and began theology until Bavarian secularisation barred the cloister.

Turning wholly to music, Aiblinger spent eight years at Vicenza under Simon Mayr, met Meyerbeer at Venice, and failed to found a classical school there. Directing Milan ballet, then Munich's Italian opera at King Max's call. He led the royal orchestra under King Ludwig, he gathered old Italian masterpieces in Italy and wrote much for All Saints church, where he was organist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-dieten:
Johann Dietenberger, a German Dominican theologian born about 1475 at Frankfurt and dead at Mainz in 1537. He was schooled at home, joined the Dominicans, and registered at Cologne in 1511, taking licentiate in 1514 and doctorate the next year after time at Heidelberg and Mainz.

Prior at Frankfurt to 1526 and at Koblenz after, Dietenberger taught Thomas at Trier from 1518, sat on the twenty theologians. They refuted the Protestant Confession at Augsburg in 1530 under Eck, and served as general inquisitor for Mainz and Cologne. His last years taught theology at Mainz academy. His catechism of 1537 and his German Bible stand as his chief works for ordinary Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-faber:
Johann Faber of Heilbronn, a Dominican controversialist and preacher born in 1504 and dead at Augsburg in 1558, entered the order at sixteen and studied at Wimpfen convent. In 1534 he was charged to preach at Augsburg cathedral, but Lutheran bans on Catholic preaching cut that work short.

At Cologne university Faber pursued higher clerical studies and in 1535 and 1536 published unedited works of English mystic Richard Rolle. Back at Wimpfen he preached against Reformers with such fruit that foes drove him out. Called to Colmar in 1539, he matriculated at Freiburg that September as Colmar preacher, and in 1545 was elected prior at Schlettstadt, serving only briefly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-g-albr:
Johann Georg Albrechtsberger, a master of music theory who taught Hummel and Beethoven, was born at Klosterneuburg in 1736 and died at Vienna in 1809. A choirboy at seven, he learned thoroughbass from his pastor at Saint Martin's, who even built him a little organ, and he practised without rest on Sundays and holidays.

At Melk Abbey Albrechtsberger's soprano won the future Emperor Leopold's praise and a ducat, and its library let him study Caldara, Fux, Pergolesi, Handel, and Graun into profound theory. Organist at Melk cathedral for twelve years, choir chief at Raab and Mariazell, then Vienna's Carmelite choir director. He became court organist in 1772, a post Joseph had long promised him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-gruebe:
Johann Grueber, a German Jesuit missionary and explorer born at Linz in 1623 and dead in 1665. He joined the Society in 1641 and reached China in 1656, serving at Peking court as mathematics professor and aide to Adam Schall von Bell. In 1661 superiors sent him with Belgian Father Dorville to Rome on order business.

Barred by sea through the Dutch blockade of Macao, the pair dared an overland road to India through China and Tibet. From Xining through Kokonor and Kalmuck lands they reached Lhasa, crossed the Himalayas to Nepal, Patna, and Agra in 214 days. Dorville died at Agra, but Grueber, with Sanskrit scholar Roth, reached Europe, proving a land link between China and India.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-ignaz-:
Johann Ignaz von Felbiger, a German school reformer and Augustinian canon regular born at Gross-Glogau in 1724 and dead at Pressburg in 1788. He was a postmaster's son ennobled through his father. Orphaned after Breslau theology study, he taught a private family in 1744, joined Sagan's Augustinians in 1746, and became abbot in 1758.

Seeing wretched local Catholic schools, Felbiger issued his first school ordinance in 1761, borrowed Hecker's Berlin Realschule and Hähn's initial-and-table method in 1762. He set up a teachers' college with a Sagan ordinance in 1763. Backed by minister Schlabrendorff, he framed a general Silesian elementary ordinance in 1765 and a Silesian Catechism in 1766 that spread widely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-joseph:
Johann Joseph Gassner, a celebrated exorcist born at Braz in 1727 and dead at Pondorf in 1779. He studied at Prague and Innsbruck, was ordained in 1750, and became Pondorf parish priest and dean in May 1776. A few years after Klosterle in 1758 his health failed despite physicians, until he guessed an evil spirit's hand and found spiritual means cured him.

Applying the method to others, Gassner drew thousands, and invitations to Constance, Ellwangen, Ratisbon, and beyond met like success. He held the devil could harm body as well as soul, so only devil-caused ills fell to him. A probative exorcism made the spirit sign its presence, then an expulsive exorcism bade it leave in Jesus's name, all in public before witnesses of standing.

Johann Joseph Ignaz von Döllinger, historian and theologian born at Bamberg in 1799 and died at Munich in 1890. He grew up in a medical academic family: his grandfather founded Bamberg's medical faculty, his father taught medicine there and at Würzburg. French books filled the house, and Ignaz learned French from his father, Italian at school, English from a Benedictine, and Spanish at university.

Entering Würzburg at sixteen, Döllinger took history, philosophy, philology, and natural science at once, a plan too vast even for his rich gifts. Means for travel and books to feed it. That receptive, many-sided schooling shaped a historian whose learning and judgment would dominate German Catholic thought, though his later break with Rome lies beyond this entry's opening span.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-ladisl:
Johann Ladislaus von Oberwart Pyrker, Hungarian churchman and poet born near Stuhlweissenburg in 1772 and died at Vienna in 1847. He came from old nobility; his father was one of eighteen hussars famed at Kunersdorf. Failing for civil service at Ofen, he joined Lilienfeld's Cistercians in 1792 and was ordained in 1796.

Pyrker rose through steward, chancellor, prior, and abbot, lifting his monastery to material and spiritual wealth, then became bishop of Zips in 1818. He became patriarch of Aquileia and primate of Dalmatia in 1820, and archbishop of Erlau at last. He founded soldiers' health resorts at Karlsbad and Gastein, a teachers' seminary at Erlau, gave ten thousand florins to Erlau cathedral. He left a painting collection that grounds Hungary's National Museum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-matthi:
Johann Matthias Kager, a German historical painter born at Munich in 1566 and died at Augsburg in 1634. He first studied under Pieter de Witte, called Candito, then spent years in Rome young. Recalled by Elector Maximilian as principal painter on a handsome allowance, he settled at Augsburg for life and became burgomaster.

Kager adorned Munich palaces and churches, but his finest work, the Last Judgment, hangs in Augsburg's Senate Hall, with David and Abigail now at Vienna also notable. He etched religious plates from his own designs dated 1600, 1601, and 1603, and Sadeler and Kilian engraved his pictures on over seventy plates. He practised architecture and miniatures, but fresco and oil were his chief work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-michae:
Johann Michael Feder, a German theologian born at Oellingen in 1753 and died at Würzburg in 1824. He studied at Würzburg's bishop's seminary from 1772 to 1777, was ordained that year, and took a theology degree. After years as Julius Hospital chaplain he became a professor of theology and Eastern tongues in 1785.

Feder took a divinity doctorate in 1786, directed the university library from 1791, and became ordinary theology professor and censor in 1795. After Würzburg's shake-up he became chief librarian in 1803, giving up theology in 1805. A stroke in November 1811, after he lost the librarianship, left him never fully recovered. His best work revised Braun's German Bible in 1803, basis for Allioli's famed version.

Johann Michael Sailer, son of a poor Bavarian shoemaker, became a noted teacher of theology and finally Bishop of Ratisbon. Born in 1751, he entered the Jesuits in 1770, continued his studies at Ingolstadt after the order was suppressed, and was ordained in 1775. He taught dogmatics at Ingolstadt and pastoral theology at Dillingen, where opponents twice cut short his work, then taught at Landshut to wide acclaim.

Pupils revered him, and Crown Prince Louis of Bavaria was among them. Sailer declined a nomination to Cologne, saw a nomination to Augsburg rejected by Rome, and reached Ratisbon as canon in 1821, auxiliary bishop in 1822, and bishop in 1829. The entry stresses his gifts as a teacher and writer, his friendships across confessional lines, and the long road his reputation traveled before Rome accepted him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-muelle:
Johann Mueller, born at Coblenz in 1801, is presented as the founder of modern physiology. The son of a shoemaker, he first meant to become a priest. He then turned to medicine at Bonn. There a student prize essay on the breathing of the fetus was judged the best ever offered in such a contest. He taught at Bonn, studied under Rudolphi at Berlin, succeeded him there in 1832, and served as university rector in 1847.

Mueller's strength lay in exact observation joined to a broad grasp of principles, and in guiding pupils into new fields. His research ranged over reflex action, blood plasma, glands, the lymph hearts of amphibians, and the ducts of the fetal kidney that now bear his name. Work on the eye in lower animals, above all insects, filled his study of comparative vision, and his teaching shaped a generation of physiologists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nikola:
Johann Nikolaus Weislinger was a German controversialist famed for the sharpness of his pen. Born in Lorraine in 1691, he studied philosophy at Heidelberg and theology under the Jesuits at Strasburg. He then served as parish priest at Waldulm from 1726 and at Kappel-Rodeck from 1730. Illness forced his resignation in 1750.

Widely read in his opponents' writings, Weislinger answered Protestant controversialists in kind, modeling his rough language on Luther's own rhetoric. His most celebrated work, Friss Vogel oder stirb, written while he was still a theology student, appeared at Strasburg in 1723 and was often reprinted. Other tracts took on Hutten and defended Catholic positions against Protestant complaints. They mocked theological showmen. He also issued a new edition of a Catholic manual on dying well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-simon-:
Johann Simon Haspinger, known in religion as Father Joachim, was a Tyrolese priest who fought as well as preached for his homeland. Born at Gries in 1776, he worked on the family farm and climbed mountains until seventeen. He then schooled at Bozen and joined volunteer marksmen against the French in 1796. He won a medal for bravery and fought at Spinges in 1797.

After Innsbruck studies he joined the Capuchins at Eppan in 1802 and was ordained in 1805, serving as chaplain among Tyrolese troops in the war against Napoleon. When the Peace of Presburg handed Tyrol to Bavaria, whose harsh treatment of friars and mountaineers bred revolt, Haspinger linked up with the peasant leader Andreas Hofer. The entry follows him from parish work and soldiering into the heart of the Tyrolese rising for God and emperor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-asser:
John Asser was a Welsh monk whose life of King Alfred remains a chief source for the king's reign. Educated at St. David's in Pembrokeshire under his kinsman Archbishop Asserius, he was invited to Alfred's court about 885. After illness delayed him, he agreed to pass half of every year with the king. He received the monasteries of Amesbury and Banwell, later a grant of Exeter, and the bishopric of Sherborne before 900.

His Life of Alfred, written in 893, joins a chronicle of English history from 849 to 887 with a personal narrative of Alfred's career. The authentic text survives only in Francis Wise's 1722 edition, printed from a tenth-century manuscript burned in 1731. Popular tales such as the burning of the cakes and Alfred's founding of Oxford are not in Asser's work, and its authenticity has itself been debated by scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bridgewa:
John Bridgewater, known as Aquapontanus, was the earliest martyrologist of Catholic England under Elizabeth. Born in Yorkshire about 1532, he took his master's degree at Oxford in 1556, was ordained, and became Rector of Lincoln College in 1563. In 1574 he resigned all his preferments and crossed to Douai with several students, preferring the old religion to what he called Calvinopapists and Puritans.

Living on the Continent at Reims, Paris, Rome, and Trier, he answered a Protestant work calling the pope Antichrist. He compiled his great Concertatio of 1588, an 850-page battle of the Catholic faith in England. It is told through lives of men famed for learning and sanctity, among them over a hundred martyrs. Reissued by Cardinal Allen in 1594, it served Dodd, Challoner, and Lingard as an original record of English Catholic suffering.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-de-taxst:
John de Taxster was a thirteenth-century Benedictine chronicler of Bury St. Edmund's. Nothing is known of his life except that he was professed there on 20 November 1244, and he probably died about 1265, when his chronicle stops. His work begins with the creation of the world, compiled in its early part from Florence of Worcester, William of Malmesbury, and Ralph de Diceto.

Its value lies in Taxster's account of his own times, later used by Everisden, Oxenedes, and Bartholomew Cotton. His chronicle for 1258 to 1263 Luard printed it in his edition of Cotton, and passages on German affairs appear in Pertz's Monumenta. The whole chronicle has never been printed and survives in only two manuscripts, one in the British Museum and one in the College of Arms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-evangeli:
John Evangelist Stadler was a Bavarian hagiographer whose Complete Lexicon of Saints gathered more lives than any work of its kind. Born at Parkstetten in 1804, he studied at Landshut and Munich. He was ordained at Ratisbon by Bishop Sailer in 1827 and taught Old Testament exegesis at Munich. He became canon of Augsburg in 1838 and dean in 1858.

Master of German, French, Italian, English, Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Persian, and Sanskrit, with Spanish and Polish added late, he poured his learning into the Heiligen-Lexikon. It was published at Augsburg from 1858 to 1882. Alphabetically arranged, it condensed the Bollandist Acta Sanctorum as far as October. It added many new lives and newly found data. Though popular rather than scientific in method, it gave readers the fullest single collection of saints' lives then available.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-fletcher:
John Fletcher was an English missionary and theologian whose sermons and translations served the Catholic mission for decades. Born at Ormskirk to an old Catholic family and educated at Douai and St. Gregory's in Paris, he became a professor at St. Omer's, where his great-uncle had been president. The Revolution caught him there, and he spent months imprisoned at Arras and Dourlens.

Released in 1795, he served at Hexham, Blackburn, Weston Underwood, and Leamington before retiring at Northampton in 1848. His works include sermons for Sundays after Pentecost with an essay on the spirit of controversy. They include a Catholic manual translated from Bossuet and a comparative view of Catholic and Protestant grounds. He also translated Campion's Ten Reasons, de Maistre on the Spanish Inquisition, and Fenelon's daily reflections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-fowler:
John Fowler was an English scholar-printer whose Louvain press served the Catholic cause under Elizabeth. Born at Bristol in 1537, he studied at Winchester and New College, Oxford. In 1559 he left rather than take the Oath of Supremacy, one of fifteen fellows who went or were ejected. He married Alice Harris, daughter of Sir Thomas More's secretary, and withdrew to Louvain.

There his learning in Greek, Latin, poetry, oratory, and theology, and his mastery of Aquinas's Summa, which he reduced to a compendium, placed him among the great scholar-printers. Wood compared him to the Stephenses. Cardinal Allen praised him as the most Catholic and most learned printer of books. English state papers show the government watching his presses at Louvain and Antwerp, which printed the English Catholic books of the age until his death at Namur in 1579.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-frederic:
John Frederick Henry Schlosser was a Frankfurt jurist and convert who made his home a center of German literary life. Born in 1780, he studied law at Jena, where he grew familiar with Schiller and Goethe. He took his doctorate in 1803 and practiced at Frankfurt, serving as counsel of the municipal court and director of the grand-ducal lyceum under Prince Dalberg.

In 1814 he and his wife Sophie entered the Catholic Church. He represented Frankfurt at the Congress of Vienna and championed the civil equality of every Christian denomination and the rights of Frankfurt's Catholics. Withdrawing from public life after 1825, he divided his year between Frankfurt and his country seat at Neuburg. He gathered leading spirits in literature, art, and science around a man charitable, hospitable, and free of denominational narrowness. He collaborated with Goethe to the end.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gother:
John Gother was an English controversialist whose Papist Misrepresented and Represented defended Catholic doctrine with Swift-like clarity. Educated a strict Presbyterian, he converted, entered the English College at Lisbon in 1668, was ordained in 1682, and returned to the London mission, devoting himself to controversial writing from 1685.

His famous work lists vulgar errors about Catholic doctrine and practice with masterly refutations, still apt today except for its remarks on papal infallibility. It drew no less an antagonist than Stillingfleet and a host of Anglican divines into a long exchange of answers and rejoinders, through which Gother single-handed more than held his ground. Dryden jested that Gother was the only person besides himself with a command of written English. He died at sea while sailing to Lisbon in 1704.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gower:
John Gower was a wealthy English poet of the fourteenth century, friend of Chaucer and author of the Confessio Amantis. Born between 1327 and 1330, probably in Kent, he owned land in Norfolk, Suffolk, and Kent, and stood well at court. In the first version of his great poem he tells how Richard II met him in a boat on the Thames. The king invited him aboard the royal barge, asking him to write something new.

Though once misidentified as a judge and as a clerk holding a rectory, Gower calls himself a simple layman, not in holy orders. He married Agnes Groundolf about 1397, living in the priory of Saint Mary Overy in Southwark, which he endowed generously. Blind about 1400, he died in October 1408; burial was in the priory chapel, where his effigy tomb can still be seen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gray-fos:
John Gray Foster was an American soldier and engineer who converted to Catholicism during the Civil War. Born at Whitfield, New Hampshire, in 1823, he graduated from West Point in 1846. He served in the Engineer Corps in Mexico, where he was wounded at Molino del Rey. He taught engineering at West Point from 1855 to 1857.

In command at Fort Moultrie when the war broke out, he moved his garrison to Fort Sumter on the night of 26 December 1860. He won a brevet majority for its defense. Made brigadier-general of volunteers in October 1861, he was baptized in New York that November. He commanded the Department of North Carolina, then Virginia and North Carolina, then Ohio until a fall from his horse. He later aided Sherman at Charleston and Savannah, commanding Florida in 1865 and 1866 before work on harbors and submarine blasting.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gropper:
John Gropper was a German jurist and theologian who drafted the reform decrees of the Cologne synod of 1536. Born at Soest in 1503, he entered Cologne University at fourteen and took his doctorate in civil law in 1525. Studying theology privately and without a master, he became known as the mouth of the Cologne clergy. He held canonries at Xanten and Soest and advised Archbishop Hermann von Wied on church and civil law.

At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 he came into closer touch with Melanchthon. For the Cologne synod he formulated the old canons on clerical duties so clearly that the synod adopted them nearly unchanged and asked him for a handbook. His Enchiridion of 1538 expounded the Apostles' Creed, the seven sacraments, the Lord's Prayer, and the Decalogue. Later editions spread across Europe, though the work eventually reached the Index of prohibited books.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-james-sc:
John James Scheffmacher was an Alsatian Jesuit theologian famed for converting Lutherans by preaching and by letters. Born at Kientzheim in 1668, he became a leading theologian of his age and an orator of power and influence. He labored for years to bring Lutherans back to the Church, winning great numbers by his work.

While teaching theology at Strasburg's Catholic university, he was appointed in 1715 to the chair of apologetics founded by Louis XIV in the cathedral. He served as university rector from 1728 to 1731. His best-known writings are letters setting out with clear, solid arguments the Catholic doctrines that experience taught him troubled Protestants most. They were collected as Letters of a German Doctor and Letters of a Theologian, alongside his Controversial Catechism, later called Light in the Darkness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-kramer:
John Kramer, also called Institor, was a Carthusian of Buxheim whose ascetic writings were much read in medieval monasteries. Born near the end of the fourteenth century, he entered the charterhouse of Buxheim in Bavaria. He lived there as a pious, obedient religious until his death between 1437 and 1440.

His Breviloquium teaches a religious the practices that keep him a faithful child of the Church and lead to perfection on earth and happiness in heaven. It then warns, by a quaint allegory of twenty birds of prey, eagle, vulture, hawk, and owl among them, against the faults of monastic life. His second work exhorts readers to avoid evil anger. Though written in a rude, uncultured style, both books show the rigorous Carthusian asceticism of the fifteenth century, softened by touches of mystical tenderness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-milner:
John Milner was an English bishop, historian, and controversialist who rebuilt Catholic life at Winchester. Born in London in 1752, he was sent at thirteen by Bishop Challoner to Douai, spent twelve years there, and was ordained in 1777. Two years later he went to Winchester to help French prisoners struck by fever, and when the pastor died of it, Milner took his place permanently.

He stayed twenty-three years, rebuilding the chapel, founding a school, and sheltering Benedictine nuns from Brussels and Franciscans from Bruges among the refugee religious flooding England. His History of Winchester of 1798 showed remarkable power and learning and sparked controversy with a cathedral prebendary. Through the double crisis of English Catholicism, internal division and revolutionary exile, Milner emerged as a writer and bishop of formidable energy, dying at Wolverhampton in 1826.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-nider:
John Nider was a German Dominican reformer and theologian of the conciliar age. Born in Swabia in 1380, he entered the Dominicans at Colmar.
