He studied at Vienna and Cologne, where he was ordained, and won wide fame as a preacher, active at the Council of Constance. After studying strict-observance convents in Italy he taught theology at Vienna from 1425.

Prior at Nuremberg in 1427, socius to his master general, and vicar of reformed convents, he became prior of strict-observance Basle in 1431. He served the Council of Basle as theologian and legate, journeying to the Hussites and pacifying them, and to Ratisbon in 1434 for further reconciliation. When Eugene IV dissolved Basle he first favored continuing the council in Germany, then yielded to the pope. He resumed Vienna lectures in 1436 and served twice as university dean before his death in 1438. His Formicarius treated philosophical, theological, and social questions of the day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-spenser:
John Spenser was an English Jesuit controversialist of the Commonwealth age. Born in Lincolnshire in 1601, Cambridge converted him, and he entered the Society of Jesus in 1627. He professed moral theology at Liege in 1642 and served the arduous camp mission before returning to England.

At Whitsuntide 1657 he took part in a much-discussed conference with the Anglican divines Peter Gunning and John Pearson, later Bishops of Ely and Chester. All of them were Cambridge men who may have known one another. An account appeared at Paris in 1658 as Schism Unmasked, Spenser its likely author. He also wrote Thirty-Six Questions to the Doctors of the Reformed Religion in 1657 and Scripture Mistaken in 1660, winning a high name as a controversialist. He died as chaplain to the Earl of Shrewsbury in 1671.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-tauler:
John Tauler was a German Dominican mystic and preacher, one of the greatest of the Middle Ages. Born at Strasburg about 1300 to a prosperous citizen, he entered the Dominicans there as a youth, drawn by the order's ascetic life. He studied at Cologne, where he knew Eckhart and probably Henry Suso. From about 1339 to 1347 he lived at Basle, center with Henry of Nordlingen of the Friends of God, lay and religious seekers of the mystical life.

Returning to Strasburg as a preacher, he won praise for a fiery tongue that kindled the world, and Rulman Merswin chose him as confessor. The Meisterbuch tells of a master of Scripture, long taken for Tauler, who was humbled by a layman. He lived two years in seclusion and preached again with such power that forty hearers fell into convulsions. Tauler died at Strasburg in 1361, his sermons remaining a treasury of Rhineland mysticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-taverner:
John Taverner was an English composer of masses and motets whose Western Wynde Mass remains his best-known work. Born in Norfolk about 1475, Boston Parish Church had him as organist from 1500 to 1525. Cardinal Wolsey then made him master of the choristers at Cardinal College, Oxford. His fame as organist and choirmaster was matched, if not surpassed, by his powers as a composer.

He stayed at Oxford until 1533, then retired to Boston. On Foxe's word in the Book of Martyrs he has been branded a heretic. But Foxe more than likely confused him with a Cromwell correspondent or with Richard Taverner, who revised Matthew's Bible. For the English service he wrote nothing, but left eight masses, Latin Magnificats, and the four-part In Nomine, adapted into two English anthems. They mark him a composer of the first rank and a pioneer for Shepherd, Byrd, and Tallis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-thayer:
John Thayer was a Boston minister who became the first native of New England ordained a Catholic priest. Born in Boston in 1755 to early Puritan settlers, he kept much of their stern character through life. Educated at Yale, he served as a Congregationalist chaplain in the Revolution under John Hancock. He then wandered Europe and was in Rome at the death of the beggar saint Benedict Joseph Labre.

Trying to dispute Labre's miracles, Thayer was instead converted on 25 May 1783. His printed account of it, one of the first by a prominent New England Protestant, created a controversial sensation in several languages. Ordained at Paris in 1789, he returned to lead Boston's new Catholic congregation but failed as pastor through an erratic, contentious temper. He then missioned in Virginia and Kentucky before settling at Limerick, Ireland, where he died in 1815, leaving funds that founded Boston's Ursuline convent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-the-fast:
John the Faster was Patriarch of Constantinople from 582 to 595, famous chiefly for claiming the title Ecumenical Patriarch. Brought up at Constantinople, he served as deacon at Hagia Sophia under John Scholasticus, then as sakellarios, or patriarchal vicar for monasteries. Little learned but famed for ascetic life, he was already called the Faster before becoming patriarch on Eutychius's death, favored by Emperors Tiberius II and Maurice.

The title dispute turned on a real distinction: earlier patriarchs had been addressed as ecumenical in compliment, but none had called himself so until John IV. In 588 he held a synod at Constantinople to examine charges against Gregory of Antioch, an act itself asserting his claim. Tolerant toward Monophysites yet persuading Maurice to burn the wizard Paulinus, he kept a high name for asceticism and charity to the poor until his death in 595.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jose-viader:
José Viader was a Catalan Franciscan who served the Indian mission at Santa Clara in California for nearly four decades. Born in Catalonia in 1765, he took the Franciscan habit at Barcelona in 1788, joined the missionary college of San Fernando in Mexico, and reached California in 1796. He worked as assistant at Santa Clara until 1833, when he returned to Spain.

For thirty-three years he was the close companion of Father Magín Catalá, handling letters and reports and standing up to soldiers and settlers who pressed on the mission. Strong and brave, he once fought off three attackers who then became his friends. Like most missionaries, he refused in 1826 to swear allegiance to the new Mexican republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-anton-g:
Josef Anton Gegenbauer was a German painter of history scenes and portraits who lived from 1800 to 1876. Born at Wangen in Württemberg, he trained at the Royal Academy in Munich and then spent years in Rome studying Raphael. Back home, the king named him court painter and set him the Royal Villa of Rosenstein to decorate.

Fresco painting was his great strength. Between 1836 and 1854 he covered the Stuttgart royal palace with sixteen fresco scenes from Württemberg history. His oil paintings ranged from Madonnas and the Crucifixion to myths such as Leda and the Swan and Hercules and Omphale. Readers get a full roll call of a busy court artist's output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-fessler:
Josef Fessler was an Austrian bishop who served as secretary of the First Vatican Council. Born to peasant parents near Bregenz in 1813, he was ordained in 1837, taught church history and canon law at Brixen and Vienna, and became Bishop of St. Pölten in 1864. Pope Pius IX chose him to run the council's secretariat in 1869.

Fessler's writings on the early Church Fathers, called patrology, were long valued by students. His book The True and False Infallibility of the Popes defended the council's teaching on papal infallibility in moderate terms. Even Bishop Hefele, who had opposed the definition, agreed with Fessler's view, and Pius IX warmly approved the book.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-josef-speckba:
Josef Speckbacher was a Tyrolean peasant soldier who fought to free his homeland from French and Bavarian rule in 1809. Born at Gnadenwald near Hall in 1767, he learned to read only as an adult, worked in the imperial salt mines, and became a crack shot. He joined Andreas Hofer's rising and took part, by his own diary, in thirty-six battles and skirmishes that year.

Speckbacher seized Hall, fought at Mount Isel, and besieged Kufstein castle, at times acting as commander and even as a spy inside the fortress. After defeat he hid in the mountains through a harsh winter and was hurt in an avalanche. He then fled to Vienna, where Emperor Francis I gave him a chain of honor and a pension.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-biner:
Joseph Biner was a Swiss Jesuit canonist, historian, and theologian famed for vast learning. Born at Gluringen in 1697, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1715 and taught canon law, the Church's legal system, at Ingolstadt, Dillingen, and Innsbruck. He threw himself into disputes with Protestant writers, so nearly all his books carry a polemical edge.

His masterpiece, Apparatus eruditionis ad jurisprudentiam ecclesiasticam, ran to eight volumes from 1754 to 1766. Arranged by centuries, it stores church council history, treaties, and essays on Jansenism and other disputes. Even critics praised its learning, though poor arrangement and the lack of an index made it hard to use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-charle:
Joseph Charles Benzinger was the Swiss founder of the Benziger Catholic publishing house. Born at Einsiedeln in 1762, he opened a small trade in religious goods in 1792, fled the French invasion, and returned in 1800 to a town stripped by pillage. With his fortune gone, he rebuilt as a bookseller and helped his county through the famine of 1817.

His sons Charles and Nicholas took over in 1833 and added lithographed religious pictures, power presses, stereotyping, and a New York house in 1853. Charles shaped the literary side and the Einsiedler Kalender, while Nicholas drove the technical advances. The firm grew into a Catholic book house known around the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ferdin:
Joseph Ferdinand Damberger was a Bavarian church historian who lived from 1795 to 1859. Born at Passau, he studied law at Landshut, then theology at Salzburg, Landshut, and Munich, taking ordination in 1818. He preached at Landshut and Munich before joining the Society of Jesus in 1837 and teaching church history at Lucerne.

Expelled from Switzerland with the Jesuits after the Sonderbund defeat in 1847, he ended his days as confessor at Schäftlarn. His great work, a synchronized history of Church and world in the Middle Ages, reached the year 1378, with its last volume finished after his death. For its day it showed wide learning, though critics found it short on rigor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-gabrie:
Joseph Gabriel Rheinberger was a Liechtenstein composer and organist who taught Europe's young musicians for forty years. Born at Vaduz in 1839, he played his parish organ at seven and wrote a three-voice Mass at eight. After the Munich conservatory, he became its professor of theory and organ in 1859 and later royal court conductor.

Rheinberger wrote some two hundred works, including oratorios, operas, cantatas, and symphonies. His twenty organ sonatas stand as the finest in that form since Mendelssohn, and his twelve Masses rank high as art, though some handle their texts weakly. The entry praises his invention, masterful craft, and noble, solid style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-georg-:
Joseph Georg Strossmayer was the Croatian bishop of Diakovo who championed South Slav culture. Born at Osijek in 1815 to German peasant settlers, he studied theology at Diakovo and Budapest, was ordained in 1838, and became bishop in 1849. At the Vatican Council he stood out as a speaker against papal infallibility, praised even by the pope for his fine Latin.

After long holding out, he published the council's decrees in 1872 and later proclaimed his submission to Rome. He spent diocesan revenues on schools, a seminary, the South Slav academy at Zagreb in 1867, its university in 1874, and a picture gallery. In politics he backed the Croatian national party and Pan-Slavism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-guegle:
Joseph Gügler was a Swiss priest and Scripture scholar who renewed theology teaching at Lucerne. Born at Udligerschwil near Lucerne in 1782, a delicate boy with no regular schooling, he read his father's books until he knew the whole Bible by twelve. He studied at Einsiedeln, Solothurn, and Lucerne, and took up theology at Landshut under Sailer.

Ordained in 1805, he became professor of exegesis, the study of Scripture's meaning, at the Lucerne lyceum and canon of St. Leodegar. With his friend Widmer he urged students to think for themselves and drop stale notions. Their new methods drew fire from defenders of the old school and from followers of Wessenberg.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-hergen:
Joseph Hergenröther was a German church historian, canonist, and first Cardinal-Prefect of the Vatican Archives. Born at Würzburg in 1824, the son of a medicine professor, he studied at Rome's German College until the troubles of 1848 cut his course short. Ordained that year, he took his doctorate at Munich and taught canon law and church history at Würzburg.

Hergenröther wrote on St. Gregory Nazianzen's teaching on the Trinity and on Protestant theories of the Church's origins. At Würzburg he joined Hettinger and Denzinger in a brilliant theology faculty whose fame spread widely. His later career carried him to Rome, where he headed the Vatican Archives as cardinal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ignati:
Joseph Ignatius Ritter was a Silesian church historian who lived from 1787 to 1857. Born at Schweinitz, he studied at Breslau, was ordained in 1811, and worked in parishes before a translation of St. John Chrysostom on the priesthood won him a doctorate. Prussia named him professor of church history at Bonn in 1823 and later professor and canon at Breslau.

As diocesan administrator from 1840 to 1843, Ritter made up for earlier leanings toward Hermes' system by a firm Catholic stand, notably on mixed marriages. He also defended the Church against Ronge's German Catholics and gave generously to needy students. His Handbook of Church History and his history of the Breslau diocese were his chief works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-maria-:
Joseph Maria Pernter was an Austrian scientist who rebuilt Vienna's weather service. Born in Tyrol in 1848, he joined the Jesuits, taught physics, and left the order in 1877 over a head ailment. He took a physics doctorate at Vienna, joined the Central Meteorological Institute in 1878, and became its director and a Vienna professor in 1897.

Pernter enlarged the staff from fifteen to thirty-one, added a laboratory, a seismic bureau, and balloon ascents, and renamed the body for meteorology and earth science. His great work on atmospheric optics gathered all published studies on sky light. He also tested hail-shooting with care and delivered the practice its death blow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-michel:
Joseph-Michel Montgolfier was the French paper maker who, with his brother Etienne, invented the hot-air balloon. Born at Vidalon-lès-Annonay in 1740, the son of a prosperous paper manufacturer, he set up his own works with his brother Augustin and improved paper, stereotyping, and air pumps. With Etienne he also built the hydraulic ram.

Watching a sheet rise over a fire, the brothers tried taffeta balloons filled with heated air. Before the Estates of Vivarais at Annonay on 5 June 1783, their globe rose about six thousand six hundred feet and landed gently a mile and a half away. The Academy of Sciences hailed a new art, and manned balloon flights soon followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-o-dwye:
Joseph O'Dwyer was an American doctor who invented intubation for diphtheria. Born at Cleveland in 1841, he studied medicine in New York, graduated in 1865, and joined the staff of the New York Foundling Asylum in 1872. There he watched children suffocate as diphtheria closed the windpipe, called the larynx, and set out to hold it open.

Wire springs and speculums failed, but a tube of his own design stayed in place, with tools to insert and remove it. After a dozen years of study, the method won over skeptical colleagues and spread worldwide. His tubes also serve in other narrowings of the windpipe, from burns to syphilis. He died in New York in 1898.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-of-exe:
Joseph of Exeter was a twelfth-century English Latin poet known as Josephus Iscanus. Born at Exeter, he studied at Gueldres about 1180, where he formed a lifelong friendship with Guibert, later Abbot of Florennes. In the following years he wrote his celebrated poem on the Trojan War in six books, De bello Trojano.

The poem, dedicated to Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, was later printed in corrupt form under the name Cornelius Nepos. Joseph joined Baldwin's crusade to the Holy Land and, after the archbishop's death in 1190, returned home. He marked the crusade in his Antiocheis, of which only fragments survive. Nothing more is known of his life or death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-othmar:
Joseph Othmar Rauscher was the Prince-Archbishop of Vienna who negotiated Austria's Concordat with Rome. Born at Vienna in 1797, he studied law and poetry, overcame his parents' objections to enter Holy Orders, and taught church history and canon law at Salzburg. In 1849 Cardinal Schwarzenberg named him Prince-Bishop of Seckau.

Rauscher took the leading part in the great episcopal assembly of 1849, drafting its program and memorials. As imperial plenipotentiary from 1852, he spent seven hard months in Rome negotiating the Concordat and entered St. Stephen's as Prince-Archbishop of Vienna in 1853. He led Austria's Catholic revival until his death in 1875.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-putzer:
Joseph Putzer was a Tyrolean Redemptorist theologian and canonist in America. Born at Rodeneck in 1836, he joined the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer in 1856 and was ordained in 1859. He reached New York in 1876, served at Baltimore and Buffalo, and in 1887 took Ilchester's chair of moral theology and canon law in Maryland.

Putzer is best known for his Commentarium in Facultates Apostolicas, a guide to faculties granted by Rome, which he revised into nearly a new work through five editions. Roman journals praised its clarity, depth, and precision. He also wrote on confessors of exempt religious and on the jubilee of 1901, leaving many manuscripts unpublished at his death in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-tieffe:
Joseph Tieffentaller was a Jesuit missionary who became the first European to describe India exactly. Born at Bozen in Tyrol in 1710, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1729 and reached India in 1740, serving chiefly in the Mughal Empire. After the order's suppression he stayed in India and died at Lucknow in 1785.

A master of Latin, Italian, Spanish, French, Hindustani, Arabic, Persian, and Sanskrit, Tieffentaller wrote a Descriptio Indiae covering twenty-two provinces with towns, fortresses, and positions fixed by quadrant. His great map book on the Ganges basin, drawn with a compass from Prayaga to Calcutta, was called an enormous labor. He also wrote on Indian religions, astronomy, and nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-von-fr:
Joseph von Fraunhofer was a Bavarian optician who founded spectrum analysis. Born at Straubing in 1787, the tenth son of a poor glass grinder, he lost both parents at twelve and was apprenticed unpaid to a mirror maker. A house collapse in 1801 brought him to Utzschneider's notice, and the king's gift of eighteen ducats bought his freedom.

Fraunhofer built better glass, lenses, and testing machines, ending England's lead in optics. He made the spherometer, the screw micrometer, and the heliometer for telescopes. His fame rests above all on the dark lines he found in the Sun's spectrum, now called Fraunhofer lines, which opened the study of light from stars and flames. He died at Munich in 1826.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-widmer:
Joseph Widmer was a Swiss theologian who revived church life at Lucerne with his friend Gügler. Born at Hohenrain in 1779, he read philosophy at Lucerne and theology at Landshut under Sailer, whose influence stayed with him for life. Ordained, he became Lucerne's philosophy professor in 1804 and its moral and pastoral theology professor in 1819.

Removed by the government in 1833, Widmer took a canonry at Beromünster and became its provost in 1841. With Gügler he opposed Wessenberg's teachings and worked to renew Swiss Catholic life. His books include The Catholic Pastor and lectures on pastoral theology, and he edited the works of Sailer, Geiger, and Gügler. He died at Beromünster in 1844.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-of-spe:
Julian of Speyer was a thirteenth-century Franciscan composer of the great saints' offices. Born at Speyer, he studied at Paris, directed music at the royal chapel under Philip Augustus and Louis VIII, and joined the new Franciscan order, accompanying Simon Angelicus to Germany in 1227. He later served as choir-master at the Paris Minorite convent.

Julian composed the rhymed Office of St. Francis between 1229 and 1235 and that of St. Anthony of Padua after 1241, works still sung by the Minorites. Their harmony, rhythm, rhyme, and sublime musical feeling are called unequaled of their kind, and their verses were widely copied, often set to his melodies unchanged. He died at Paris about 1250.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julien-garnie:
Julien Garnier was a French Jesuit called the Apostle of the Senecas. Born at Connerai in 1642, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1660, sailed to Canada in 1662, and became the first Jesuit ordained there in 1668. He served the Oneida briefly, then the Onondaga, whose chief Garaconthié rebuilt his chapel of St. Mary at his request.

From 1671 Garnier preached among the Senecas, staying even after fire destroyed his chapel and village, and he pleaded with Governor de la Barre for moderation toward them in 1683. Recalled during the wars, he returned after the Montreal treaty of 1701 and stayed until 1709. His notes and letters remain a chief source on the Seneca Iroquois. He died at Quebec in 1730.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-caesar:
Julius Caesar Scaliger was an Italian humanist who settled in France and attacked Erasmus. Born at Riva on Lake Garda in 1484, he came to France as physician to the Bishop of Agen and took French citizenship. His violent Oration for Cicero against Erasmus of 1531 defended Cicero's absolute perfection and called Erasmus a parasite and parricide.

Scaliger's calmer De causis linguae latinae of 1540 found 634 errors in Valla and earlier grammarians. His seven books on poetics, published after his death in 1561, made imitation the base of poetry after Aristotle and ranked Virgil above Homer and Seneca beside the Greek tragedians. A botanist as well, he urged plant classes by form, not use. He died at Agen in 1558.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-ficker:
Julius Ficker was an Austrian historian of law, politics, and diplomacy. Born at Paderborn in 1826, he read history and law, first at Bonn, then Münster and Berlin, and at Frankfurt in 1848 he befriended the historian Böhmer. Count Thun called him to Innsbruck as professor of general history in 1852, and in 1863 he moved to the law faculty, drawing devoted pupils.

Ficker broke new ground in each field, from imperial archives at Pisa to the origins of the Sachsenspiegel and the science of charters in his Beiträge zur Urkundenlehre. Against Sybel he argued that Austria, blending many peoples, best suited the old empire's heir in Central Europe. Ennobled in 1879, he later edited Böhmer's Acta Imperii selecta. He died at Innsbruck in 1902.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kajetan-georg:
Kajetan Georg von Kaiser was a Bavarian chemist whose work centered on fermentation. Born at Kelheim on the Danube in 1803, he became professor of technology at the University of Munich in 1851. In 1868 he moved to the technical high school in the same city as professor of applied chemistry. A saccharometer he invented in 1842 measured the percentages in wort, the liquid from which beer is brewed.

Besides journal articles, he published a Munich paper of 1846 on beer testing and the errors it invites. He also edited the collected writings of his friend Johann Nepomuk von Fuchs, adding an obituary of the chemist and mineralogist. An obituary of Kaiser himself praised a Catholic belief that stayed invulnerable through every trial, including the years 1870 and 1871. Fermentation chemistry, not controversy, was the ground of his reputation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-ludwig-v:
Karl Ludwig von Haller was a professor of constitutional law, born at Berne in 1768 and dead at Solothurn in 1854. Grandson of the poet Albrecht von Haller, he had little schooling and entered the Bernese chancery at fifteen. Self-study filled the gaps, and at nineteen he became clerk of a public commission. As diet and legation secretary he traveled to Geneva, Ulm, Lugano, Milan, and Paris, meeting Bonaparte and Talleyrand.

The new freedom made him an opponent of the Revolution. His Helvetische Annalen attacked the revolutionary authorities so bitterly that it was suppressed and he fled. His Restauration der Staatswissenschaft, six volumes from 1816 to 1834, rejects revolutionary doctrine. In 1821 his conversion to Catholicism became public and cost him his office; his letter to his family ran through some fifty editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-lueger:
Karl Lueger, Vienna's burgomaster, political leader, and municipal reformer, was born there in 1844 and died there in 1910. His father was a peasant's son keeping the Institute of Technology; his mother was a cabinet maker's daughter. After the Theresianum and law school, he practiced from 1874, winning rank by quick judgment and courtroom eloquence.

Entering politics in 1872, he turned against a Liberalism enriching capitalists at the small tradesman's cost. Elected to the council in 1875 and 1876, he resigned over exposed corruption and led the anti-corruption movement from 1878. His United Christians elected him burgomaster in 1895, though he first declined for want of a majority. After stronger September returns and a fifth election in 1897, the emperor confirmed him, and his later years went to guiding the party and remaking Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-maria-fr:
Karl Maria Friedrich Ernst von Weber was a composer born at Eutin in 1786 and dead in London in 1826. His father, an impoverished nobleman turned strolling manager, gave the boy stage routine but hindered his education. He still learned violin, piano, and harmony well, guided by Michael Haydn and Abbé Vogler. At Vogler's recommendation he conducted the Breslau opera in 1804, but youth kept him from discipline and he left within a year.

After serving Württemberg princes and exile in 1810, he spent three years composing and concertizing. In 1813 he took the Prague opera, and in 1816 Saxony's king called him to Dresden to organize a German opera company. At Dresden, steeped in folk song and liberation poetry, he founded the romantic school of music. He became a force for throwing off the foreign yoke in politics and art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-muller:
Karl Müller was a Düsseldorf professor and Nazarene painter, born at Darmstadt in 1818 and dead at Neuenahr in 1893. The Nazarenes won Düsseldorf new renown abroad with popular, beautiful renderings of religious devotion. His delicate, almost soft style carried the naturalness and fresh piety his subjects demanded. In 1837 Schadow chose him, aged nineteen, with his brother Andreas and Deger, for Remagen's Apollinarisberg frescoes.

In Rome from the end of 1839, he matured his talent among the treasures of Rome, Florence, Pisa, and Assisi. Four years later he brought home a German religious style lightly touched with southern elements. His Crowning and Birth of Mary, finished in 1850, ranked him with the elder Deger. The Crowning's lower part, apostles by the grave amid lilies and roses, became widely known. The Birth of Mary sought to satisfy Raphael and Dürer at once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knights-of-th: This 1913 reference article on the Knights of the Redeemer — a chivalric order. Charles Moeller surveys its brief record. Little more than its name survives. The entry keeps its modest fame. The crusading age knew its cross. Its 13th-century cross is famed. Its brief record is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-konstantin-vo: This 1913 reference piece on Höfler — the Prague historian. Patricius Schlager honors his famous works. His pen chronicled the Bohemian past. The university prized its learned son. The archives keep his name. His 1897 death is famed. His 1897 works are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kremsmunster: A 1913 entry on Kremsmünster — the Austrian abbey. Oswald Hunter-Blair gives its storied past. Its monks guard the ancient library. The ages bless the holy house. The Danube guards its walls. Its 777 founding is famed. Its library is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-laurenz-forer: This 1913 reference article on Forer — the Jesuit writer. Anthony Maas catalogs his works. Little is known of his career. The seventeenth century was his era. The order prized its learned son. His 1690 works are famed. His 1690 writings are famed. His 1690 Jesuit pages are famed.

character:
Samuel Smiles, the Victorian apostle of self-help, turned from success to Character in this book of moral essays. Smiles argues that character, not genius, rules life: men of integrity command trust and imitation in every station. Chapters treat the influence of character, duty, industry, courage, self-control, and companionship, drawing examples from statesmen, soldiers, artists, and working men.

Quotations from Emerson, Luther, and Burke head the chapters, and short lives do the persuading. Smiles insists that ordinary people, denied chances of greatness, can still act honestly in small things. Character followed his best-selling Self-Help and shares its faith that nations rise on the cultivated citizens they produce. It is earnest, anecdotal instruction for the ambitious Victorian reader.
chaucer:
Adolphus William Ward wrote this life of Geoffrey Chaucer for the English Men of Letters series, a set of short literary biographies. Ward, a Cambridge scholar, built the account on public records and the Chaucer Society's research. He warns readers that many dates in the poet's life stay uncertain. Documents, not legend, set the limits of his story.

Four chapters divide the work, covering Chaucer's times, his life and writings, his character as a poet, and a short epilogue. Ward traces a courtier, soldier, customs official, and member of Parliament who also wrote the Canterbury Tales. He weighs which poems are truly Chaucer's and which later hands added. A glossary and index close the volume for student use. Readers who want a compact, careful Victorian life of the first great English poet, with the evidence shown, will find this volume serviceable and clear.
cicero-de-officiis-miller:
Cicero wrote On Duties in late 44 BC, in the last months of his life, as a letter of advice to his son Marcus. Walter Miller's English translation is the text here. The old statesman, shut out of power after Caesar's murder, turned to teaching his son how to live in public life.

The three books weigh what is honorable, what is useful, and what to do when the two seem to clash. Cicero insists the useful and the honorable are one in the end. He treats justice, kindness, courage, and the duties of rulers and citizens. The book trained Europe's gentlemen and statesmen for two thousand years.
clotel-or-the-president-s-daughter:
William Wells Brown, who had escaped slavery himself, published Clotel in 1853, and it is often called the first novel by an African American author. The title figure is Clotel, daughter of Currer, an enslaved woman who had kept house for Thomas Jefferson and borne him two daughters. When Jefferson leaves for Washington, Currer and the girls are sold at auction in Richmond.

Brown follows Clotel and her sister Althesa through sales, separations, and escapes, mixing their story with speeches, songs, and newspaper matter against slavery. The president's daughter of the title ends as property in the republic her father helped found. Brown meant the irony to burn, and the novel still works as abolitionist argument in story form.
cowboy-dave-or-the-round-up-at-rolling-r:
Cowboy Dave, or the Round-Up at Rolling River, by Frank V Webster, is a western for boys from a writer whose list fills a page of ranch and school stories. Webster, author of Only a Farm Boy, Bob the Castaway, and Comrades of the Saddle, sets his hero among cattle at the season when herds are gathered, counted, and branded. The round up of the title is the year's hardest and most public work.

Dave's proving ground is that work itself: riding, roping, and judgment under the eyes of older hands. Missing cattle, disputed ownership, and the river country around Rolling River supply the friction that boys' westerns require. Webster wrote to a formula his readers trusted. A young rider's honesty is tested against rustlers and accidents. A reputation is made the way a brand is set. It is done in the open, and for good.
denzil-quarrier:
George Gissing set Denzil Quarrier in suburban London and a provincial town hungry for politics. Lilian Quarrier keeps a tasteful home on the edge of Clapham Common and waits each evening for her husband. Denzil is rich, restless, and eager for a public career. Their quiet domestic life opens the book in autumn dusk.

Quarrier's ambition draws the couple toward an election contest and the bargaining that surrounds it. Gissing watches how money, newspapers, and local pride shape a candidate's rise. Lilian's devotion is tested as public success demands ever more compromise. The novel asks what a man may hide, and what he may sell, to win a seat and a name. Its pleasures lie in sharp social observation and a marriage watched under growing strain.

early-australian-voyages-pelsart-tasman-:
John Pinkerton's Early Australian Voyages retells the first European encounters with Australia through three Dutch-age sailors, in the 1886 Cassell edition. Pinkerton opens with the long guessing game about a southern continent, from Plato's Atlantis to Bacon's. Then come the voyagers. Pelsart was wrecked with the Batavia on the western coast. Tasman reached Van Diemen's Land and New Zealand. Dampier's voyage, at the century's end, woke England to New Holland.

An introduction surveys the later colonies, from penal Sydney in 1788 to Queensland in 1859, and the continent's strange plants and animals. Pinkerton abridges the old narratives for Victorian school and home readers. The book is exploration history in epitome: shipwreck, mutiny, discovery, and the slow naming of a continent.
elsie-venner:
Oliver Wendell Holmes called Elsie Venner a medicated novel in his own second preface, and warned readers seeking mere amusement away. The story, first serialized in the Atlantic Monthly as The Professor's Story, follows Elsie, a strange, silent girl whose mother was bitten by a rattlesnake before her birth. Holmes builds his plot on that prenatal poisoning: Elsie carries something serpentine in her nature, fascinating and dangerous to the young teacher who loves her.

His prefaces argue the real question openly: how far is a person responsible for a disordered will she did not choose? Original sin, heredity, and moral blame meet in a Massachusetts village tale. Holmes the physician-novelist wrote fiction as an experiment, and Elsie Venner remains his boldest case study.
golden-bough-abridged-1922-frazer:
James George Frazer wrote The Golden Bough, a huge study of magic and religion. The 1922 abridged edition packs his core argument into one volume. Frazer taught at Cambridge and read reports from across the world.

He argues that magic came first, then religion, then science. Kings who were killed for the land's health fill his pages. He compares rites from Africa, Europe, and beyond in one sweep. Later scholars fault his method but not his scope. The book shaped myth study, poetry, and film for a century of readers. Its reach still shows in classrooms today.
gospel-philip-zinner:
Among the codices found at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945 sits a short gospel of sayings and rites. The Gospel of Philip, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that Valentinian text in clear English. The early Christians who prized it read the faith through signs and unions.

Philip speaks of baptism, anointing, and the bridal chamber as doors to a higher world. Its sayings are dense and strange, circling love, name, and image again and again. Scholars use the text to map how one bold school of Christians read the gospel. Mattison's free version puts the odd, rich work in any reader's hands.
gospel-truth-zinner:
Joy at finding what was lost runs through a Valentinian sermon from the first Nag Hammadi codex. The Gospel of Truth, in Mark Mattison's public-domain rendering, gives that meditation in English. It is no tale of Jesus's life, but a preacher's deep talk on rescue.

Error is a fog, the speaker says, and knowledge of the Father is the sun that burns it off. The book speaks of the cross as a tree of fruit and of names written in a living book. Its prose is the most poetic in the whole Nag Hammadi shelf. Mattison's free version lets that music sound in English.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ABCGoodMorningA: Dated June 16, 1977, this letter was written to a contact at ABC-TV at 7 West 66th Street in New York. It encloses a critique connected with a work identified as 'Posner.' The letter discusses a de Mohrenschildt memo and the Dutch journalist Willem Oltmans, both figures in Kennedy assassination research. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text. It survives as a piece of the correspondence that circulated among assassination researchers in the 1970s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADeSilvaPeer_:
Peer de Silva ran the CIA's Saigon station during the early Vietnam years, and Sub Rosa: The CIA and the Uses of Intelligence was his account of the intelligence trade. Anthony Marro reviewed the book, which was published by New York Times Books.

De Silva wrote as an insider defending the craft: what intelligence is for, how it is gathered, and how policymakers misuse it. Reviews like Marro's show how the reading public of the exposure era received a station chief's self-defense. The single review is preserved among the archive's intelligence clippings for students of that debate.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CooperJohnSherm:
Senator John Sherman Cooper of Kentucky served on the Warren Commission, the panel that investigated President Kennedy's murder. A news article preserved here quotes Cooper saying there was no point in reopening the investigation. He also defended the commission's report against its critics, standing by the work he had helped to produce.

Cooper's remarks carry weight because he was inside the inquiry, not commenting from outside it. He had heard the witnesses and weighed the evidence himself. The article captures a commission member holding his ground years after the report came out, while public doubt about its findings kept growing around him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CubanPower_Cuba: A federal indictment in United States v. Orlando Bosch Avila was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, case number 68-420-Cr-WM. Bosch was a leading figure in the militant anti-Castro exile movement. The archived record preserves the indictment's caption, court, and case number. The surviving evidence does not spell out each charge. The document stands here as the formal opening of that prosecution.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Nagy-TalaveraNi:
Wallace Turner reported for the New York Times from San Francisco, in a story dated February 20, on Nicholas M. Nagy-Talavera. Nagy-Talavera was a Hungarian refugee who had fled to the United States in 1957. He said he then served as a CIA information source for two years.

His troubles, in his account, began with a 1959 visit to Cuba. The article traces how a refugee's work for the agency followed him into later difficulties. Stories like his filled the era's newspapers: defectors and exiles whose intelligence ties were both livelihood and liability. Turner's report preserves the man's claims and the outline of his case as he presented it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NashRambler_Nas: Special Agent Earle Haley of the FBI's Dallas office wrote this memorandum on November 23, 1963, the day after the assassination. It was filed under Dallas number 89-43, the assassination file. The memo's subject line is garbled in the scan, so what Haley reported cannot be stated. The file is kept under a Nash Rambler heading, a car reference from the inquiry. What survives is the date, the author, and the file number.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PLetter_P_Lette:
Peter Lemkin wrote this personal letter from Coronado, California, to a man named Pertti, on April 12, 1989. His subject is the investigations into the assassination of Swedish prime minister Olof Palme. The letter is followed by unrelated material on the Lockerbie bombing, the destruction of Pan Am Flight 103. The file is a multi-document compilation.

Two famous unsolved attacks sit side by side in one envelope's worth of paper. Lemkin writes as a private student of the Palme case, sharing what he has gathered. The Lockerbie pages that follow belong to a different inquiry entirely. Compilations like this show how researchers filed by sender rather than subject, so one man's letter could carry two cases at once.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TLetter_T_Lette: nsia-TLetter T Letter: the declassified government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, preserved as released. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WritersOther_Wr: W. C. Sullivan recommended, in an FBI memo dated November 15, 1966, that the bureau cooperate with writer Richard J. Whalen. Whalen was preparing a piece for the Saturday Evening Post. Sullivan ran domestic intelligence work, and his memo shows the bureau choosing which journalists to help. Such choices shaped what the public read about the FBI and the Kennedy investigation.
govdocs-archive_org-spirit-mind-vol-1-2-: Nicolai Levashov's Spirit and Mind, volumes 1 and 2, reached English readers in translation from the Russian. Levashov taught a system joining the spirit, the mind, and hidden structures of living things. The library holds the set as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. The two volumes give his followers' core text in full, for readers studying his movement.
govdocs-archive_org-the-mystery-of-the-o: Hyranio Garbho takes up a long argument in The Mystery of Oera Linda: is the Oera Linda Book real? The manuscript claims to be an ancient Frisian chronicle. Most scholars judge it a nineteenth-century fabrication. Garbho's work examines the authenticity debate itself. The question matters because believers built movements on the book. His study serves readers who want the evidence weighed rather than the legend repeated.
govdocs-archive_org-the-ruling-class-gae:
Gaetano Mosca, an Italian political scientist, published The Ruling Class in 1896. Its claim is simple and bleak: in every society, a small organized minority rules the large disorganized majority, whatever the constitution says.

Mosca argues that the ruling group keeps power through organization, shared interests, and a political formula that makes its rule seem natural and right. Elections change faces, he says, not the structure underneath. The book founded elite theory and helped create modern political sociology. Its full text here lets readers test Mosca's claim against the democracies of our own day.
govdocs-archive_org-the-spiritist-fallac:
René Guénon published The Spiritist Fallacy in 1923, his first long attack on the occult fashions of his day. Spiritism claimed that mediums and séances could speak with the dead, and Paris was full of both.

Guénon grants that strange psychic events may occur, then denies that they prove anything about spirits or the afterlife. From the Traditionalist standpoint, he separates real metaphysics from parlour wonders and fraud. The book is a cornerstone of his early work. Readers still use it as the sharpest statement of his case against the séance room.
govdocs-archive_org-the-ultimate-flower_: A short story called The Ultimate Flower opens in the foothills of the Andes, inside a child's memories. From the earth, a hand emerges. That strange image sets the tale's tone, mixing a remembered childhood landscape with something buried and returning. Little else about the story is recorded here. It survives as a single piece of short fiction from the archive's holdings, strange first and explanatory never.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_able-arc:
Able Archer 83 was a NATO command exercise held in November 1983, rehearsing the move to nuclear war. The Censored History of Able Archer 83 argues that its full story is still blacked out in official files.

Soviet leaders watched the exercise closely, and some feared it covered a real attack plan, pushing the superpowers close to war by mistake at the end of 1983. The briefing book collects what has been released and marks what remains censored after forty years. For readers of Cold War history, it shows how much of a famous near-miss the public is still not allowed to read.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CI:
In September 2016 the National Security Archive posted a 1987 CIA special intelligence assessment on the murder of Orlando Letelier. Letelier was a former Chilean diplomat, and he was killed with his colleague Ronni Moffitt in a car bombing in Washington, D.C. in 1976. The assessment reached a blunt conclusion about who gave the order.

The CIA reported that its file review gave convincing evidence that General Augusto Pinochet personally ordered his intelligence chief to carry out the murder. It called the bombing an act of state terrorism on American streets. The posting marked forty years since the attack and put the agency's own words in public view.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Before the 2020 presidential election, the Archive's Cyber Vault project compared the two major parties on technology policy. This posting, dated October 26, 2020, reviews the Democratic and Republican platforms side by side. It asks how each party proposed to handle cyber issues.

Party platforms are promises in writing, and they are rarely read closely on technical subjects. Laying the two texts together shows where the parties agreed, where they split, and what each left vague. For students of cyber policy, the comparison preserves the stated positions of both camps at the moment voters chose between them.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_indonesi:
In 1965 Indonesia's military and allied groups killed hundreds of thousands of people in an anti-communist purge. The United States Embassy in Jakarta tracked that mass murder as it unfolded. This briefing book, posted in October 2017, publishes the embassy's declassified record.

Evidence in the posting is brief beyond the posting date and subject. What the title establishes is central, though: American diplomats were not guessing from afar. They followed the killings closely enough to report them. Their cables are now a primary source for one of the twentieth century's largest mass murders, and for what Washington knew while it happened.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: The Rockefeller Commission investigated CIA abuses in 1975, and its report was supposed to reassure the public. This briefing-book page reports that President Gerald Ford's White House altered that report before release. A whole section on CIA assassination plots was removed, the title states. The evidence supplied here is that headline claim alone, with no documents described. Even so, the claim is specific and serious: the first official inquiry into the agency was itself censored by the executive it examined.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Ireland brought a resolution to the United Nations in the late 1950s urging that nuclear weapons not spread to more countries. That Irish Resolution became a forerunner of the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty. This briefing-book page marks the sixtieth anniversary of the Irish initiative with the Archive's records. The evidence here is the title alone, so the documents cannot be named. The subject deserves its marker: the global nonproliferation regime began partly as a small country's idea, pressed patiently year after year.

Through the 1980s, intelligence reports on Pakistan's nuclear program kept raising tension between Washington and Islamabad. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted in April 2012, on newly released documents from the Reagan years. The reports suggested Pakistan was moving toward a bomb.

The tension had a second cause: Pakistan was also America's partner in supporting Afghan fighters against the Soviets. Officials had to weigh a secret weapons program against a needed alliance, year after year. The documents show that balancing in real time. It is a clean case of nonproliferation policy bending around a war Washington cared about more.

William Burr edited this briefing book, number 834, published in July 2023, on the nuclear football from Eisenhower to George W. Bush. The football's emergency action decrees were called, by American officials themselves, of doubtful legality or even illegal.

Documents show the football formally assigned to Vice President Walter Mondale, an unusual step. Pentagon officials also worried that Vice President Lyndon Johnson had not been briefed on the football at the time of Kennedy's assassination. That gap, at the moment of maximum danger, is the kind of detail only records preserve. The set follows the briefcase as an institution, president by president.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness:
President Dwight Eisenhower spoke of rolling back Soviet control of Eastern Europe, but his private conclusion was bleaker. Ronald D. Landa edited this briefing book, number 581, published in February 2017. It presents an unpublished Defense Department draft history of American attempts to keep the pot simmering in the region.

Eisenhower concluded that neither American military operations nor popular uprisings were feasible against Soviet control. CIA Director Allen Dulles agreed, saying people do not revolt in the face of tanks, artillery, and tear gas, and that revolutions now happen at the top. The documents explain the gap between liberation rhetoric and the caution that governed real policy when Hungary rose in 1956.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p: The last superpower summits were the meetings between American and Soviet leaders that closed the Cold War, above all Ronald Reagan's and George H. W. Bush's encounters with Mikhail Gorbachev. A National Security Archive briefing book page collects the Archive's work under that heading, the same name as the editors' award-winning book on those summits. The evidence here is the page capture itself rather than summit transcripts, so the entry points readers toward the Archive's larger collection on the diplomacy that ended the rivalry without a war.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber: North Korea runs one of the world's most aggressive state hacking programs, funding itself through bank theft and ransomware while probing foreign networks. A National Security Archive cyber brief collects its material under the heading of North Korean cyber operations. It belongs to the Archive's Cyber Vault effort. That effort gathers the public record on state cyber activity. The evidence preserved for this entry is the page capture alone. It serves as an index point for the brief's subject. It is not a document set a reader can search directly.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cybervault_Cyber_:
American military cyber operations grew up fast and largely in secret, and a National Security Archive cyber brief gathers material on how the Department of Defense built and ran them. The brief, edited by Michael Martelle, sits inside the Archive's Cyber Vault project, which works against the overclassification of records about cyberspace.

The brief is paired with a featured article on overclassification and its impact on cyber conflict and democracy, by Jason Healey and a co-author. Their point frames the documents: when nearly everything about cyber operations is secret, the public and even policymakers cannot judge the risks. Readers get both primary material on defense cyber work and a clear argument for why so much of it stays hidden, and what that secrecy costs.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Guatema:
Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police, known as the AHPN, holds millions of records from the country's civil war years and has been used to prosecute human rights crimes. In August 2018, the National Security Archive reported the archive in crisis: its director, Gustavo Meono Brenner, had been abruptly removed by the Guatemalan government.

The removal was one of several moves the Archive said the government and a United Nations office had arranged together. More than fifty remaining staff were put on temporary contracts. Control of the archive also moved, from the national archives, where it had sat since 2009, to the Ministry of Culture and Sports. For readers, the posting shows how an archive can be weakened without being closed, by changing its leadership, its staff terms, and its chain of command.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_southern-cone_Dec: The Trump administration agreed to hand Argentina a trove of declassified American records. They concern the human rights violations of its 1976 to 1983 military dictatorship. A National Security Archive briefing book page announces that turnover. Its headline spells out the whole transaction. Such releases give Argentine courts and families American intelligence files on the junta's crimes, evidence gathered by the government that once worked with the generals. Only the page capture survives here, marking the promise whose fulfillment companion postings describe.
harriet-and-the-piper:
Kathleen Norris's Harriet and the Piper opens at Crownlands, a creamy brick estate on the Hudson. Richard Carter bought the place and let his mother invent a family tradition for it. Two hundred years of Carters, Madame Carter implied, stood behind the name. The beautiful house deserved its neighbours, if not its pedigree.

Harriet Field, a governess-secretary of quiet strength, enters the Carter household. The piper of the title is Ward Peyne, a charming musician whose past Harriet alone knows. His return threatens the daughter of the house, and Harriet must pay for knowledge she never sought. Norris writes domestic melodrama about class, secrecy, and a woman's honour. Crownlands' lawns and garages frame an old question: who shall pay the piper, and how much of another's debt can one good person carry?
hebbel-agnes-bernauer:
A bathhouse keeper's daughter marries Duke Albrecht of Bavaria in secret, and his father orders her drowned as a witch. Hebbel's Agnes Bernauer, given here in German, builds its tragedy on a true fifteenth-century story. Love stands against reason of state, and the state wins by murder.

Agnes herself barely resists; the horror lies in the calm logic that condemns her. Counselors argue necessity, and necessity grinds pity to dust. Hebbel called such collisions the real subject of tragedy, and this play proves his theory. It remains his most moving work for many readers. The drowning at Straubing still echoes through German memory and drama.
her-father-s-daughter:
Gene Stratton-Porter set Her Father's Daughter in California, where Linda Strong, orphaned daughter of a famous naturalist, keeps his canyon botany alive. The contents open with shoes, move to the cotyledon of Multiflores Canyon, and promise a house of dreams and a revolution started by Linda. She knows where clematis and wild iris grow along her brook.

Linda battles a rival at school, helps the newspaperman Donald Whiting, hides her authorship of nature articles, and fights to keep her father's canyon from developers. Stratton-Porter pours her own field knowledge into Linda's yucca trials, bug-catching, and iris plantings. The novel argues that a girl's science and stubbornness are strengths, and it was among her most popular later books.
heu-heu-or-the-monster: Heu-Heu, or The Monster, H. Rider Haggard's African tale. The monster's story. This book preserves that adventure. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
hiram-the-young-farmer:
Burbank L Todd's Hiram the Young Farmer begins with the call of spring at Mrs Atterson's boarding house, where clerk Hiram is stifled by town work and a lost card causes commotion. The contents promise the lure of green fields, a bargain made, beating hoofs, and a girl riding into the tale. Hiram buys a run-down farm and learns farming by doing it.

Early crops, pasture fences, and a heavy cloud of debt season the middle chapters, while Hiram's quick wits rescue neighbors, including a boatload he dares not move until his plan ripens. Todd wrote practical optimism for rural boys of the Progressive era: scientific farming, honest dealing, and a sweetheart named for the fields. The book reads like a farm manual wearing a novel's coat.
homer-iliad-butler:
Homer's Iliad, composed around the eighth century BCE, stands at the head of Western literature. Samuel Butler translated the epic into plain English prose. The poem covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War.

Achilles, insulted by King Agamemnon, withdraws from battle in anger. His friend Patroclus fights in his place and is killed by Hector. Grief drives Achilles back to battle and to Hector's death. Butler believed prose served Homer better than forced English verse. His clear version won many readers. Pride, rage, and pity drive the oldest epic we have.
homer-odyssey-butler:
Homer's Odyssey follows the Iliad as the second great epic of ancient Greece. Samuel Butler translated it into straightforward English prose. Odysseus has fought at Troy and now struggles to get home.

Ten years of wandering bring him monsters, storms, and tempting islands. He outwits the Cyclops, resists the Sirens, and loses every companion. Meanwhile his wife Penelope holds off suitors in Ithaca with patient cunning. Butler argued, unusually, that the poem's author might have been a woman. His prose stays brisk and lucid. The voyage remains the pattern for adventure stories everywhere.
hopes-and-fears-or-scenes-from-the-life-: Hopes and Fears, or scenes from the life of a spinster, by Charlotte Yonge. The single woman's tale. This book preserves that Victorian novel. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
huntingtower: Huntingtower, John Buchan's adventure. The tower's secret. This book preserves that novel. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
in-camp-on-the-big-sunflower:
Lawrence J. Leslie's In Camp on the Big Sunflower is a boys' camp story set by a river, where Max, Owen, Steve and Bandy-legs spend their days. An alarm in the camp opens the book, with Toby staring as if he had seen a ghost while Max and Owen walk the river bank hunting fresh-water clams.

Chapters promise treasure hunting, unknown shell gatherers, a puzzler for Max, a great find, danger on the trail, and a man trap set again. A new cook springs a surprise, and the mystery is solved by the conclusion. Leslie writes in the cheerful, outdoor manner of the camp-story genre, and young readers who like rivers, camps and puzzles will enjoy the Sunflower crew.
in-the-quarter:
Robert W. Chambers's In the Quarter is a novel of young American artists in Paris, opening one evening in May 1888 at the Café des Écoles. Marble-topped tables are wet with beer, the din is appalling, and students shout news from the Salon: Thaxton is in with a number three, while Rhodes and Clifford are out.

Songs about mistresses, fathers, the Code and Bullier's dance hall fill the café, as the young men lament the difficulty of reconciling filial duty with pleasure. Chambers, himself a Paris art student in his youth, writes the Latin Quarter from inside, with its studios, cafés and ambitions. Readers who enjoy novels of bohemian Paris will find In the Quarter fresh, noisy and atmospheric.
indian-summer:
William Dean Howells's Indian Summer opens on the Ponte Vecchio at Florence, where Colville lounges against a jeweller's booth and stares at the Arno. It is a late January afternoon, bright and warm at first, then dimmed by flying grey clouds and threatening rain.

The yellow torrent swells around the bridge piers, rolling toward the Cascine beneath ranks of poplars. Howells, author of The Rise of Silas Lapham, sets his middle-aged American among Florentine domes, towers and society, in a story of late love and second chances. Readers who enjoy Howells's realistic, gently ironic novels will find Indian Summer among his most graceful.
introduction-to-the-compleat-angler:
Andrew Lang wrote this introduction to Izaak Walton's Compleat Angler for the 1896 Dent edition, and it stands alone here as a small book of its own. Lang retells Walton's long, quiet life: born at Stafford in 1593, dead in 1683, having lived under Elizabeth, two Charleses, James, and the Commonwealth. He adds Walton's character as shown in his Lives of poets and churchmen.

The essay then comments on fishing ancient and modern, quoting Walton's predecessors and contemporaries. Lang, a poet and folklorist who fished himself, defends the old book's peaceable charm against a hurried age. Readers get both a biography and a seasoned angler's apology for the gentle art, in Lang's easy, learned prose.
isaac-bickerstaff-physician-and-astrolog:
Richard Steele invented Isaac Bickerstaff, physician and astrologer, as the presiding voice of his Tatler papers, and this volume gathers the Bickerstaff pieces with Henry Morley's introduction. Morley explains the borrowed name: Swift had used Bickerstaff to hoax the almanac-maker Partridge with a prediction of his death. Steele took the astrologer over when the Tatler began in April 1709 and made him a counselor of manners from Shire Lane.

Through Bickerstaff, Steele attacked dueling, defended marriage and women's honor, and told tales of love and loss, including the papers Happy Marriage and A Wife Dead. The essays helped invent the modern periodical essay: short, humane, and amused. Addison's Spectator grew from this soil, but Bickerstaff's warmth is Steele's own.
jack-archer: Jack Archer, G, a. Henty's Crimean War tale, the young soldier. This book preserves that historical novel. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
jane-oglander: Jane Oglander, Marie Belloc Lowndes's novel. Jane's tale. This book preserves that story. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
janice-day-the-young-homemaker:
Helen Beecher Long made Janice Day the capable center of Janice Day, the Young Homemaker, a girls' novel set in the midwestern town of Greensboro. Janice, motherless and serious-minded, keeps house for her father Broxton Day, a banker, and gets his breakfast before school on Knight Street. The first chapter watches cats frolic over catnip scattered by Arlo Weeks Junior before dawn.

A hunt for a treasure-box of her mother's keepsakes gives the early chapters their thread. Long writes domestic adventure at household scale: cooking, neighbors, church, and small mysteries solved by a girl who reads her Bible chapter and her cookbooks with equal care. The Janice Day books offered their first readers a heroine whose glory was competence at home.
jezebel-s-daughter:
Jezebel's Daughter is a novel by Wilkie Collins, the English master of the sensation story. The sample opens with Collins's own letter to his Italian translator, Alberto Caccia. There he explains that this book is not the planned sequel to The Fallen Leaves. That sequel had to wait, he says, until the first part reached the widest body of readers.

Collins also defends his freedom to treat social topics that some English readers called forbidden. A novelist, he argues, deserves the same liberty as a newspaper writer or a preacher. He trusts time and a growing audience to judge his work fairly. That defiant preface frames the novel that follows, from a writer who refused to let critics fence in his art.
john-leech-s-pictures-of-life-and-charac:
John Leech's Pictures of Life and Character is William Makepeace Thackeray's essay on his friend Leech, the Punch artist. It first appeared in the Quarterly Review in December 1854. Thackeray begins by remembering the gloomy picture galleries of his own childhood. Boydell's Shakespeare prints, he says, were black and ghastly, full of staring eyes and pointing fingers.

Against those horrors he sets Leech's cheerful drawings of everyday Victorian life. The essay ranges over waxworks, worsted pictures, and West's gallery for contrast. Leech's hunters, dandies, and schoolboys caught life as it was lived around him. Thackeray writes as one artist honoring another, with warmth and long knowledge of the man. The piece stands as both criticism and friendship's tribute.
john-ward-preacher:
John Ward, Preacher is a novel by Margaret Deland, first copyrighted in 1888. Deland dedicates it to Lorin Deland, calling the book already more his than hers. A line from Omar Khayyam stands at the front: the soul that sought heaven and hell found both in itself. The story opens at Ashurst rectory, the evening before Helen Jeffrey's wedding day.

A wedding is rare excitement in Ashurst, which prides itself on being half asleep. Dr. Howe jokes that the last wedding came twelve years before. Against this quiet setting Deland sets her title figure, the new preacher whose presence stirs the parish. The opening calm is deliberate: a household in the garden, suppressed excitement, and a rector counting quiet years.
jonas-on-a-farm-in-winter:
Jonas on a Farm in Winter is a children's book by Jacob Abbott, author of the Rollo books. This edition carries the date 1851 in Roman numerals. Abbott explains in his preface that the book continues a series begun with Jonas's Stories and Jonas a Judge. A companion volume covers Jonas on a farm in summer.

Abbott says the books aim to amuse young readers and to teach them at the same time. They show honest integrity and plain practical good sense at work in childhood's ordinary life. The early chapters are named Morning, Commanding and Obeying, and Franco. Farm work in winter gives Abbott his scenes for lessons in obedience, judgment, and steady conduct.
kate-bonnet-the-romance-of-a-pirate-s-da:
Kate Bonnet: The Romance of a Pirate's Daughter is a novel by Frank R. Stockton, issued at New York in 1902. A. J. Keller and H. S. Potter drew the pictures. One caption quotes Dickory telling Kate about a wonderful pirate fight he saw. The opening chapters bring two young people, a ship, and a fish together.

A fruit-basket and a friend, two clocks, and a pair of shoes and stockings fill the next chapter titles. Kate plans, in chapter seven's plain title. Stockton, famed for gentle humor in stories like The Lady or the Tiger, here turns to the sea. His pirate's daughter promises a lighter, kinder sort of pirate romance, told with his usual dry wit.
kepler:
Kepler is Walter W. Bryant's short life of the astronomer Johannes Kepler, in the Pioneers of Progress series of 1920. Bryant wrote from the Royal Observatory at Greenwich. His chapters open with astronomy before Kepler, from Chaldaean eclipse prediction to Greek star lore. Early life, university days, and Kepler's turn to astronomy follow.

The central chapters bring Kepler to Tycho Brahe, the great observer whose data he inherited. Kepler's laws of planetary motion get a chapter of their own. Closing chapters cover his last years, with lists of dates, books, and a glossary for young readers. Bryant explains hard astronomy in plain stages, as befits a series for schools. The book honors the man who found how the planets truly move.
kernel-cob-and-little-miss-sweetclover:
Kernel Cob and Little Miss Sweetclover is a children's book by George Mitchell, illustrated by Tony Sarg, from 1918. Mitchell dedicates it to four named children: Ursula, Dordie, Hutch, and Bob. The story opens with Jackie and his sister Peggs, who live with their aunt. She is very old, Jackie thinks: maybe thirty-two.

The aunt, busy with her own affairs, has forgotten that children need playthings. The house holds no soldiers, dolls, animals, engines, or picture books. So the children make believe, turning their small garden into a world of pies and adventures. Kernel Cob and Miss Sweetclover, figures of their invention, lead the play. Mitchell writes a gentle tale of imagination making riches out of nothing.
king-winter:
King Winter is a short verse tale for children, printed by Gustav W. Seitz of Hamburg. No author is named. The story begins on a cold, grey day, when frost makes each step ring on the ground.

A mother sits by the fire with her children around her knees. They beg her for a story about King Winter and Jack Frost, his helper. She tells how King Winter lives far north in the Frozen Zone. He holds court in a snow palace and sits on an icy throne. Simple rhymes and pictures carry the lesson about the cold season. Children learn the north, frost, and snow through a family scene.
lady-rose-s-daughter:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published her novel Lady Rose's Daughter in 1903. Howard Chandler Christy drew its pictures. Ward was already known for Eleanor and Robert Elsmere.

Picture captions hint at the drama inside. Lady Henry gasps and falls back in her chair in one scene. Sir Wilfrid makes a firm promise in another. An older man speaks gently of Rose's child near the end. The daughter of Lady Rose must live under her mother's shadow. Ward turns that burden into a serious social novel. Christy's drawings stress faces and drawing room tension. Ward's plot turns on loyalty between mothers, daughters, and old friends.
left-tackle-thayer:
Ralph Henry Barbour published Left Tackle Thayer in 1915. Barbour also wrote Left-End Edwards and Left Guard Gilbert. Charles M. Relyea drew the pictures for this school story.

A new boy arrives at Brimfield school in the first chapter. Captain Innes, practice cuts, and a runaway wheel follow. A mysterious auto and buried treasure widen the plot beyond football. Brimfield meets defeat before the season resolves. Barbour's sports tales mixed school honor, friendship, and hard games for boy readers. Clint Thayer's school career continues Barbour's Brimfield series. Games matter, but character tests decide the real wins.
legends-of-vancouver:
E. Pauline Johnson, also called Tekahionwake, wrote Legends of Vancouver. A preface praises a poet who honors the city's Native heritage. Committee members helped her push the book through the press.

Johnson retold Squamish and other coastal legends in English prose. Mountains, inlets, and islands around Vancouver carry the stories. She heard many tales from Chief Joe Capilano, her friend. Her retellings join Indigenous tradition with her own poet's voice. The book remains a beloved part of Vancouver's literary identity. Two Brothers and the Siwash Rock appear among its tales. Johnson's Mohawk heritage shaped her telling of coast stories.
letters-from-mesopotamia-in-1915-and-jan:
Robert Palmer's letters from Mesopotamia cover 1915 and January 1916. The book was printed for private circulation only. Its title page records that Palmer was killed at the battle of Um el Hannah, aged twenty-seven.

Palmer went out with a draft from the 6th Hants to reinforce the 4th Hants. His regiment had been in India since November 1914. His letters home describe service in the Mesopotamian campaign of the First World War. A poem on war's evils stands at the front. Family printing preserved a young officer's voice that the war cut short. Private printing kept the book within family and friends. Such memorial volumes preserved many soldiers' letters that newspapers never saw.
letters-of-a-woman-homesteader:
Elinore Pruitt Stewart's Letters of a Woman Homesteader appeared in 1914. Houghton Mifflin published it at Boston and New York. A publishers' note introduces Stewart's hard road to Wyoming.

She lost her husband in a railroad accident, the note says. Left with a two-year-old daughter, she worked in Denver as a cleaner and laundress. Then she took work as a housekeeper and claimed a homestead. Her letters turn that rough life into cheerful, funny reports. Readers meet a widow who built a new life on the frontier. Her humor turns drudgery into a kind of triumph. Stewart later wrote more letters from her Wyoming ranch life.
life-of-abraham-lincoln-little-blue-book:
John Hugh Bowers wrote this short life of Abraham Lincoln in 1922. Haldeman-Julius issued it as Little Blue Book Number 324. The ten cent pocket series came from Girard, Kansas. Bowers taught history at the State Teachers' College in Pittsburg, Kansas.

His opening praises Lincoln's rise from humble beginnings by honest effort. The log cabin, rail-splitting ax, and few borrowed books appear early. Studying by pine-knot light formed the boy's character, Bowers argues. Great suffering, he writes, taught Lincoln great sympathy for others. A flatboat trip to New Orleans widened the young Lincoln's world. The slave mart at New Orleans revolted his sympathetic soul, Bowers writes.
life-of-daniel-boone-the-great-western-h:
Cecil B. Hartley wrote this life of Daniel Boone, frontiersman. Boone appears as the great western hunter and first settler of Kentucky. The book adds Boone's own autobiography, dictated by himself. Boone believed he was ordained to settle the wilderness.

Early chapters trace his grandfather's emigration to Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Boone's boyhood, brief schooling, and a terminating anecdote follow. The family then removes to North Carolina's Yadkin River country. Indian adventures and border hazards fill the career that follows. Byron's verse describes the Yadkin country Boone entered as a boy. His grandfather first settled the family in Bucks County.
life-of-father-hecker:
The Reverend Walter Elliott wrote this life of Father Hecker in 1891. The Columbus Press published it in New York. Archbishop Corrigan granted the book its official imprimatur. Elliott calls himself Hecker's first biographer in the preface.

He writes with the joy of a son, he confesses. Hecker's own journals, letters, and recorded sayings dominate the book. Elliott reckons Hecker has three words here to his one. His own words, he says, are merely hinges and latches. Archbishop Hewit served as censor deputatus for the edition. Hecker's recorded sayings, Elliott hopes, swing open heaven-made wisdom.
life-of-luther:
Julius Köstlin wrote this life of Luther, translated from German. A Cranach portrait in Weimar's town church fronts the volume. Köstlin calls Luther Germany's most powerful religious influence. No German, he argues, so faithfully mirrored his people's character.

His larger two-volume work of 1875 gathered the full materials. That study supplied references, historical and critical, for this life. Protestants read Luther with love and veneration, Köstlin writes. Others treat him as a rock of offence, he admits candidly. Cranach's portrait comes from Weimar's town church collection. Köstlin's dedication borrows Luther's praise of a god-fearing, home-keeping wife.
lightfoot-the-deer:
Thornton W. Burgess tells children the story of Lightfoot the deer. Peter Rabbit meets Lightfoot in the opening chapter. Lightfoot explains how his new antlers grew. Sammy Jay soon brings him word of danger.

A long game of hide and seek with a hunter follows. Paddy the Beaver becomes Lightfoot's partner in escaping danger. Hounds pursue him until a long swim shakes them off. The hunting season ends, and love arrives with a stranger deer. Visitors come to Paddy's pond as the watcher chapters multiply. A great fight and an unseen watcher precede the surprising discovery.
lives-of-john-donne-henry-wotton-rich-d-:
Izaak Walton's second volume of lives opens with Richard Hooker. This issue rests on John Major's edition of 1825. Major printed from the 1675 edition, corrected by Walton's own pen. Austin Dobson added marginalia and supplementary notes later.

Hooker authored the learned Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity. A friend persuaded Walton to write his life, he says. George Herbert, prebendary of Salisbury, receives the next life. Dr. Robert Sanderson, Bishop of Lincoln, closes the volume. Cowper's verse praises Hooker's lasting monument in his books. I. G. dated the editorial note on Walton's birthday, 1898.
london-pride-or-when-the-world-was-young:
M. E. Braddon published this historical novel in 1896. She had written Lady Audley's Secret, Vixen, and Ishmael before. Chapter One, A Harbour from the Storm, opens the contents. Within Convent Walls and Letters from Home follow.

A bitter winter opens the tale in the Royal tragedy's year. Sleet rattles against an old leathern coach at dusk. Puritan houses, priest's holes, and King's Bench courts await inside. Fashion's top and London-Oxford roads carry the historical action. Dido, Philaster, and the Millbank ghost haunt the contents. High stakes and King's Bench revelations drive the later chapters.
london-river:
H. M. Tomlinson published these Thames essays in 1921. Knopf and Garden City Publishing issued the volume. He dedicates it to his mother and his father's memory. The Foreshore opens the contents on the City's north side.

Poverty Corner begins a shipping parish invisible to strangers. A midnight voyage and the ship-runners follow the river down. An old Lloyd's Register closes the collection. Tomlinson finds deep water memories hidden inside ordinary Fenchurch Street. Seamen alone use Poverty Corner's name among themselves, Tomlinson notes. A stranger lighting a pipe there might guess nothing of it.
love-letters-between-a-nobleman-and-his-:
Love-Letters Between a Nobleman and His Sister is an early novel by Aphra Behn. Behn was among the first English women to earn her living by writing. Her story is told in letters between lovers caught in scandal. The argument here sets part of the tale amid the Huguenot wars in France.

There a young nobleman serves under the Prince of Condé, here called Cesario. He loves Myrtilla, a lady famed for beauty, youth, and wit. Love, flight, and court intrigue drive the letters forward. Behn mixed real scandal with romance and politics. Her book helped shape the young English novel. It still reads as bold, lively, and ahead of its time.
love-the-fiddler:
Love, the Fiddler is a book of short stories by Lloyd Osbourne. The first tale, 'The Chief Engineer,' opens on Commonwealth Street. Frank Rignold loves Florence Fenacre, a widow's daughter, with all his heart. Yet Florence, though she has never said no, will not say yes.

Other stories tell of Ffrenches First, golden castaways, and the mascot of Battery B. Osbourne mixes love tales with sea and adventure yarns.
