Moliere's comedy The Miser, known in French as L'Avare, appears here in English prose translated by Charles Heron Wall, with a short introduction and explanatory notes. The play was first acted on September 9, 1668. Moliere borrowed from Plautus and imitated other authors, the introduction says, yet surpassed them in handling his subject.

Harpagon, the miser of the title, loves money in place of every natural affection and treats his own children as enemies. Moliere played Harpagon himself. The cast list sets the scene in Harpagon's Paris house, with his son Cleante and daughter Elise, their lovers Valere and Marianne, the broker Master Simon, and the cook-coachman Master Jacques. Act I follows the introduction.
the-moccasin-maker:
E. Pauline Johnson's story collection The Moccasin Maker was first gathered and issued soon after her death in 1913. Sir Gilbert Parker supplied an introduction, and Charles Mair an appreciation of Johnson. The contents list thirteen pieces, among them My Mother, A Red Girl's Reasoning, The Legend of Lillooet Falls, and The Derelict.

Parker's introduction describes Johnson as a writer of Indigenous and white ancestry who lived for years on the Iroquois Reserve with her chief father and white mother. She held, he writes, to her Indigenous blood with full pride, and took deep joy in her people's legends, history, and language. Sympathy comes easily to her case, Parker argues, yet her work needs no generosity to stand.
the-modern-traveller:
Only front matter is present here for The Modern Traveller, a comic travel poem published by Edward Arnold in London in 1898, so the verses themselves do not appear. The title page credits the work to H. B. and B. T. B., the same initials behind More Beasts (For Worse Children). A list of the authors' earlier books gives prices for the Bad Child's Book of Beasts and its sequel.

A table of contents follows, listing four numbered sections with page numbers only and no titles. Section I begins at page 5, Section II at page 7, Section III at page 18, and Section IV at page 28. Those bare numbers are all the guidance the present pages offer.
the-mucker:
Edgar Rice Burroughs's The Mucker is introduced by its publishing history. The novel ran serially in All-Story Cavalier Weekly under Munsey copyright in 1914, and its sequel, The Return of the Mucker, followed in All-Story Weekly in 1916. A first Ballantine edition of January 1966, printed in New York, supplies the present pages.

Part I opens with Chapter I, Billy Byrne. Billy is a product of Chicago's West Side streets, from Halsted to Robey and Grand Avenue to Lake Street, knowing every bartender by first name. His schooling began in an alley behind a feed store, among pickpockets and second-story men who drank beer from a battered tin pail. At six, Billy was rushing the can for that band, and learning life from them.
the-mysterious-rider:
Zane Grey's 1921 novel The Mysterious Rider opens under a September sun sinking over the black Colorado range. Purple haze thickens in the timbered notches while grey, billowy foothills roll down from the high country. Aspens blaze gold, red vine colours the sage, and Old White Slides, an avalanche-scarred mountain, towers above the scene.

A list of illustrations before the chapter quotes the story's tensions. A round-up shows one hundred head of stock lost, news that rancher Belllounds receives with a roar. A girl is warned away from a club-footed cowboy named Moore, and a rider called Wade soliloquises that he could not let her marry Buster Jack. Grey is billed as author of Riders of the Purple Sage.
the-mystery-at-putnam-hall-the-school-ch:
Arthur M. Winfield's The Mystery at Putnam Hall carries the subtitle The School Chums' Strange Discovery. Only a frontispiece, title page, and a publisher's list are present here. The cadets' mystery itself does not appear. Winfield is identified on the title page as Edward Stratemeyer, author of the Rover Boys series. Grosset and Dunlap published the volume in New York.

The frontispiece shows cadets approaching, buckets of water in hand. The facing list advertises the Putnam Hall Cadet series in cloth. It names The Cadets of Putnam Hall and The Rivals of Putnam Hall. The Champions of Putnam Hall and The Rebellion at Putnam Hall complete the four. The Mystery at Putnam Hall itself is named only in the frontispiece caption.
the-mystery-of-cloomber:
Arthur Conan Doyle's The Mystery of Cloomber is narrated by John Fothergill West, a law student at St. Andrews. His preface-like opening promises a concise, business-like statement, with no paragraph adding to or detracting from the truth. Literary success, he insists, is not his aim; endorsement by those who know the matter would satisfy him completely.

Sixteen chapters with long descriptive titles map the story in the contents. The Wests migrate from Edinburgh, a strange tenant comes to Cloomber, and Major-General J. B. Heatherstone enters the tale. Statements and narratives by other hands fill many chapters. A corporal's coming, a castaway barque, and three foreign men on the coast follow. A day-book completes a mystery assembled from documents as much as from action.
the-nature-faker:
Richard Harding Davis's story The Nature Faker begins with Richard Herrick, a wealthy young man of gentle disposition who had no sense of humour. Marrying Miss Catherweight was his one aim in life. For three years she tried to talk him out of it, and at last married someone else to convince him.

Rejected lovers are supposed to drink or travel; statistics say they instead fall for the beloved's best friend. Herrick truly loved her, so he became a lover of nature instead, assuring friends that nature never disappoints. He bought an abandoned Connecticut farm and made it a model place, with model dairies, incubators, gardens of every style, and a two-hundred-acre game preserve stocked with squirrels, rabbits, and raccoons.
the-new-mcguffey-first-reader:
Only the Project Gutenberg header for The New McGuffey First Reader is present here, so none of the reading lessons appear. The header names the file as the first in the Gutenberg series of McGuffey Readers, electronic text number 1489, dated October 1998. Dianne Bean of Phoenix, Arizona, prepared the text.

Her note explains what the plain text omits: the book's music notations, diacritical markings, and samples of handwriting could not be carried into this form. Several pages were torn in the copy used, and the gaps are marked as missing words in the file. The header invites anyone holding a good copy to help fill the blanks or supply the engravings.
the-new-mcguffey-fourth-reader:
Only the Project Gutenberg header for The New McGuffey Fourth Reader is present here, so none of its lessons or readings appear. The header names William H. McGuffey as compiler and places the file second in the Gutenberg series of McGuffey Readers, electronic text number 1490, dated October 1998. Dianne Bean of Phoenix, Arizona, prepared it using OmniPage Pro scanning software.

Standard Gutenberg notices fill the rest of the pages shown. They explain that the texts are usually created from multiple editions. All those editions are in the public domain. No particular paper edition is followed exactly. Books are also released a month ahead of their official dates, allowing time for better editing. Nothing of the reader's own contents is included.
the-next-of-kin-those-who-wait-and-wonde:
Nellie L. McClung's The Next of Kin, subtitled Those Who Wait and Wonder, was published at Toronto by Thomas Allen and in Boston and New York by Houghton Mifflin in November 1917. McClung, author of Sowing Seeds in Danny and In Times Like These, opens the book with a poem headed Hope, addressed to the women who wait at home in wartime.

Down through the ages, the poem begins, the accepted picture is of the woman who weeps, tears her birthright and sorrow her portion. McClung announces a change. There is a limit to tears, and a new note is sounding: women who wept without hope now see hope dawn in their lonely hearts. Their message flashes across the world to their weeping sisters.
the-note-books-of-samuel-butler:
Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon, kept notebooks from early in life, jotting down anything he wanted to remember. Henry Festing Jones chose and arranged the selections for the 1912 London edition, which carries a portrait taken in 1898. Butler said his thoughts flew so fast that he had to shoot them before they escaped.

Jones explains in the preface that Butler stored his rewritten notes on loose sheets, like a museum of ideas. In 1874 Butler began an index, cut notes he had already used in print, and rewrote the rest. What remains is a sharp, funny store of remarks on life, art, and human habits.
the-odyssey-of-homer: Homer's Odyssey appears in English prose by S. H. Butcher and Andrew Lang, both Oxford scholars. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the epic itself does not appear. The contents promise prefaces, an introduction, and all twenty-four books of the poem. Those books carry Odysseus from Troy through shipwreck, monsters, and the underworld, back to Ithaca and Penelope. The Butcher and Lang version was long prized for its stately English prose.
the-old-man-in-the-corner: Baroness Orczy wrote The Old Man in the Corner, a set of detective tales. Only the contents are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. The list runs to twenty chapters, ending with An Alibi. Titles name The Fenchurch Street Mystery, A Millionaire in the Dock, The Robbery in Phillimore Terrace, The York Mystery, and The Mysterious Death on the Underground Railway. Other cases are set in Liverpool and Edinburgh, and one concerns a theft at the English Provident Bank.
the-opinions-of-a-philosopher:
Robert Grant published The Opinions of a Philosopher in New York in 1895, with an etching by W. H. Hyde. The narrator's wife Josephine calls him a philosopher in his old age. At forty, with gray at his ears, he admits he now looks at the world as through a glass, though not darkly.

He insists he is no cynic like Diogenes, who lived in a tub and hugged statues of snow to prove his scorn for custom. A natural sunniness, he says, guards him against sour thought. Grant's sketch sets up a genial observer who muses on modern manners while denying that he is a real philosopher at all.
the-outdoor-chums-or-the-first-tour-of-t: Captain Quincy Allen published The Outdoor Chums, or The First Tour of the Rod, Gun and Camera Club, in 1911. Front matter and a contents list are present, and no story text follows. Chapters open with Planning the Campaign, Ready for the Start, and The Race for a Camp-Site. Later titles promise The Shack of the Muskrat Trapper, Where Is Bluff?, A Night Alarm, How Jerry Was Treed, and In a Bear's Hollow.
the-pageant-of-summer:
Richard Jefferies wrote The Pageant of Summer, shown here in the 1914 Chatto and Windus edition from London. The essay opens in a ditch bank in early summer. Green rushes, long and thick, tell the hour of the year as plainly as a shadow on a dial. On the fingers they leave a green scent, and their stems rise like classical columns, heavy with sap.

Jefferies moves from rushes to angelica, hedge parsley, and wild parsnip, each plant noted for height, scent, and use to birds. The may bloom has fallen and June roses are near. His close looking turns a common hedge into a full pageant of summer life.
the-philanderer:
George Bernard Shaw wrote the play The Philanderer. Act One opens in the drawing room of a flat in Ashly Gardens, in London's Victoria district, past ten at night. The walls carry theatrical portraits: Kemble as Hamlet, Mrs. Siddons as Queen Katharine, Irving as Richard III, and Ellen Terry, though nothing of Ibsen or Duse. A statue of Shakespeare stands in the turret window among flowers.

On a sofa sit Grace Tranfield, about thirty-two, slight and delicate yet firm-chinned and self-respecting, and Leonard Charteris, a few years older. He wears a velvet jacket, cashmere trousers, a garnet scarf held by a turquoise ring, and leather sandals. The two are making love, and Shaw's long stage picture sets character before a word is spoken.
the-plunderer:
Henry Oyen's The Plunderer was published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York, under copyrights of 1920 by the George H. Doran Company and 1919 by the Curtis Publishing Company. Oyen is named as the author of Big Flat, Gaston Olaf, and The Snow Burner. The story opens in the office of Tibbetts and Payne, manufacturers' agents.

Roger Payne has reached a decision as the chapter begins. With the stenographer gone, he swings his long legs onto his flat-top desk. He shouts across the office to his partner Jim Tibbetts, who is footing a column of cost figures. Payne has spent two years in the business, since a day on a western irrigation dam when he installed a cement machine Tibbetts was selling. Those two years felt like a prison to him. His tanned face, the narrator notes, marks him as a man out of place among office furniture.
the-poems-of-sidney-lanier: The Poems of Sidney Lanier reaches this record through an old Project Gutenberg header, numbered Etext 579 and dated July 1996. Only that header and its production note are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. The note explains the text was typed twice. One copy came from an 1898 printing of the 1891 edition, the other from a 1918 printing of the 1916 edition. The two copies were then compared to remove errors, with differences noted in an appendix. No title page, contents, or verse can be seen in what is present.
the-poetaster:
Ben Jonson's The Poetaster, or His Arraignment, is introduced by a long essay on Jonson's life and standing. The essay calls him the greatest English dramatist except Shakespeare. It names him the first literary dictator and poet laureate of his age. His personality, it says, affected the later course of English letters more strongly than any other man's of his time.

Jonson was born at Westminster early in 1573, nearly ten years Shakespeare's junior. His grandfather had come from Annandale, over the Solway. His father lost an estate under Queen Mary, entered the church, and died a month before his son was born. The widowed mother married a bricklayer, and the boy was apprenticed to the trade. Then the antiquary William Camden noticed him at Westminster School. The essay also recounts his soldiering in Flanders, where by his own account he killed an enemy before both camps and took the spoils.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
Bunker-Hill Battle and Other Poems (1874 to 1877) form this section of Holmes's Poetical Works, bracketed as Volume 3 of the 1893 set. Occasional pieces fill the list. They include a tribute to Dr. Samuel G. Howe, Old Cambridge, and a welcome to the nations at Philadelphia on July 4, 1876. How the Old Horse Won the Bet appears too.

The section opens with Grandmother's Story of Bunker-Hill Battle, told as she saw it from the belfry. At eighty, the speaker says, remembering stirs living embers. Words that are ashes to the young are burning coals to her. She recalls the rattle of the April running battle and the red-coats of Lord Percy's hunted soldiers. A deadly chill comes over her as the day returns. A thousand men lay bleeding then on the slopes of Bunker's Hill, heralded by cannon booming from river and shore on a peaceful summer morning.
the-postmaster-s-daughter:
Louis Tracy's The Postmaster's Daughter, dated 1916, lists eighteen chapters that promise a village mystery. They include The Face at the Window, P. C. Robinson Takes a Line, and Scotland Yard Takes a Hand. The Case Against Grant and The Truth at Last come later. Chapter I opens on John Menzies Grant, who has breakfasted, filled his pipe, and strolled bare-headed into his garden.

The month is June, the glorious rose-month of the last summer before war-clouds darkened England's sky. The narrator notes that thousands of men were strolling into thousands of gardens at nine that morning. Few men favoured with youth, health, leisure, and money looked as perplexed as Grant. His actions spoke as plainly as words. A spacious French window cut into an old-fashioned room stands open behind him to the flower-scented breeze.
the-prime-minister: Anthony Trollope's The Prime Minister was first published in monthly parts in 1875 and 1876 and in book form in 1876. The pages shown give a contents list for Volume I, so the novel itself is not on view. Early chapters name the leading figures: Ferdinand Lopez, Everett Wharton, and Mr. Abel Wharton, Q.C. The Duke of Omnium appears by chapter XVIII, thinking of himself. Later titles include The Duchess's New Swan, The Marriage, The End of the Honeymoon, and The Duke's Misery. A Silverbridge election closes the volume's list.
the-prince-and-the-pauper:
Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens with a storyteller's frame. The tale, Twain writes, was told to him by one who had it from his father, and so back for three hundred years. It may be history, or only legend. It may have happened, or not, but it could have happened. The wise may have believed it in the old days, or only the simple loved and credited it.

A contents list then maps the whole exchange of places. It begins with the birth of the prince and the pauper and Tom's early life. Tom meets the prince, and the prince's troubles begin. Later chapters follow Tom as patrician and as king, the prince with tramps, peasants, and a hermit, and Hendon to the rescue. Prison, a sacrifice, and the road back to London close the list.
the-princess-de-montpensier:
Madame de Lafayette's story The Princess de Montpensier, published without her name in 1662, is introduced by Oliver C. Colt. The tale is set almost a hundred years earlier, during the wars of the counter-reformation. Catholic rulers, encouraged by the Papacy, were bent on wiping out the followers of Luther and Calvin. Colt notes that many persons in the tale actually existed. The weak, vicious king and his malign mother are real, as is a Duc de Montpensier known for cruelty to Huguenots.

The heroine herself, Colt explains, is fictional, and so is the Comte de Chabannes. The real Duc de Guise married for politics, not for a princess's wishes. Colt remarks that women were then traded in marriage with little regard to their feelings. Marriages without love encouraged love outside marriage. For all its courtly restraint, he finds in the tale the seeds of many later romantic novels.
the-private-memoirs-and-confessions-of-a:
James Hogg, a Scots shepherd poet, wrote this dark novel with no name on it in 1824. Its full name is The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner. Hogg framed it as a found text, with an editor's tale round a sinner's own words.

Robert Wringhim holds that the saved can sin and still be safe in grace for good. A tall, strange friend urges him to kill those he deems foes of the true faith, one by one. The tale is the double tale before the word for it was coined, a Scots classic.
the-project-gutenberg-complete-works-of-: A contents list heads the Project Gutenberg Complete Works of Gilbert Parker, naming thirty titles. The Judgment House stands first, followed by Pierre and His People, Romany of the Snows, and Mrs. Falchion. Later entries include Pomp of the Lavilettes, The Seats of the Mighty, The Right of Way, and two poetry volumes, Embers and A Lover's Diary. The pages provided then open The Judgment House with Parker's note that it pictures no living or dead individuals. No novel text follows in the leaves at hand.
the-prose-marmion-a-tale-of-the-scottish: Sara D. Jenkins adapted Scott's Marmion into prose as The Prose Marmion, a tale of the Scottish border, published at Ithaca in 1903. Her introduction sketches Scott's life: born in Edinburgh five years before American independence, lamed in his second year, and raised partly on his grandfather's farm at Sandyknow. He loved ballads, romances, and old plays too well for philosophy or dead languages, and was apprenticed to law against his taste. The pages at hand hold that introduction only; the adapted tale itself is not shown.
the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-vo: The leaves provided for Volume VI of Swift's Prose Works hold a prospectus of the whole twelve-volume set, not the Drapier's Letters themselves. It lists Volume I, A Tale of a Tub, and Volume II, the Journal to Stella, edited by Frederick Ryland. Volume VI is named as The Drapier's Letters, edited by Temple Scott, with reproductions of Wood's coinage. Gulliver's Travels and the Historical Writings fill later volumes. No page of the letters appears in the pages at hand.
the-queen-like-closet-or-rich-cabinet-st: Hannah Wolley offers her collection of receipts for preserving, candying, and cookery to ingenious women readers, in a second edition printed at London in 1672 for Richard Lowndes. The title promises a rich cabinet stored with rare receipts, and a dedication to a virtuous patroness begins the volume. Only the title pages, printer's information, and opening of the dedication are present here, so the receipts themselves do not appear.
the-quest-of-the-sacred-slipper:
Sax Rohmer builds a thriller around a sacred slipper. Hassan of Aleppo guards the relic. Thirty-four chapters hold attempts on a safe and a phantom scimitar. A girl with violet eyes recurs through the headings. The narrator boards a steamship named Mandalay at the start. He notices a disturbance as passengers join at Port Said.

Headings trace oblong boxes and prophetic rings. Hashishin watchers, screams, and shrivelled hands follow. A pool of death waits near the close. A final meeting with Hassan ends the contents. The pace is pure serial adventure throughout. Museums and strong-rooms serve as battlegrounds. Readers who enjoy early pulp thrillers will feel at home.
the-radio-boys-on-the-mexican-border:
Gerald Breckenridge places his Radio Boys near the Mexican border. A. L. Burt Company issued the series volume at New York in 1922. The title pages list companion adventures. Those books cover secret service duty and revenue guards. They also cover an Inca treasure hunt and a lost Alaska expedition.

Contents begin with practical directions. They explain how to install an amateur radio receiving telephone. The story then opens with a cry in the air. An enemy is near at hand. Only the opening pages and the start of the contents are present here. The border pursuit itself does not appear on these pages.
the-rangeland-avenger:
Max Brand's western first ran in Western Story Magazine in 1922 under another title and a pen name, then appeared in book form in 1924 with the title used here. Four gold seekers cross the mountains together, each bringing a different strength to the party.

Sandersen dreams and hopes past all reason, Quade supplies tireless labor, Lowrie knows camp and trail craft, and young Hal Sinclair keeps spirits alive with songs and talk to his horse. Their search has failed, water holes have run dry on a desert shortcut, and thirst now drives the plot. Readers get a stark survival opening before any avenging begins.
the-red-rat-s-daughter:
Guy Boothby, author of Doctor Nikola, published his adventure at London in 1899 with Ward, Lock and Company, illustrated by Henry Austin. Chapter one introduces John Grantham Browne, a rich young man whose cynical wit can wound his friends.

Boothby reckons Browne's income in pounds per year, month, day, and even minute to explain his skepticism about other people's motives. His father, plain Brown without the final letter, rose from bare-legged street boy in a manufacturing town to a fortune by seldom making mistakes. Inherited wealth and sharp tongues set the stage for intrigue around the title's mysterious daughter.
the-register:
William Dean Howells's farce, taken from an 1911 Houghton Mifflin collection of his plays, is set in an upper room of a Boston boarding-house in Melanchthon Place. Henrietta Spaulding decorates the room while her friend Ethel Reed despairs from a sofa in the next room.

Ethel insists her heart is truly broken this time and that her forehead burns, while Henrietta answers that the same despair has happened often before. Dinner, she suggests, would do more good than mourning. The quick dialogue promises a light comedy of courtship in which household gods and hurt feelings share the stage.
the-reminiscences-of-an-astronomer: Simon Newcomb published his memoirs in 1903. The contents survey a long scientific life. Ancestry and early schooling come first. A botanic doctor and phrenology follow. Acquaintance with Professor Henry marks a turning point. Harvard, observatories, and great telescopes fill the later list. Only the title page is present here. The opening of the detailed contents appears with it. The reminiscences themselves do not appear on these pages.
the-ridin-kid-from-powder-river: Henry Herbert Knibbs published his western in 1919. Houghton Mifflin issued it. Contents follow young Pete through early chapters. Firearms and new fortunes come first. Warnings, justice, and new vistas follow. Bookkeeping, an open holster, and a false trail come next. A black sombrero and a spider darken the middle. A devil-wind leads toward the closing chapters. A rider stands at a lamplit bar there. Only the title pages and contents list are present here. The kid's story itself does not appear.
the-rime-of-the-ancient-mariner:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge divides his ballad into seven parts and begins at a wedding feast. An ancient mariner with a long grey beard and glittering eye stops one of three guests on the way to the bridegroom's open doors.

The guest protests, the mariner's hand drops, yet the glittering eye holds him still like a child of three, seated on a stone and unable to choose but hear. Sun, kirk, hill, and lighthouse pass as the ship drops merrily from harbor. Few English poems open with a grip so quiet and so complete.
the-rise-of-iskander:
Benjamin Disraeli opens at sunset over the plain of Athens, where a Greek twilight suffuses olive groves and a Turkish squadron rides at anchor in the Piraeus. Women stream to a fountain, horsemen gallop throwing javelins, and birds, insects, flowers, and a nightingale fill the purple air.

A solitary figure stands on the Acropolis among ruins of the Temple of Minerva, gazing over columns and Caryatides that baffle modern proportion. Iskander's rise begins inside a meditation on lost Greek greatness under Ottoman rule. Disraeli's lush scene-setting announces a romance of liberation.
the-roadmender: Michael Fairless's papers, first printed in The Pilot, were republished by Duckworth at London in 1911 and dedicated both to his mother and to earth his mother. Contents list three pieces only: the title meditation, a piece called out of the shadow, and one at a white gate, with page numbers suggesting short reflective works. Here only the title pages, dedication, and contents list are present, so the meditations themselves do not appear.
the-romance-of-rubber:
John Martin edited a booklet published by the United States Rubber Company to teach coming generations how rubber is grown, gathered, and made useful. Contents cover discovery, Charles Goodyear, the hevea tree, Wickham's idea, plantation development and life, and harvesting.

Chapter one teases readers who can say what Columbus discovered in 1492 but not what he found on his second voyage to Haiti while hunting gold. Industry writing for children turns a commodity into adventure. The company's hope, stated plainly, is that future citizens who understand rubber will value the industry more.
the-romance-of-the-colorado-river:
Frederick S. Dellenbaugh tells the Colorado River's story here. He joined the United States expedition of 1871 and 1872. His account runs from discovery through later explorations. Powell's voyages through the great canyons receive special weight. Detailed contents credit Ulloa in 1539 first. Alarcon ascends the river and names it in 1540. Diaz renames it, and Cardenas finds the Grand Canyon.

A caption describes the Bright Angel Trail in detail. It drops some six thousand feet into the canyon. Thomas Moran painted the watercolor behind the view. Dellenbaugh dedicates the book to his expedition comrades. He remembers the 1871 and 1872 work with gratitude. Exploration history comes from a participant here. He floated the river himself on those voyages.
the-runaway-skyscraper:
Murray Leinster's The Runaway Skyscraper begins with a clock running backward. The clock stands on the Metropolitan Tower. Its hands had moved in their customary deliberate fashion. Then office workers heard creaking and groaning. A slight shiver ran through the tower. Something gave with a crash. The big hands began to move backward.

Calm seems to return at once. Elevators run and lights burn as usual. Clerks go back to their ledgers and typewriters. Arthur Chamberlain resumes dictating a letter. His stenographer is Estelle Woodward. Chamberlain is a young New York engineer. He is short of money, as young engineers often are. His letter protests a demand from the Gary and Milton Company. They want immediate payment for his office furniture. He calls their demand untimely and unjust.
the-satyricon-of-petronius-arbiter:
Petronius Arbiter's Satyricon appears here in William Burnaby's translation. C. K. Scott Moncrieff supplied an introduction. He casts it as an open letter to a young gentleman, titled On Reading Petronius. His image is the Inchcape Rock seen from above St Andrews. On a bright afternoon almost nothing shows. After dark, a clear beam can pierce the sky.

Moncrieff argues that Petronius stands unremarked in clear, confident ages. Imperial Rome was such a night of civilization, he says. So were Renaissance Italy and Restoration England. The surviving manuscript was copied in Renaissance Italy. It was discovered at Trau in Dalmatia during the years 1650 to 1700. Editions followed at Padua, Paris, Upsala, Leipzig, and Amsterdam. Burnaby then made it English, with another hand helping.
the-scarlet-letter:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter is preceded by an introductory sketch called The Custom-House. The contents outline the novel that follows it. Chapters move from the prison door and the market-place onward. Hester at her needle, Pearl, and the governor's hall appear early. The leech and his patient come later. The revelation of the scarlet letter closes the list, before a conclusion.

Hawthorne begins the sketch with a small confession. An autobiographical impulse has twice seized him in addressing the public, he says. The first time, he described his life in the deep quietude of an Old Manse. Now he talks of three years' experience in a custom-house. He found a listener or two before, he jokes. That encourages him to seize the public by the button again.
the-schemes-of-the-kaiser:
Juliette Adam's The Schemes of the Kaiser reached English readers in J. O. P. Bland's translation from the French. E. P. Dutton and Company published it in New York in 1918. It was printed in Great Britain. Adam's preface is brief and combative. She claims a Military Cross, she jokes, for forty-five years of hand-to-hand fighting. Her opponents were Bismarck and William the Second.

Chapter one is dated 1890 and opens on April 12. Adam calls William an all-pervading nuisance. One man has burdened the intelligence of humanity and the world's press, she complains. Bismarck's machiavelism demanded constant vigilance, she says. The new emperor is worse, like an infant prodigy. His ways resemble a shopkeeper's, she writes. He fills the earth with circulars on government and puffs his own magnanimity.
the-scholemaster: Roger Ascham's Scholemaster was printed at London by John Daye in 1570. The full title promises a plain and perfect way of teaching children Latin. They would learn to understand, write, and speak the tongue. The book was specially purposed for private bringing up of youth. Gentlemen's and noble men's houses are named as its setting. The pages shown give the title and the start of a dedication to Sir William. No teaching text follows, so Ascham's method itself is not shown.
the-secret-of-the-tower: Anthony Hope published The Secret of the Tower in 1919. Hope also wrote The Prisoner of Zenda and Rupert of Hentzau, the title page notes. The pages shown give a contents list of eighteen chapters. The text stops at the heading of chapter one, so no narrative follows. Doctor Mary's paying guest opens the list. The magical word Morocco appears partway through. The secret of the tower itself is chapter twelve. Dead majesty, the chief mourners, and the gold and the treasure close the book.
the-secret-power:
Marie Corelli's The Secret Power opens high above Southern California. A cloud floats slowly above a mountain peak. It is vast, fleecy, and white as sea foam. Chapter one follows that cloud across the Sierra Madre heights. The sinking sun catches its edge like fire.

Below sits a roughly built hut on a sloping hollow. Its door stands open, with two benches outside on burnt grass. Papers and books are neatly piled on one bench. A man sits on the other, reading and writing by turns. His features hide behind a heavy beard. Loose woollen trousers and a white shirt make his whole outfit. He jots numerals in a small note-book, frowning at the slowness of writing. A wonderful silence lies everywhere, Corelli writes.
the-secret-sharer:
Joseph Conrad's The Secret Sharer opens with a captain alone on his ship. Fishing stakes line the water on his right hand. They resemble a mysterious system of half-submerged bamboo fences. Barren islets stand to his left, suggesting ruined stone walls. The sea looks solid in its stillness, he writes.

The ship lies anchored outside the bar, at the mouth of the river Meinam. A tug has just left her on the first stage of the homeward journey. The narrator watches its smoke fade behind a pagoda's grove. Then he is alone with his ship at the head of the Gulf of Siam. No sound comes from her, and nothing moves around them. In that breathless pause, ship and captain seem to measure their fitness. A long and arduous enterprise lies before them both.
the-seeker: Harry Leon Wilson published The Seeker with Doubleday, Page and Company in New York in 1904. Wilson also wrote The Spenders and The Lions of the Lord. Rose Cecil O'Neill illustrated the book. Wilson dedicated it to his friend William Curtis Gibson. An epigraph from Holy Writ asks whether the potter has power over the clay. A verse from The Chemistry of Character follows, naming John, Peter, Robert, and Paul. An illustration caption reads, My dear, Bernal is saying good-bye. The pages shown stop there, with no chapter text following.
the-silly-syclopedia-a-terrible-thing-in: Noah Lott, billed as an ex-relative of Noah Webster, wrote The Silly Syclopedia. G. W. Dillingham Company published it in New York in July 1905. Louis F. Grant embellished it with numerous and distracting cuts and diagrams. The title page calls the book a terrible thing in the form of a literary torpedo. It is launched for hilarious purposes only, it declares. It is inaccurate in every particular, the page boasts. The pages shown stop at that title matter and a verse fragment. No definitions themselves appear here.
the-solitary-summer:
Elizabeth von Arnim dedicated The Solitary Summer to the man of wrath, with some apologies and much love. The book proceeds as a diary by months. Its May section opens on May second. Last night after dinner, in the garden, she announced her wish. She wanted to be alone for a whole summer, she said.

She would get to the very dregs of life and be as idle as possible, she declared. Her soul would then have time to grow. Nobody would be invited, and callers would be told she was out or sick. She would spend the months in garden, plain, and forest. The Man of Wrath answered by removing his cigar. Mind you do not get your feet damp, he advised. The spring had taken hold of her body and soul, she writes.
the-song-of-the-blood-red-flower: Johannes Linnankoski's Finnish novel, first published in 1920 under the title Laulu Tulipunaisesta Kukasta, appears here in English translation. Only the title page and contents are present in this record. Chapter names include The Fairy of the Forest, Gazelle, A Mother's Eyes, and Father and Son. Flower titles such as Pansy, Rowan, Daisy, and Hawthorn join The Rapids, so the story itself does not appear.
the-sorrows-of-young-werther:
J. W. von Goethe's novel of unhappy love appears here in R. D. Boylan's translation, edited by Nathen Haskell Dole. A short preface presents the editor as a collector of poor Werther's story. He asks readers for admiration for his spirit and tears for his fate. He also offers the little book as a friend to anyone suffering the same distress.

Book One begins with Werther's letter of May 4, rejoicing that he has gone away from the friend he loves. He looks back on Leonora and her sister and admits his part in the tangle. He vows to improve, enjoy the present, and let the past rest. The following letters steadily undo that resolution.
the-star-spangled-banner:
John A. Carpenter recounts the British campaign of August 1814 that produced the national anthem. His narrative opens with a letter from Admiral Cockburn. Cockburn wrote to Secretary Monroe on August 18. He threatened to destroy coastal towns that could be attacked. The threat answered American destruction in Upper Canada. Baltimore, Washington, and Annapolis all lay within reach. The British fleet waited in the Patuxent River.

British troops landed at Benedict, marched through Nottingham to Upper Marlborough, and were entertained there by Dr. Beanes, the local physician. Meanwhile Francis Scott Key serves as aide-de-camp. Key was a Washington lawyer. He assigned regiments at Bladensburg in the hot, dusty days. Those days ended in American defeat. Washington's public buildings burned. Carpenter follows the events toward Key's famous night.
the-stolen-singer: Martha Bellinger wrote this novel, illustrated by Arthur William Brown and published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company of Indianapolis under a 1911 copyright. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The contents list sixteen chapters. They run from twilight in the park and Hambleton of Lynn onward. Melanie's dreams and a voyage on the Jeanne d'Arc follow. A rope ladder and a camp on the beach come next. Echoes from the city close the list. The story itself does not appear.
the-story-of-a-bold-tin-soldier:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this Make Believe story for children, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, in ten chapters that carry a toy soldier through a bean battle, rescues of the Calico Clown and the Sawdust Doll, and a sad accident. Chapter one opens at night in a big department store. The scene is the toy section, after customers and clerks have gone home.

A word of command, Attention, rings out, and the Calico Clown peers around a pile of building blocks asking what is going on. The Candy Rabbit hopes the Sawdust Doll has come back. The Monkey on a Stick climbs up to announce that it is not true. Around them the toys come alive for their nightly adventures.
the-story-of-a-pioneer: Anna Howard Shaw tells her pioneer life. Elizabeth Jordan helped write it. Shaw dedicates it to America's women pioneers. An adapted poem tells of cutting a path through tangled brush. Only the title pages and contents are present here. The contents list fourteen chapters. They begin with first memories and wilderness years. High school, college, and the wolf at the door follow. The great cause and Aunt Susan come next. The presidency of the National and suffrage campaigns close the list. Shaw's narrative itself does not appear.
the-story-of-a-summer:
Cecilia Cleveland published this journal of a summer at Chappaqua with G. W. Carleton and Company of New York in 1874, dedicating it affectionately to her cousins Ida and Gabrielle. A prefatory note insists the little volume is not a made-up tale at all. It is a plain record of one pleasant summer's stay.

That record, Cleveland explains, holds facts never published before. They concern a man who once filled much of the public mind. The journal shows the part of his busy life spent at home. It belonged to his home circle, not to the public. Written first for the amusement of herself and friends, the journal was printed at persuasion for readers who wanted that private view.
the-story-of-isaac-brock-hero-defender-a:
Walter R. Nursey published this life of Major-General Sir Isaac Brock in Toronto with William Briggs in 1908, calling Brock in its title the hero, defender, and saviour of Upper Canada in 1812. A word to the reader opens the volume. Nursey makes a bold claim there. No student of history, he says, can deny it. Brock ranks as the finest defender the flag has known in western Canada. He fought and won when the odds were all against him.

Nursey sets the scene of 1812. Nearly all British soldiers were off fighting Napoleon in Europe. The duty of upholding Britain's honour in America fell on Brock. He was the undismayed man behind the gun, Nursey writes, when a determined enemy threatened the integrity of British America.
the-story-of-the-malakand-field-force-an:
Winston S. Churchill tells the story of the Malakand Field Force. It was an episode of frontier war on India's north-west frontier. He inscribes the book to Major-General Sir Bindon Blood. The operations were carried out under Blood's command. The inscription is dated from the cavalry barracks at Bangalore. Churchill wrote it on December 30, 1897. He thanks Blood warmly. The service was the finest experience of his life, he says.

Chapter one, The Theatre of War, opens under verses from Sir A. Lyall's Amir's Message about narrow, steep paths and deep snow-fed streams. Churchill then surveys the Himalayas. They run along India's northern and north-western frontiers. The region is nearly four hundred miles broad. It stretches more than sixteen hundred miles long. It is the greatest upheaval of the earth's surface from chaotic ages.
the-story-of-waitstill-baxter: Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote this Maine novel, illustrated by H. M. Brett and published in October 1913 under her married name of Riggs, dedicating it to her husband. Only the title pages and contents appear in this record. The chapters are arranged by seasons. Spring brings the Saco water, the sisters, and Deacon Baxter's wives. Summer brings the joiner's shop and haying time. Autumn brings a brace of lovers. Lois burying her dead closes the year. Waitstill's story itself does not appear.
the-substitute-prisoner:
Max Marcin, author of Britz of Headquarters, published this novel with Moffat, Yard and Company in October 1911. Chapter one opens on a man's agitation. A strange woman enters his home at a compromising hour. Had she come to threaten him, or to plead?

He has never seen her before. Yet her presence signifies something. She is bound up, near or far, with his own tangled affairs. The thought drives him to look closer. Surprise and terror mingle in him. Marcin's opening stays inside the man's mind. He gazes stupidly at his visitor. The scene sets up the mystery of the substitute prisoner. Who is she? What does she want? What tangle connects them?
the-sunny-side-of-ireland-how-to-see-it-: John O'Mahony wrote this railway guide to the south and west of Ireland, in a second edition, rewritten and enlarged, from Alex. Thom and Company of Dublin, with seven maps and over 160 illustrations and a chapter on the region's natural history by R. Lloyd Praeger. Only the title pages and the first line of the first edition's preface appear here. That line begins an attempt. It aims to make one part of Ireland better known. The Great Southern and Western Railway serves that part. The guide itself does not appear.
the-surgeon-s-daughter:
Sir Walter Scott's tale, part of the second series of Chronicles of the Canongate published in 1827, is introduced from Abbotsford in September 1831. Scott says he has nothing to add except that the tale's principal incident was narrated to him at breakfast by his friend Mr. Train of Castle Douglas, and that his military informant on Eastern matters, Colonel James Ferguson, is concealed under the Gaelic form Mac-Erries.

An appendix prints the narrative Train afterwards drew up in writing, though it reached Abbotsford only in July 1832. It begins with Davie Duff, called the Thane of Fife. Duff rose from humble parentage by industry and economy. He built an ingenious manufactory. He sat on his native burgh's council board. From that seed Scott grew his story. It tells of a surgeon's daughter and the East.
the-sword-maker: Robert Barr, author of Tekla and Cardillac, published this historical novel with Frederick A. Stokes Company in June 1910. Only the title page and table of contents appear here. The contents list twenty-two chapters. An offer to open the river leads off. Dissension in the ironworkers' guild follows. Father Ambrose makes a journey. The Countess von Sayn and the Archbishop of Cologne appear. Mutiny and missing gold come next. The prisoner of Ehrenfels follows. Journeys ending in lovers meeting close the list. The story itself does not appear.
the-tailor-of-gloucester: Beatrix Potter's tale, copyrighted by Frederick Warne in 1903 and renewed in 1931, appears here through her prefatory letter to Freda. Potter writes to Freda, who loves fairy-tales and has been ill. She has made her a story of her own. It is a new one. Nobody has read it before. The queerest thing is its source. Potter heard it in Gloucestershire. It is true, she says. The tailor, the waistcoat, and the cry of no more twist are all real. The tale itself does not appear beyond the letter.
the-tale-of-brownie-beaver: Arthur Scott Bailey wrote this animal tale for children in nineteen chapters. A queer place to live leads off. How to fell a tree follows. Sticks and mud and a freshet come next. Brownie saves the dam. A newfangled newspaper and a sign on the tree follow. Jasper Jay's story and a new suit close the tale. Only the title page and that contents list are present in this record, so Brownie Beaver's adventures themselves do not appear.
the-tale-of-mr-jeremy-fisher:
Beatrix Potter's Mr. Jeremy Fisher was published by Frederick Warne in 1906. Jeremy is a frog who lives in a little damp house among buttercups beside a pond. Water lies slippy-sloppy in his larder, yet he likes getting his feet wet and never catches cold. When rain splashes on the pond, he decides to dig worms and go fishing for minnows.

He hopes to catch more than five fish and invite his friends Mr. Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise and Sir Isaac Newton to dinner, though the Alderman eats salad. Dressed in a macintosh and shiny goloshes, Jeremy hops off to his round green boat. Potter gives small children a polite, cheerful fisherman setting out on a wet-day adventure.
the-teeth-of-the-tiger: Maurice Leblanc's Teeth of the Tiger, an Arsène Lupin adventure dated 1914, is laid out here in title page and contents, with just the first line of chapter one. Twenty-one chapters are listed, promising a dead man, a doomed man, an iron curtain, the devil's post-office, and an heir to a hundred millions. The opening line places M. Desmalions, the Prefect of Police, at half-past four, still waiting. Beyond that threshold the adventure does not go in this record, so Lupin's tiger-toothed case stays unopened.
the-tin-soldier: Temple Bailey's Tin Soldier, copyrighted in 1918 by the Penn Publishing Company and reprinted by Grosset and Dunlap, is laid out here in title page and contents. Book One, called On the Shelf, opens in a toy shop and moves through chapters named Cinderella, Drusilla, The Question, The Slacker, and The Promise. The frontispiece promises 'I shall come back for more.' Bailey's wartime romance of a toy-shop Cinderella and a soldier can be mapped from these leaves, but her story does not begin in the pages present.
the-torch-bearer: Agnes E. Ryan's Torch Bearer, a look forward and back at the Woman's Journal, is framed here by that paper's own masthead. The Journal called itself a weekly devoted to woman's educational, industrial, legal, and political equality, and especially to her right of suffrage. Founded in 1870 by Lucy Stone and Henry B. Blackwell, it lists Alice Stone Blackwell as editor-in-chief. Ryan's history of the suffrage paper begins after these leaves, so this record preserves its banner rather than her account.
the-town-traveller:
George Gissing's Town Traveller opens at half-past eight on a lodging-house morning, when Moggie, the general servant, knocks at Mr. Gammon's door. Mrs. Bubb wants to know whether he knows the time, and Gammon answers with a sleepy hallo. The contents promise much more than a late breakfast: a missing uncle, a china shop, Polly and Mr. Parish, a head waiter, and Polly's wrath and defiance across twenty-seven chapters.

Later headings bring Lord Polperro's representative, a husband's return, a will, and the traveller at rest. Gissing, better known for grim novels of poverty, here writes a lighter mystery of a commercial traveller hunting a vanished relative through London boarding-houses and shops. Gammon the crafty, as one chapter calls him, turns detective among landladies, waiters, and the formidable Polly.
the-training-of-a-public-speaker: Grenville Kleiser, formerly instructor in public speaking at Yale Divinity School, published The Training of a Public Speaker with Funk and Wagnalls in February 1920. The pages present give his title page and his list of earlier guides, such as How to Speak in Public. They also give the first contents entries. Those are Rhetoric and Eloquence, The Exordium or Introduction, The Narration, and Division and Argument. Kleiser trained speakers by system, but his instruction starts past the leaves shown, so this record preserves the course plan, not the course.
the-uncommercial-traveller: Charles Dickens's Uncommercial Traveller appears in a 1905 London edition from Chapman and Hall, with illustrations by Harry Furniss and A. J. Goodman. The front matter and contents are what this record holds; the essays themselves are not included. Twenty-six chapters are listed, beginning with the traveller's line of business and a shipwreck. Wapping Workhouse, a cheap theatre, night walks, and shy neighbourhoods follow. Later entries cover Dullborough Town, nurse's stories, Chatham Dockyard, and the boiled beef of New England, sketching Dickens's range across London streets, workhouses, and remembered places.
the-underworld-the-story-of-robert-sincl: James C. Welsh published The Underworld with Frederick A. Stokes in New York in 1920, subtitled The Story of Robert Sinclair, Miner. This record holds the title page and contents only, so the novel's text does not appear. Fourteen chapters are listed, opening with The Thong of Poverty and A Turn of the Screw. Later headings follow a young rebel, a prophet's coming, work at the pit-head, and an accident. Heroes of the underworld and a strike build toward a final chapter called The Awakening.
the-value-of-a-praying-mother:
Isabel C. Byrum published The Value of a Praying Mother with the Gospel Trumpet Company, in a first printing dated 1911. Her preface sends the book out as precious seed, hoping it falls into good soil and bears a hundredfold. Parents, she says, wish noble children, yet many miss the knowledge needed to shape young lives well.

True incidents carry the teaching, since principles stated abstractly can be hard to apply. Names are mostly withheld because the people still live, though one child, Bessie Worthington of Michigan, is identified with her parents' consent in the preface's telling. Byrum also shows how extreme environments affect a child, and how one praying mother's results reveal a secret of success.
the-vanished-messenger:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens his thriller on platform twenty-one of Liverpool Street Station, a remote and little-used corner of the terminus. Shortly before nine on the night of April 2, almost nobody is about. The station-master and an inspector wait, along with a dark, thick-set traveller whose dressing-case bears the name Mr. John P. Dunster.

No train is due for hours, which makes the gathering stranger. A tall young stranger in grey tweeds and a straw hat arrives, having missed the boat train, and makes straight for Dunster. His request for a private word lands with sudden keenness in the older man's eyes. Oppenheim builds the mystery from timetable gaps and watchful officials.
the-vicar-s-daughter: George MacDonald's The Vicar's Daughter was first published by Tinsley Brothers in London in 1872. An illustration caption shows the narrator bringing a baby to be kissed. The pages present here stop at the contents, so the novel's text does not appear. Chapters listed include an introductory chapter, I Try, My Wedding, and Judy's Visit. Later headings name Connie, Connie's Baby, and The Foundling Refound, then Wagtail Comes to Honor. The list breaks off at chapter twelve in what is preserved.
the-village-watch-tower:
Kate Douglas Wiggin's Village Watch-Tower, first published in 1895, reaches this edition with a long introductory essay about its author. The essayist notes that Wiggin's name now rings few bells, while Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, in print since 1903, wins instant recognition. Jack London wrote from Manchuria in 1904 that Rebecca had won his heart.

Wiggin was born in Philadelphia in 1856 and raised mostly in Maine, the backdrop of much of her fiction. She moved to California, joined the free kindergarten movement, and opened San Francisco's first free kindergarten on Silver Street. The introduction traces her teaching school, first husband's death, and return east, framing a story collection that never matched Rebecca's fame.
the-vizier-of-the-two-horned-alexander:
Frank R. Stockton published The Vizier of the Two-Horned Alexander in 1899, grounding his tale in legendary history. A prefatory note credits the chronicles of Tabari, the first Muslim writer of a general history of the world. Tabari was born in the year 244 of the Hejira, lived mostly at Baghdad, and carried his history from the creation to the year 302.

Tabari tells startling experiences of El Khoudr, vizier to the Two-Horned Alexander, and those experiences motivate Stockton's further adventures. The note insists this monarch is not Alexander the Great: ancient histories place him in Abraham's time. Baring-Gould is cited for tracing famous legends to that reign. An illustrations list promises lent gold, Moses asking embarrassing questions, and astonishment at Abraham's era.
the-wentworth-letter:
Joseph Smith, Jun., wrote the Wentworth Letter for the Times and Seasons of March 1, 1842, at the request of John Wentworth, editor of the Chicago Democrat. Wentworth wanted the sketch of the rise, progress, persecution, and faith of the Latter-day Saints for a friend writing a history of New Hampshire. Smith asks only that the account be published entire, ungarnished, and without misrepresentation.

Smith begins with his birth at Sharon, Vermont, on December 23, 1805, and his family's moves to Palmyra and Manchester, New York. At about fourteen, troubled by clashing religious plans of salvation, he took James's promise that God gives wisdom liberally to those who ask. In a grove he was enwrapped in a heavenly vision of two glorious personages.
the-whistling-mother:
Grace S. Richmond's Whistling Mother is narrated by a son unabashedly bragging about his mother. She stands five feet six, keeps active, shoots well, drives her own car, and rides like a Cossack. An illustration caption carries the book's motto: a man is immortal till his work is done. Her sons feel especially lucky, the narrator says, now that the war game's on.

The story starts with Hoofy Gilbert crossing a dorm hall, downcast over a letter from home. College fellows are writing to break the news that they mean to enlist, asking families to say go, and God bless you. Some mothers answer with sobs and cannot bring themselves to send Bob, Sam, or Hector. Richmond sets cheerful courage against wartime dread.
the-white-feather:
P. G. Wodehouse addresses The White Feather to his brother Dick in a prefatory note. The story, he explains, falls a year and a term after The Gold Bat, and Wrykyn school's intervening history appeared in magazine stories. He jokes that Messrs Black declined to publish those stories, keeping away with painful lightness of foot, itself an exhibition of the white feather.

The pages present here give that note and a partial contents list, so the school story itself does not appear. Chapters follow Sheen at home, Sheen receiving visitors and advice, and the better part of valour, before the white feather chapter itself. A naval battle, Sheen beginning his education, and schoolfellows going up the river follow in the visible headings.
the-white-sister: F. Marion Crawford's White Sister appears with its copyright note stating that an eleven-hundred-word excerpt was printed in Cosmopolitan Magazine. The pages present here give that note and a chapters heading, so the novel itself does not appear. No chapter titles or narrative wording accompany the heading. Readers learn that the book was popular enough to excerpt in a major magazine before or during its book life. Crawford's story of the white sister stays untold in what is preserved here.
the-window-gazer:
Isabel Ecclestone Mackay opens The Window-Gazer with an old rhyme. It tells of those who buy life's show and those who stand outside and gaze in. Mackay also wrote Mist of Morning and The Shining Ship. Chapter one strands Professor Spence on an upturned keg, shivering in sudden fog. Fifteen minutes earlier the coast city was ordinary, and he had successfully hunted out Johnston's wharf from a wilderness of wharves.

Mr. Johnston, making boats in his shed, had complimented the professor on finding the place at all, since some take hours or days. Now the fog has swallowed wharf, boat-builder, streets, sea, and ships together. Mackay begins her novel with a reasonable man made helpless by weather in a city he had just congratulated himself on mastering.
the-wings-of-icarus-being-the-life-of-on:
Laurence Alma Tadema published The Wings of Icarus with Macmillan in New York and London in 1894. The subtitle promises the life of one Emilia Fletcher, revealed by herself in three forms: thirty-five letters to Constance Norris, a fragmentary journal, and a postscript. The letters run from July 18 of one year to March 26 of the next.

Letter one is written at midnight from Fletcher's Hall, Graysmill. Emilia sits in a strange room in a strange land, her life lying behind her, she says. Heat hangs heavy, moths flutter round her candle, and she cannot save them all. Darkness hides everything outside the window. The letter breaks off mid-question to her beloved Constance, setting an intimate, unsettled tone.
the-women-who-came-in-the-mayflower:
Annie Russell Marble wrote The Women Who Came in the Mayflower as a memorial, her foreword explains. It also honors women who arrived later on the Ann and the Fortune. They upheld home life in early Plymouth Colony. Marble offers glimpses of communal life from 1621 to 1623. Portraits of individual matrons and maidens follow.

Marble makes no attempt at genealogy. She regrets that proof is lacking for many facts. Conflicting statements appear, and she sometimes gives both views. Elsewhere she offers the more probable guess. Readers meet the women behind Plymouth's survival, often overlooked in colony histories.
the-wonders-of-prayer:
The Wonders of Prayer, revised by D. W. Whittle in an 1885 edition, collects accounts of answered prayer. Famous names headline the title page. George Muller, D. L. Moody, and C. H. Spurgeon are listed. Abraham Lincoln, Martin Luther, and John Knox also appear. The introduction to the first edition vouches for every incident. Nothing doubtful, it insists, was allowed into print.

Each case, the editor says, was carefully investigated. The stories came from his own experience or from correspondents. Results, he claims, arrived only through persevering faith. The book presents prayer as powerful and practical. Readers get a nineteenth-century evangelical record of providence at work.
the-works-of-frederick-schiller:
A collected Works of Frederick Schiller, translated from the German, spans history, plays, poems, and philosophy. The contents list his History of the Thirty Years War in five books. Plays include The Robbers, William Tell, and Mary Stuart. A novel, The Ghost Seer, also appears. A preface to the sixth edition calls this the best collected Schiller open to English readers.

Earlier translations of single plays and poems were gathered into the set. The preface praises Schiller as both historian and dramatist. Nature, it says, qualified him equally for each calling. Readers can move from his histories to his dramas in one volume. The collection shows the full range of Germany's great playwright-poet.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-peter:
Peter's first letter, book sixty of the World English Bible, goes to chosen exiles scattered abroad. Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia are named. Peter calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ. He blesses God for a living hope. That hope rests on Christ's resurrection from the dead.

Believers, he writes, await an inheritance that cannot fade. It is reserved in heaven and guarded by God's power. Present trials grieve them for a little while. Tested faith, Peter says, is worth more than gold. The letter comforts suffering Christians with praise still to come. Its tone is pastoral rather than argumentative.
the-world-english-bible-web-esther:
Esther, book seventeen of the World English Bible, opens at a Persian king's vast court. Ahasuerus rules from India to Ethiopia, over 127 provinces. In his third year he feasts his princes and servants. The display of royal wealth lasts 180 days. A further seven-day feast follows for everyone in Shushan. Garden hangings of white, green, and blue are described.

Such splendor sets the stage for a court drama. Queen Vashti's refusal and Esther's rise come next. A Jewish orphan will stand between her people and destruction. Readers get palace intrigue with high stakes. God's name never appears, yet deliverance drives every scene.
the-wrecker:
Robert Louis Stevenson and Lloyd Osbourne set The Wrecker's prologue in the Marquesas Islands. It is a winter afternoon in Tai-o-hae, the French port of entry. Trade winds blow strong and squally over the beach. A fifty-ton French schooner of war rolls at her moorings. Tropic rain has fallen hard earlier that day. Torrents still streak the green mountain above town.

Winter there, the narrator notes, is only a name. Rain brings no refreshment to the islanders. Convict gardeners work on at the residency garden. Everyone else sleeps through the heavy afternoon. Stevenson builds an indolent, watchful South Seas atmosphere. Mystery and wrecking schemes grow naturally from such colonial ports.
the-yellow-wallpaper:
Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote this short tale in 1892, and it ran in a magazine that year. She wrote it from her own ill health and the rest cure a doctor had laid on her. The tale is told in the first person, as a secret diary kept in a sick room.

A young wife, kept from work and books by her husband and her doctor, rests in a room with foul yellow paper. Day by day she sees a woman creep and crawl in the pattern of the paper. The tale is the root work of feminist horror in America.
the-yeoman-adventurer: George Gough's The Yeoman Adventurer is shown through its dedication and contents list in this record. Gough dedicates the book to A. D. Steel-Maitland, a member of Parliament. Seventeen chapters follow a yeoman into adventure. He serves as a highwayman in one chapter title. Bonnie Prince Charlie appears in another. Mistress Margaret Waynflete and a conjurer's cap also feature. The story chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present here.
the-young-forester:
Zane Grey's The Young Forester opens with Ken explaining his chosen profession to his brother. Ken loves outdoor life and hunting. Talk of forestry keeps sliding into grizzly bears, Hal teases. Their father blames dime novels for Ken's ideas. The brothers are camping on the Susquehanna River near Harrisburg. Fishing and tramping fill their days while they await their father's visit.

Ken hopes to win permission for Arizona that summer. Hal begs to be included in the plan. Mustangs, bears, and lions fill his imagination of the West. Grey, himself devoted to the outdoors, writes forestry as adventure. Young readers learn that foresters guard, not just hunt, western wild lands.
the-young-pitcher: Zane Grey's The Young Pitcher, dated 1911, is represented here by its contents list and a chapter heading. Ken, the hero, clashes with Graves in chapter twelve. Games against State University and Herne are listed. A matter of principle and Ken's day also appear. Chapter one, The Varsity Captain, is announced at the end. Its text does not follow in the pages present in this record.
the-zeppelin-s-passenger:
E. Phillips Oppenheim opens The Zeppelin's Passenger over afternoon tea in wartime England. A young officer admits he heard nothing during the night. He slept from eleven until reveille, he says. Route marching had tired him out completely. He calls missing the excitement a jolly sell. His companion, Captain Griffiths, stayed up until two o'clock. Griffiths is tall, awkward, and sallow for a soldier.

His hard, unsympathetic voice adds little to tea-table talk. Bony fingers and greying black hair complete the portrait. Something passed overhead in the night, clearly. Oppenheim seeds espionage suspense inside polite conversation. A Zeppelin raid's aftermath will draw these officers into intrigue.
thoughts-on-man-his-nature-productions-a:
William Godwin published Thoughts on Man at London in 1831, subtitled with particulars respecting the author. A Shakespeare line about rousing a lion serves as epigraph. Godwin's preface says the essays gather thoughts formed over thirty-four years, since his Enquirer volume.

He admits long stretches away from print and insists he rarely wrote for periodicals. His mind, he says, was constitutionally meditative, and duty required setting these fruits in order. Readers get a philosopher addressing plain men in clear terms, deliberately avoiding the obscure phraseology he scorns in self-styled profound thinkers.
together:
Robert Herrick opens his novel at a wedding in a little chapel on a warm June morning. The bride stands tall and straight before the minister, looking at him rather than at the man beside her. Her father releases her arm and steps behind her as quiet falls.

Woodbine thrusts through the open window, and earthy odours of new growth fill the air. The bride feels poised between her whole past and a mysterious future, suddenly seeing her chosen husband as a stranger. Readers get a marriage novel that begins inside a bride's awed, divided consciousness during the ceremony itself.
told-after-supper: Jerome K. Jerome's Told After Supper is identified in an electronic text header dated December 1999, prepared by David Price from the 1891 Leadenhall Press edition. The header calls it number fifteen in a series of Jerome texts. It also explains the volunteer project's donation appeals and release schedule. No title page or story from Jerome's book follows in what is present. Readers learn the book's identity, preparer, and source edition from these lines, but none of Jerome's after-supper tales themselves appear here.
tom-slade-motorcycle-dispatch-bearer: Percy K. Fitzhugh sent Tom Slade to war as a motorcycle dispatch bearer, in a Grosset and Dunlap book copyrighted in 1918 and approved by the Boy Scouts of America. R. Emmett Owen illustrated it. A frontispiece shows Tom's searchlight finding a hatless, coatless German soldier. Contents promise service as required, aid and comfort to the enemy, an old compass, going over the top, and a mysterious fugitive. The front pages and contents are what is present here, so Fitzhugh's war story itself does not appear.
toni-the-little-woodcarver: Johanna Spyri, author of Heidi, wrote Toni, the Little Wood-Carver, translated by Helen B. Dole and published by Thomas Y. Crowell at New York in 1920. An illustrated title page names Toni himself. A publisher's panel lists Spyri's Alpine stories in uniform editions. Gritli's Children, Rico and Wiseli, Uncle Titus, Veronica, and Little Curly Head fill that list, several translated by Louise Brooks or Dole herself. The title page and publisher's list are what is shown in this record, so Spyri's story of Toni itself does not appear.
treat-em-rough-letters-from-jack-the-kai:
Ring W. Lardner's Treat 'Em Rough collects comic letters from Jack, a soldier writing home to his friend Al. Frank Crerie illustrated the Bobbs-Merrill edition. Jack calls himself the Kaiser killer, though his first letter comes from Camp Grant, far from any trench.

Writing on September 23, Jack describes a recreation room full of men scribbling letters home. Half of them, he jokes, can barely talk English, let alone write it. He has felt sick since arriving Wednesday, and his left arm aches from a shot. Lardner builds the humor from Jack's mangled spelling and cheerful confidence, a recruit's-eye view of army camp life.
trials-and-confessions-of-a-housekeeper:
T. S. Arthur's Trials and Confessions of a Housekeeper, printed at Philadelphia in 1859, gathers a housekeeper's experiences into short chapters. The introduction explains that part of the matter appeared earlier as Confessions of a Housekeeper. The enlarged book mixes grave and instructive pieces with amusing ones, all drawn from life.

Chapter heads promise a speculation in china ware, something about cooks, cheap furniture, and a picked-up dinner. Later chapters take up shirt buttons, pavement washing in winter, house cleaning, and broiling a lobster. Arthur assures women readers they will recognize their own perplexities. The book treats running a household as skilled, trying work worth recording.
two-on-a-tower:
Thomas Hardy's Two on a Tower appears in the 1923 Macmillan reprint, with a map of Wessex. Hardy first published the novel in 1902, and this edition lists reprints through 1923. His preface states the aim plainly: two tiny lives and their feelings, set against the vast background of the stars.

The smaller magnitude, Hardy hoped, might prove the greater to readers as human beings. Instead, he reports, the public fastened on the novel's morals and called it improper. A Crashaw motto on love's horoscope heads the title page. The preface alone shows Hardy defending a slight romance built on a vast contrast of scale.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1950-july-decembe:
Page 181 opens the July-to-December 1950 catalog, which keeps the same title-first arrangement as its spring partner. Literature, art, and film renewals fill the list, music again excluded. Claimants appear with a letter code in parentheses after each renewal.

The first full entry renews an ABC Book designed and cut on wood by C. B. Falls. He copyrighted it on October 19, 1923 and renewed it himself on October 23, 1950. Cross-references under Eleanor Plaisted Abbott point to her story collection and its renewal. Because renewal fell due twenty-eight years on, this half year mostly revisits books of 1923.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1951-july-decembe:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott's Silver Moon leads the July-to-December 1951 list. She copyrighted the book on October 12, 1923, and Mrs. Fordyce Coburn renewed it on September 26, 1951. Herbert Vaughan Abbott's Life of Johnson follows close behind in the alphabet.

The catalog keeps the year's new pattern: Class A works under author, editor, compiler, or title headings. Every entry pairs the original registration with the renewal, number and date on both sides. Renewal claimants here are often widows, executors, or publishers rather than the authors themselves. The half year shows the machinery by which 1923 books gained a second term in 1951.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1952-july-decembe:
Love letters lead the second half of 1952. Pierre Abailard stands first, with the letters of Abelard and Heloise edited by Lloyd E. Smith as Little Blue Book number 871. The pamphlet was copyrighted on August 31, 1925 and renewed under number R99511.

Around it, the catalog keeps to Class A works arranged under main headings. Cheap classics, law digests, and novels all pass through the same entry form: title, original date and number, renewal number and date, then claimant. The presence of a pocket-sized Abelard shows how renewal covered the whole book trade, from treatises down to five-cent classics sold on newsstands.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1953-july-decembe:
Scope widens in the July-to-December 1953 issue. The catalog now names books, pamphlets, serials, and contributions to periodicals as its field. Headings run under author, issuing body, or title, and cross-references come from claimants as well as creators.

Allan Abbott, joint author of a Columbia Research Bureau English test, supplies an early entry with renewal number R124205. School testing materials sit beside novels and digests in the same alphabet. The entry form stays constant: both registrations, original and renewal, with dates and numbers. Teachers' tests and trade books alike needed renewal at twenty-eight years, and this half year records both kinds.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1954-july-decembe:
A music publisher opens the second half of 1954, though the entries concern printed works. ABC Music Corporation appears as a cross-reference, pointing readers to Maurice Baron and his collection of popular spirituals. Claimant and issuing-body headings now stand level with author headings.

The field stays books, pamphlets, serials, and contributions to periodicals. Each entry reports both the original registration and the renewal, so the twenty-eight-year gap can be checked line by line. Song collections filed as books, school texts, and fiction all renew side by side. The half year captures American print of 1926 reaching its renewal deadline in 1954.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1955-july-decembe:
Eleanor Hallowell Abbott opens the July-to-December 1955 list with But Once a Year. The work was copyrighted on September 21, 1928, and the entry begins her renewal record under her own heading. Fiction by a popular magazine novelist thus leads a half year of legal and technical renewals.

The catalog's form is settled by now: books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical pieces, alphabetically under author, issuing body, or title. Cross-references cover claimants, joint authors, editors, and name variants. Both registrations appear in each entry. A reader checking a story's status can move from this list to the claimant's name without leaving the alphabet.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1956-july-decembe:
Charles G. Abbot's The Sun, in a revised edition, leads the July-to-December 1956 list. The Smithsonian solar physicist copyrighted the revision on January 11, 1929 and renewed it himself, the author code marking the entry. A standard astronomy text thus opens the half year.

The catalog arranges its books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions by author or issuing body, with serials by title. Claimant references stand interfiled in the alphabet rather than gathered apart. Each entry reports the original registration beside the renewal. Science titles from 1929, like Abbot's sun book, show how textbooks lived long enough to need a second term.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1957-july-decembe:
Abbott entries resume at the top of the July-to-December 1957 list, continuing the run of legal and literary renewals. The catalog's plan matches the year's first half: one alphabet under author or issuing body, with serials filed by title. Claimant and variant-name references are interfiled throughout.

Each entry joins the original registration to its renewal, so a work's first and second terms can be read as one record. The second half of a renewal year often holds the year's biggest publishers' lists, filed in bulk. This issue closes the 1957 pair, covering renewals registered in the last six months for works reaching twenty-eight years since 1929.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1958-july-decembe:
An Abbot heading, cut off in mid-name at the page top, opens the July-to-December 1958 catalog. The issue repeats the year's established plan: books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions in one alphabet. Authors and issuing bodies supply the headings, serials file by title, and claimant references are interfiled.

Original and renewal registrations are printed together in every entry, the pattern holding steady across the decade. Works first copyrighted in 1930 make up most of this half year's business. For a modern searcher, these lists answer a narrow, vital question: did anyone claim the second term, and if so, who claimed it and when.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1959-july-decembe:
The second half of 1959 opens under an Abbot heading and closes the decade's run of catalogs. Its plan matches the spring issue: one alphabet, author or issuing body headings, serials under title. Renewal claimants, joint authors, and editors all earn interfiled references.

Entries pair each original registration with its renewal, numbers and dates together. Works of 1931 fill most of the list, their first terms ending as the renewal window opened. A publisher's backlist, a novelist's early books, and a church's pamphlets could all turn on entries in this half year. The catalog's dry columns decided what stayed owned into the 1960s.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1960-july-decembe:
An Abbott heading opens the July-to-December 1960 list, the second true catalog for the year. The issue follows the same plan as its spring partner: one alphabet for books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Author and issuing-body headings dominate, with serials under their titles.

Every entry joins the original registration to the renewal, so dates can be checked across the twenty-eight-year span. Claimant references stand interfiled, helping a searcher who knows the renewing publisher but not the author. Works of 1932 close out their first terms here. Together the two 1960 halves record a full year of second-term claims.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1961-july-decembe:
Abbott again heads the alphabet in the July-to-December 1961 issue. The catalog covers books, pamphlets, serials, and contributions to periodicals for which renewals were registered in the half year. Its arrangement and entry form match the spring volume exactly.

Both the original and the renewal registration are reported in each entry, with claimant references interfiled. Works of 1933 predominate, since renewal fell due twenty-eight years after first registration. A novelist's early novel and a law digest could share a page here, equal in the eyes of the register. The list served lawyers and librarians who needed certainty about a title's status.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1962-july-decembe:
ABC Music Corporation heads the July-to-December 1962 alphabet, a reminder that printed music and song folios renewed as books. The catalog's field remains print: books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Headings run under author or issuing body, with serials filed by title.
