Every entry reports the original registration beside the renewal, and claimant references are interfiled. Most works here were first registered in 1934. A searcher tracing a song folio or a novel from that year would find its fate here. Either a named claimant renewed it, or it passed into the public domain by absence.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1963-july-decembe:
A see-reference to the Ancient and Mystical Order stands first in the July-to-December 1963 list, under the initials A.M.O.R.C. The catalog then proceeds through its single alphabet of authors and issuing bodies. Serials and certain other works file by title.

Renewals registered in the half year cover books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Every entry joins the original registration to the renewal, with claimant and variant-name references interfiled. Works of 1935 supply most of the list. The second half of a year often gathered corporate renewals in bulk, as firms cleared their backlists before the window closed at year's end.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1964-july-decembe:
The July-to-December 1964 list opens with a cross-reference under the initials A. M. O. R. C., pointing into the alphabet. Behind it stands the usual half year of renewed print: books, pamphlets, serials, and contributions to periodicals. Arrangement and entry form match the spring issue.

Original and renewal registrations appear together in every entry, so a work's two terms read as one record. Claimants, joint authors, editors, and variant names all receive interfiled references. Works of 1936 dominate the list. The catalog closes 1964 having recorded which of that year's books their owners thought worth a second twenty-eight years.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1965-july-decembe:
Another see-reference under A.M.O.R.C. leads the July-to-December 1965 catalog. The Rosicrucian order's steady renewals gave its initials a near-permanent place at the alphabet's head. Around the reference, the half year's books, pamphlets, and serials file under their authors and issuing bodies.

The entry form holds: original registration and renewal printed together, references interfiled. Most works here date from 1937. A modern researcher checking a Depression-era novel's status would read this list closely. A renewal claimed in late 1965 kept a book protected for decades more. Silence in these columns meant the opposite.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1966-july-decembe:
For the second straight half year, Michael Aaron's entries lead the alphabet, in the July-to-December 1966 catalog. A prolific author's renewals could anchor both halves of a year when his works were registered across many months. The plan around him is unchanged: one alphabet, issuing bodies beside authors.

Books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions renewed in the half year fill the issue. Original and renewal data stand together in each entry. Works of 1938 predominate. A claimant reading these pages in 1966 could confirm a rival's renewal or spot a lapsed title, which is exactly the legal certainty the register was printed to provide.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1967-july-decembe:
Michael Aaron leads a third catalog in the July-to-December 1967 issue, his renewals again filed first in the alphabet. The list covers the half year's renewed books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions. Authors and issuing bodies head the entries, serials go under title, and references are interfiled.

Each entry prints the original registration beside the renewal, numbers and dates paired. Works first copyrighted in 1939 supply most entries. For works of that year, this issue and its spring partner are the authoritative printed record of second-term claims, consulted by publishers weighing reprints and by scholars dating a text's protected life.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1968-july-decembe:
A pseudonym heading, Abbey, opens the July-to-December 1968 list. Pen names file in the same alphabet as legal names throughout these catalogs, with references tying them to their owners. The issue covers the half year's renewed books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions.

Entries give the original registration and the renewal together, dates and numbers on both sides. Works of 1940 supply most of the list. By 1968 the renewal trade was well organized, and big publishers' entries arrive in long runs. A title absent here had, in most cases, entered the public domain when its first term ended that year.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1969-july-decembe:
Edith Abbott, the social work scholar, heads the July-to-December 1969 alphabet with a sociology title. Her presence is a reminder that university-press scholarship renewed beside trade fiction in these lists. The catalog covers the half year's books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions in the usual single alphabet.

Original and renewal registrations are printed together in each entry. Works of 1941 dominate the list. Claimant references are interfiled, so a search under a publisher's name lands at the author's heading. The year's two halves together record the fate of 1941's print: which works their owners carried into a second term.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1970-july-decembe:
A law-reports heading, the A.L.R. Blue Book line, opens the July-to-December 1970 catalog. Legal reference publishing renewed its indexes and digests with special care, since their value compounded across decades. The list otherwise follows the established plan of one alphabet for all renewed print.

Books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions fill the issue, each entry pairing original and renewal registrations. Works of 1942 predominate. Claimants appear as interfiled references, so the renewing firm can be found even when the author is obscure. This half year closes the register's account of 1942's copyrights reaching their renewal deadline.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1971-july-decembe:
A cumulative index heading for the A.L.R. law reports opens the July-to-December 1971 catalog. Such indexes renewed in many years of this series, their entries marking the legal trade's housekeeping. The list covers the half year's books, pamphlets, serials, and periodical contributions in one alphabet.

Original and renewal registrations stand paired in every entry, with claimant references interfiled. Works of 1943 predominate. For a publisher planning a reprint in 1971, this register was the first check. A renewal entry meant negotiation with the claimant. No entry usually meant the work could be used freely.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1972-july-decembe:
For a third consecutive half year, an A.L.R. cumulative index heading opens the catalog, this time for July-to-December 1972. The recurrence shows how legal reference sets renewed piece by piece, volume and index alike. Around the heading, the half year's books, pamphlets, and serials file as usual.

Every entry joins original and renewal registrations, with interfiled references. Works of 1944 dominate. A researcher tracing one title can also read the neighborhood. The same firms recur, and the same kinds of books renew. A publisher's care for its backlist becomes visible across the alphabet's first pages.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1973-july-decembe:
Order changes with the July-to-December 1973 catalog. The headnote announces arrangement by registration number, warning that numbers run continuously across all classes, so gaps appear for any one kind of material. Entries no longer file by author at all.

The first entry, R554644, renews War Injuries of the Extremities by Paul W. Roder, copyrighted on July 20, 1945, with a pharmaceutical house as claimant. Medical and technical titles suit the number-first system, which favors office lookup over browsing. Each entry still pairs original and renewal data. Works of 1945 dominate this first number-ordered half year.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1974-july-decembe:
Faith Baldwin's Sleeping Beauty, in its third installment, supplies an early entry in the July-to-December 1974 catalog. Renewal R571960 covers the serial piece under her full name, Faith Baldwin Cuthrell. Serial fiction renewed installment by installment in these lists.

The catalog arranges entries by registration number, so authors scatter through the sequence. Original and renewal data still appear together in every entry. Works of 1946 predominate. A searcher now needs the renewal number, or patience: the alphabet that served for two decades is gone. The change favors the Copyright Office's own filing over the browsing habits of outside readers.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1975-july-decembe:
Bracketed markers for non-renewal entries pepper the July-to-December 1975 list, twelve at a time in places. Between them, the Books and Pamphlets renewals run by number. An early entry renews the Jessup-Redfield law and practice in New York surrogates' courts, in two volumes.

Edwin M. Bohm's revision was copyrighted on April 28, 1947, and Baker, Voorhis and Company renewed it as proprietor. Works of 1947 supply the list. Law, medicine, and fiction renew side by side under the number system. The markers remind readers that the full register held other classes between these book entries, classes this section omits.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1976-july-decembe:
Christine Louise Richards renewed her Exhibition of Original Paintings herself in the July-to-December 1976 list. The work was copyrighted on August 27, 1948, and her renewal, R636003, dates to July 1, 1976. An author's own renewal, marked with the author code, sits beside corporate claims.

Smith's Bible Dictionary follows in the sequence, renewed for its additions and revisions. The Books and Pamphlets section runs by number, with bracketed markers for skipped entries. Works of 1948 dominate. Individual artists and great publishing houses meet in these columns on equal terms, each entry a small legal act preserving a work.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1977-july-decembe:
Law, Totalitarianism and Democracy supplies an early entry in the final catalog, July-to-December 1977. The casebook, by Sidney Post Simpson, Julius Stone, and M. Magdalena Schoch, was copyrighted on March 24, 1949. West Publishing renewed it as proprietor in April 1976.

Cradle Rhymes by Gladys M. Horn and Rachel Taft Dixon follows in the number sequence. The Books and Pamphlets list runs to the series' end with bracketed markers for skipped entries. Works of 1949 close the twenty-eight-year renewal story that began with 1922's books in 1950. The whole run maps a half-century of American print staying, or failing to stay, in copyright.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Background opens the holder-of-data part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Crime law grew up guarding things a thief could carry off. Facts and figures do not work that way. Their worth rose sharply as work moved from factories to screens.

The piece draws a line between data and the meaning drawn from it. Copying a file steals the pattern, not the thought, which may live on elsewhere. So old theft rules fit badly. Facts can also flow freely in a way goods cannot. Guarding a holder's stake must sit beside the stake of the people the facts describe. That clash leads straight to the privacy part that follows.
un-un-res-james-warburg-before-the-subco:
James Warburg, a banker and former adviser to President Roosevelt, testified in 1950 before a Senate subcommittee reviewing the United Nations Charter. The panel was asking whether the young UN needed stronger powers. Warburg gave the boldest answer it heard, and his words still startle readers today.

He argued that world peace needs world law backed by a world federation. He told the senators that mankind would have world government one way or another, by consent or by conquest. The testimony captures a brief postwar moment when such ideas were debated in earnest in Washington.
up-the-hill-and-over:
Isabel Ecclestone Mackay, author of The House of Windows, wrote the novel Up the Hill and Over and dedicated it to her mother. Chapter one opens with a dusty traveller singing a comic song about the fifteen miles between Wimbleton and Wombleton. The heat and the road get the better of him, and he collapses on a green slope above a cool swimming pool.

Below him on the grass lies a small boy with a packet of schoolbooks. The traveller calls down and asks how far it is to Wimbleton, but the boy seems deaf and gives no answer. Mackay starts her story as a roadside meeting between a tired grown man and a silent child. The verse on the title page, about the scent of clover and another dawn, sets the book's hopeful tone.
vondel-vondel-s-lucifer:
Joost van den Vondel staged Lucifer in 1654, and English readers meet the Dutch tragedy here in translation. The proud archangel chafes at man's new place in God's great plan. Envy turns to open revolt, and heaven itself splits into armed camps.

Vondel writes the fall of the angels in grand, ringing verse. Pride, envy, and wounded honor drive Lucifer step by step to ruin. Some say Milton knew the play before writing Paradise Lost. Whether or not he borrowed from it, Lucifer stands as the finest drama of the Dutch Golden Age and its author's crown.
wagner:
John F. Runciman wrote this short life of Wagner for Bell's Miniature Series of Musicians. G. Bell and Sons issued the second edition at London in 1913. His contents divide the life by places. Youth runs from 1813 to 1834. Magdeburg, Riga, and Paris follow, then Dresden, then Zurich and Paris again. Munich and Triebschen come next, and Bayreuth ends the list. A section on the works closes the book.

Runciman opens by asking readers to feel how remote Wagner's world is. At his birth in 1813, Bach had been dead some sixty years, and Mozart about twenty. Haydn had been dead about ten. Beethoven stood at the full splendour of his powers. Weber and Schubert still had their finest work to do. Art's history, he warns, cannot be measured in years: some ages creep and others leap. The little book traces the leap that one man made in opera.
wanted-a-match-maker:
Paul Leicester Ford wrote Wanted: A Match-Maker, a light novel of love and scheming. He dedicated it to Bond and Edith Thomas, as a record of friendship. Its picture list shows the heroine Constance Durant springing out to lift a fallen head. She takes a seat at a bedside, and sits on the floor with a companion. A doctor comes to call, with an apology for intruding.

The story opens in talk. Mrs. Durant tells her friend Josie that she would never wish Constance to marry without love. Then she lets a long pause say more. With some petulance, she complains that the modern girl is so hard to impress. Mrs. Ferguson sympathizes and praises Constance's advantages. Ford sets a mother's matchmaking against a daughter's cool head, in the drawing rooms of New York. The comedy turns on who will outwit whom.
war-rhymes-by-wayfarer:
Wayfarer's War Rhymes opens with Modern Diplomacy, or How the War Started, a chain of limericks dated August 1914. Austria speaks first. She orders Serbia to its knees with an apology. Serbia threatens to call in its uncle the Czar. The Kaiser vows to teach the Serb his place. The Czar answers that his cousin will grow older and wiser. France sees her long-waited chance to win back Alsace-Lorraine after forty-four summers.

Belgium closes the round. She promises to wake from her nap and put up a scrap, when great armies pour over her fence. The verses turn the July crisis into music-hall patter, each nation rhyming its threats. Behind the jokes stands the shock of that summer. Five powers talked themselves into a world war in five-line stanzas. The rhymes show how ordinary readers, far from the chancelleries, made sense of the outbreak through satire.
we-of-the-never-never: Jeanie Gunn, billed as Mrs. Aeneas Gunn, wrote We of the Never-Never. She dedicated it to the bush folk of the Never-Never, Australia's Northern Territory. Pages present here hold a title line, that dedication, and a bare contents list, so her narrative itself is not shown. The list names a prelude, then nineteen numbered chapters with no titles given. Readers learn only the frame of a famous bush memoir. Its teller was the first white woman to live in that remote country.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
R. F. Weymouth's third edition of 1913 gives First Peter, book 60 in his modern speech New Testament. Peter writes to God's people scattered as strangers across Pontus, Galatia, and other Roman lands. He greets them as chosen and set apart by God's Spirit. Grace and peace open the letter.

The next verses praise God for new birth and a living hope through Christ's rising. That hope points to a stored reward that cannot spoil or fade. Trials, Peter says, test faith the way fire tests gold. Weymouth keeps the lines smooth and clear. Readers meet a letter of comfort for people under strain.

Second Peter stands as book 61 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech set, third edition, 1913. Simon Peter writes to those who share the same faith as the apostles. He says God's power has given all that life and goodness need. Great promises let believers share in God's own nature.

Peter then builds a chain of traits to add to faith. Good character comes first, then knowledge, self-control, and patience. Godliness, brotherly love, and full love close the list. A man who lacks these, he warns, has gone blind to his past cleansing. Weymouth renders the call in firm, plain speech that readers can follow with ease.
what-answer:
Anna E. Dickinson published the novel What Answer? in 1868. The story opens on a bright Fifth Avenue crowd in New York. Rich dress, fine carriages, and proud faces fill the street. A young man at a window draws greetings and admiring talk from the passers by.

He is praised as handsome, rich, and a fine match. One voice adds a odd note, wishing he had been born poor. Yet the rich scene is cut by sight of the poor in thin clothes and by a funeral passing through. Dickinson sets wealth and want side by side at the start. Love and race and war stand behind the question of her title.
what-social-classes-owe-to-each-other: The pages present here stop at the title page and an early contents list, so William Graham Sumner's argument does not appear. Sumner first published What Social Classes Owe to Each Other in 1883. The listed chapters state bold claims as titles. One says poverty can be the best policy. One says a free man is a sovereign who cannot take tips. One denies that wealth is wicked, even wealth past a neighbor's. The titles sketch Sumner's stern creed of self-help.
whig-against-tory-or-the-military-advent:
Whig Against Tory, a tale of the Revolution for children, came out in 1851. The book is framed as talks in a family: three boys, William, Henry, and John, beg their father for a war story. The father, called General P., asks if he ever told them about Enoch Crosby. None of the boys knows the name.

Crosby, their father says, was no general but a spy for the American side. He corrects the word to informer, since such men won key facts about the enemy and the Tories. The boys learn what the word Tory means as the tale starts. Talk, questions, and a spy's deeds teach the war to young readers.
winchester: The pages here hold the title page and a series advertisement for Winchester, a Beautiful England volume, with no guide text present. Sidney Heath described the city and E. W. Haslehust pictured it. Blackie and Son printed the book in 1911 in London, Glasgow, and Bombay. The advertisement lists sister volumes ready in the series. Oxford, Canterbury, the English Lakes, and the Thames appear among them. Windsor Castle and Cambridge also have volumes. The list sketches a set of short, pictured guides to famed English places.
wisdom-s-daughter: Only the dedication and a partial contents list are present here for H. Rider Haggard's Wisdom's Daughter, first published in 1923, so the romance itself does not appear. Haggard calls it the life and love story of She-Who-Must-Be-Obeyed. He gave it to the memory of Andrew Lang, to whom She and Ayesha had been dedicated. The contents open in the halls of heaven. Noot the prophet, a battle and flight, and the kiss of fate follow. A sea battle and the shame of Pharaoh appear later.
with-buller-in-natal-or-a-born-leader:
G. A. Henty's With Buller in Natal, or A Born Leader, opens with a preface on the trouble of writing war tales near the event. Full and fair history must wait, he says, since men in different parts of a field see different fights. Thin official despatches leave gaps no writer can yet fill. Henty tried to blend the rival accounts of Natal fighting into a clear line.

His story centers on a little band of lads from Johannesburg. The war is the background, and Buller's men are not the stars. The contents open with the bursting of the storm and a terrible journey. This record shares its preface with a twin record of the same book. Youth, loyalty, and battle fill the tale.
within-the-law-from-the-play-of-bayard-v:
Marvin Dana turned Bayard Veiller's stage play into this novel. Chapter one opens on a girl staring at a panel of light in a wall. Her brain feels numb, and she clings to that numbness. Feeling nothing gives her a short rest from horror. The chapter list then promises kleptomania, marked money, a spurned bridegroom, and a shooting.

Crime and law shape every turn promised by the contents. Chapter titles move from prison-like despair toward traps, confessions, and a final mix of anguish and bliss. Readers get a melodrama about a woman trapped by charges, police plots, and her own choices.
within-you-is-the-power:
Henry Thomas Hamblin wrote this short book on inner spiritual power. His preface says a hidden power lets people rise to better things. He calls the deeper part of a person the greater Self. It stands above the everyday self, much as a mountain stands above a plain. The book aims to help readers use mind and spirit wisely.

Chapters cover fate, success, health, habit, and happiness. Hamblin does not promise an escape from trouble. Each life must meet sorrow, he says. Yet a person who knows unity with universal life can stand firm. Character building sits at the centre.
woodroffe-world-as-power:
Woodroffe set out his Tantric view of the world in 1921. The World as Power argues that all things are Shakti at play. Matter and mind alike take form as the divine energy moves.

The Calcutta judge builds a bridge between Western thought and Tantra. He reads physics, life, and soul through one lens of power. Nothing is dead stuff in his scheme, and nothing stands apart. His synthesis is bold, learned, and warm toward its Indian sources. Readers watch a whole cosmos rethought from a Tantric base of power. The book's calm nerve in making huge claims still impresses today.
woodstock-or-the-cavalier:
Sir Walter Scott set this novel in the year 1651, after the English Civil War. His 1832 introduction recalls strange events at Woodstock in 1649. Scott had read of them long before, then lost the source. He later found an account in Hone's Every-day Book. A tale of the year sixteen hundred and fifty-one follows the introduction.

Scott had already used the war in Peveril of the Peak, set far away. Woodstock let him return to richer ground near the war's heart. Party spirit, loyalty, and trickery drive the plot. Readers get romance built on real Civil War strife.
